abstract: We describe two parallel analog VLSI architectures that integrate optical flow data obtained from arrays of elementary velocity sen(cid:173) sors to estimate heading direction and time-to-contact. For heading direction computation, we performed simulations to evaluate the most important qualitative properties of the optical flow field and determine the best functional operators for the implementation of the architecture. For time-to-contact we exploited the divergence theorem to integrate data from all velocity sensors present in the architecture and average out possible errors.

paragraphs: This paper describes two parallel analog chip architectures that combine measurements of visual motion. Their inputs come from arrays of elementary velocity sensors, which together provide optical flow data. The architectures use that distributed information to estimate heading direction and time-to-contact, two quantities relevant to movement through an environment.

For heading direction, the authors use simulations to study the most important qualitative properties of the optical flow field. Those simulations help them select the functional operators used in the architecture. The design process therefore connects the structure of the visual motion signal to the computations implemented by the hardware.

For time-to-contact, the architecture uses the divergence theorem to combine information from all of its velocity sensors. Pooling those measurements is intended to average out possible errors. The two designs illustrate complementary uses of distributed sensing: selecting operations suited to the overall flow pattern and integrating many local measurements into a shared estimate. Parallel analog circuitry provides the common implementation framework.
summary.tldr: Two parallel analog architectures integrate optical flow measurements to estimate heading direction and time-to-contact.

title: Parallel analog VLSI architectures for computation of heading direction and time-to-contact

abstract: Neuromodulation can change not only the mean firing rate of a neuron, but also its pattern of firing . Therefore, a reliable neu(cid:173) ral coding scheme, whether a rate coding or a spike time based coding, must be robust in a dynamic neuromodulatory environ(cid:173) ment. The common observation that cholinergic modulation leads to a reduction in spike frequency adaptation implies a modifica(cid:173) tion of spike timing, which would make a neural code based on precise spike timing difficult to maintain. In this paper, the effects of cholinergic modulation were studied to test the hypothesis that precise spike timing can serve as a reliable neural code. Using the whole cell patch-clamp technique in rat neocortical slice prepara(cid:173) tion and compartmental modeling techniques, we show that cholin(cid:173) ergic modulation, surprisingly, preserved spike timing in response to a fluctuating inputs that resembles in vivo conditions. This re(cid:173) sult suggests that in vivo spike timing may be much more resistant to changes in neuromodulator concentrations than previous physi(cid:173) ological studies have implied. 112 A. C. Tang, A. M. Bartels and T. J. Sejnowski

paragraphs: A neural code based on precise spike timing must remain reliable as neuromodulators change neuronal behavior. Cholinergic modulation creates a particular concern because it reduces spike-frequency adaptation, the tendency for firing to slow during continued stimulation. That change appears capable of shifting spike times and disrupting information carried by their timing.

The authors test this concern using whole-cell patch-clamp recordings from rat neocortical slices together with compartmental modeling. They examine responses to fluctuating inputs that resemble conditions in a living brain. The character of the input is central: the study asks whether timing survives modulation when the neuron receives physiologically realistic fluctuations.

Under those conditions, cholinergic modulation preserved spike timing. This finding supports the possibility that precise timing can remain a reliable component of neural coding despite changes in modulation. The authors interpret it as evidence that spike timing in vivo may be more resistant to neuromodulator changes than earlier physiological work suggested. The direct observation comes from the slice and modeling conditions, while the implication concerns robustness in the living brain.
summary.tldr: Recordings and modeling show preserved spike timing under cholinergic modulation when neurons receive fluctuations resembling in vivo input.

title: Cholinergic Modulation Preserves Spike Timing Under Physiologically Realistic Fluctuating Input

abstract: Epidemiological data is traditionally analyzed with very simple techniques. Flexible models, such as neural networks, have the potential to discover unanticipated features in the data. However, to be useful, flexible models must have effective control on overfit(cid:173) ting. This paper reports on a comparative study of the predictive quality of neural networks and other flexible models applied to real and artificial epidemiological data. The results suggest that there are no major unanticipated complex features in the real data, and also demonstrate that MacKay's [1995] Bayesian neural network methodology provides effective control on overfitting while retain(cid:173) ing the ability to discover complex features in the artificial data.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether flexible predictive models reveal relationships in epidemiological data that simpler statistical methods might overlook. Its subject is the relationship between tobacco, alcohol, and cancer. Flexibility creates an opportunity to detect unexpected patterns, but it also makes it easier to fit accidental features of the available observations.

The study compares the predictive quality of neural networks and other flexible models on both real and artificial epidemiological data. Those two settings serve complementary purposes: the real data address the substantive application, while the artificial data test whether a method can discover complex structure when such structure is present. Effective control of overfitting is central to the comparison.

The results suggest that the real data contain no major unexpected complex features. At the same time, the Bayesian neural network methodology controls overfitting while retaining the ability to uncover complex patterns in artificial data. Together, these findings support using flexible models with regularization to investigate complexity without assuming that more elaborate relationships must exist.
summary.tldr: Bayesian neural networks control overfitting while detecting artificial complexity, but reveal no major unexpected complexity in the real epidemiological data.

title: A Comparison between Neural Networks and other Statistical Techniques for Modeling the Relationship between Tobacco and Alcohol and Cancer

paragraphs: Storage capacity describes how much a neural architecture can store in its weights. This paper studies that capacity for a fully connected committee machine as the number of hidden nodes, K, becomes large. The question concerns the architecture's capacity scaling, rather than the performance of a particular training procedure.

The authors analyze the geometry of weight space in relation to the network's internal representations. They then examine the large-K behavior of quantities called order parameters, which summarize aspects of that structure. This route connects capacity to the organization of possible weight configurations and their internal representations.

The resulting leading-order capacity grows in proportion to K times the square root of log K. The result satisfies an existing mathematical bound. By contrast, the replica-symmetric solution from the conventional Gardner approach violates that bound. This comparison gives the geometric analysis a concrete consistency check: its asymptotic prediction respects a constraint that the alternative calculation fails to meet. The stated scaling applies in the large-hidden-layer limit.
summary.tldr: A geometric analysis finds large-K committee-machine capacity proportional to K√log K, consistent with an existing mathematical bound.

title: The Storage Capacity of a Fully-Connected Committee Machine

abstract: We derive the correspondence between regularization operators used in Regularization Networks and Hilbert Schmidt Kernels appearing in Sup(cid:173) port Vector Machines. More specifica1ly, we prove that the Green's Func(cid:173) tions associated with regularization operators are suitable Support Vector Kernels with equivalent regularization properties. As a by-product we show that a large number of Radial Basis Functions namely condition(cid:173) ally positive definite functions may be used as Support Vector kernels.

More specifica1ly, we prove that the Green's Func(cid:173) tions associated with regularization operators are suitable Support Vector Kernels with equivalent regularization properties. As a by-product we show that a large number of Radial Basis Functions namely condition(cid:173) ally positive definite functions may be used as Support Vector kernels.

paragraphs: This paper establishes a mathematical connection between regularization networks and support vector machines. It relates the operators used to specify regularization in one framework to the kernels used in the other. The connection explains how these apparently different mathematical choices can encode equivalent regularization properties.

The central result concerns Green's functions associated with regularization operators. The authors prove that these functions can serve as suitable support vector kernels. This makes the relationship constructive: a regularization operator supplies a route to a corresponding kernel, with a stated equivalence in the regularization it imposes.

A further result expands the available kernel choices to a large family of radial basis functions, specifically conditionally positive definite functions. The significance is theoretical rather than an application benchmark: the paper gives a principled link between choosing regularization and choosing a kernel. That link helps interpret kernels through their regularization properties and identifies additional functions that can be used in support vector methods.
summary.tldr: The paper proves that Green's functions of regularization operators yield support vector kernels with equivalent regularization properties.

title: From Regularization Operators to Support Vector Kernels

abstract: We describe a Bayesian approach to model selection in unsupervised learning that determines both the feature set and the number of clusters. We then evaluate this scheme (based on marginal likelihood) and one based on cross-validated likelihood. For the Bayesian scheme we derive a closed-form solution of the marginal likelihood by assuming appropriate forms of the likelihood function and prior. Extensive experiments compare these approaches and all results are verified by comparison against ground truth. In these experiments the Bayesian scheme using our objective function gave better results than cross-validation.
originalAbstract: We describe a Bayesian approach to model selection in unsupervised learning that determines both the feature set and the number of clusters. We then evaluate this scheme (based on marginal likelihood) and one based on cross-validated likelihood. For the Bayesian scheme we derive a closed-form solution of the marginal likelihood by assuming appropriate forms of the likelihood function and prior. Extensive experiments compare these approaches and all results are verified by comparison against ground truth. In these experiments the Bayesian scheme using our objective function gave better results than cross-validation.

paragraphs: Unsupervised model selection can involve deciding both which features matter and how many clusters the data contain. This paper presents a Bayesian approach that determines these two elements together. Treating them jointly makes the representation of the data part of model selection, alongside the choice of clustering structure.

The Bayesian scheme uses marginal likelihood as its objective. The authors derive a closed-form expression by assuming suitable forms for the likelihood and prior. This analytical result is conditional on those modeling choices. They compare the scheme with an alternative based on cross-validated likelihood, giving two different ways to evaluate candidate unsupervised models.

Extensive experiments compare the approaches, and the results are checked against ground truth. In those experiments, the Bayesian scheme using the proposed objective performs better than cross-validation. The finding supports that particular scheme in the tested settings; it does not establish that every Bayesian selection method will outperform cross-validation. The main contribution is a tractable joint selection approach backed by direct empirical comparisons.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian objective jointly selects features and cluster count, outperforming cross-validated likelihood in the reported experiments.

title: Generalized Model Selection for Unsupervised Learning in High Dimensions

abstract: Multiagent learning is a key problem in AI. In the presence of multi- ple Nash equilibria, even agents with non-conﬂicting interests may not be able to learn an optimal coordination policy. The problem is exac- cerbated if the agents do not know the game and independently receive noisy payoffs. So, multiagent reinforfcement learning involves two inter- related problems: identifying the game and learning to play. In this paper, we present optimal adaptive learning, the ﬁrst algorithm that converges to an optimal Nash equilibrium with probability 1 in any team Markov game. We provide a convergence proof, and show that the algorithm’s parameters are easy to set to meet the convergence conditions.
originalAbstract: Multiagent learning is a key problem in AI. In the presence of multi- ple Nash equilibria, even agents with non-conﬂicting interests may not be able to learn an optimal coordination policy. The problem is exac- cerbated if the agents do not know the game and independently receive noisy payoffs. So, multiagent reinforfcement learning involves two inter- related problems: identifying the game and learning to play. In this paper, we present optimal adaptive learning, the ﬁrst algorithm that converges to an optimal Nash equilibrium with probability 1 in any team Markov game. We provide a convergence proof, and show that the algorithm’s parameters are easy to set to meet the convergence conditions.

paragraphs: Agents with aligned interests can still struggle to coordinate when a game has several Nash equilibria. Reaching an equilibrium does not by itself mean selecting an optimal coordinated policy. The challenge becomes greater when agents initially do not know the game and each receives noisy payoff observations, making both learning the environment and learning how to act necessary.

The paper introduces optimal adaptive learning to address these connected problems in team Markov games. Its central result is convergence to an optimal Nash equilibrium with probability one in any game within that class, under the convergence conditions. This is a claim about eventual learning behavior, with optimality of the equilibrium included in the guarantee.

The authors supply a convergence proof and state that the algorithm's parameters are easy to set to satisfy the required conditions. The contribution therefore combines an algorithm with a theoretical account of successful coordination. It shows how the uncertainty involved in identifying the game can be handled alongside the task of learning to play an optimal equilibrium.
summary.tldr: Optimal adaptive learning provably converges with probability one to an optimal Nash equilibrium in any team Markov game under its convergence conditions.

title: Reinforcement Learning to Play an Optimal Nash Equilibrium in Team Markov Games

abstract: Given a probability measure P and a reference measure µ, one is often interested in the minimum µ-measure set with P -measure at least α. Minimum volume sets of this type summarize the regions of greatest probability mass of P , and are useful for detecting anoma- lies and constructing conﬁdence regions. This paper addresses the problem of estimating minimum volume sets based on independent samples distributed according to P . Other than these samples, no other information is available regarding P , but the reference mea- sure µ is assumed to be known. We introduce rules for estimating minimum volume sets that parallel the empirical risk minimization and structural risk minimization principles in classiﬁcation. As in classiﬁcation, we show that the performances of our estimators are controlled by the rate of uniform convergence of empirical to true probabilities over the class from which the estimator is drawn. Thus we obtain ﬁnite sample size performance bounds in terms of VC dimension and related quantities. We also demonstrate strong universal consistency and an oracle inequality. Estimators based on histograms and dyadic partitions illustrate the proposed rules.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to find the smallest region containing at least a specified amount of probability. Size is measured using a known reference measure, while probability comes from an unknown distribution. Such regions summarize concentrated probability mass and can support anomaly detection or the construction of confidence regions.

The available information consists of independent samples from the unknown distribution. The authors introduce estimation rules analogous to empirical risk minimization and structural risk minimization in classification. Their analysis connects performance to how uniformly sample-based probabilities approximate true probabilities across the candidate family of sets. This makes the complexity of that family central to the guarantees.

The paper derives finite-sample performance bounds involving VC dimension and related quantities. It also establishes strong universal consistency and an oracle inequality, providing additional theoretical guarantees for the estimators. Histogram-based estimators and dyadic partitions illustrate the rules. The contribution translates familiar learning-theory principles into a method for estimating compact probability regions from samples.
summary.tldr: The paper develops sample-based estimators of minimum-volume probability regions with finite-sample bounds and consistency guarantees.

title: Learning Minimum Volume Sets

abstract: We demonstrate that log-linear grammars with latent variables can be practically trained using discriminative methods. Central to efﬁcient discriminative training is a hierarchical pruning procedure which allows feature expectations to be efﬁ- ciently approximated in a gradient-based procedure. We compare L1 and L2 reg- ularization and show that L1 regularization is superior, requiring fewer iterations to converge, and yielding sparser solutions. On full-scale treebank parsing exper- iments, the discriminative latent models outperform both the comparable genera- tive latent models as well as the discriminative non-latent baselines.
originalAbstract: We demonstrate that log-linear grammars with latent variables can be practically trained using discriminative methods. Central to efﬁcient discriminative training is a hierarchical pruning procedure which allows feature expectations to be efﬁ- ciently approximated in a gradient-based procedure. We compare L1 and L2 reg- ularization and show that L1 regularization is superior, requiring fewer iterations to converge, and yielding sparser solutions. On full-scale treebank parsing exper- iments, the discriminative latent models outperform both the comparable genera- tive latent models as well as the discriminative non-latent baselines.

paragraphs: This paper shows that log-linear grammars containing latent variables can be trained practically with discriminative methods. Latent variables provide hidden distinctions within the grammar, while discriminative training focuses on choosing the desired analysis of an observed sentence. Combining them creates a computational challenge because training must account for those hidden alternatives.

The key technique is hierarchical pruning. It makes the feature expectations needed by gradient-based training efficient to approximate, allowing the training procedure to handle the latent grammar. The authors also compare L1 and L2 regularization. In their comparison, L1 needs fewer iterations to converge and produces sparser solutions, with fewer retained nonzero parameters.

On full-scale treebank parsing experiments, the discriminatively trained latent models outperform comparable generative latent models and discriminative models without latent variables. These comparisons support the value of combining hidden grammatical structure with discriminative learning. The practical contribution is the pruning procedure that makes this combination trainable, alongside evidence favoring L1 regularization in the studied setting.
summary.tldr: Hierarchical pruning makes discriminative latent-variable grammar training practical and improves parsing over the reported generative and non-latent comparisons.

title: Discriminative Log-Linear Grammars with Latent Variables

abstract: For infants, early word learning is a chicken-and-egg problem. One way to learn a word is to observe that it co-occurs with a particular referent across different situations. Another way is to use the social context of an utterance to infer the intended referent of a word. Here we present a Bayesian model of cross-situational word learning, and an extension of this model that also learns which social cues are relevant to determining reference. We test our model on a small corpus of mother-infant interaction and find it performs better than competing models. Finally, we show that our model accounts for experimental phenomena including mutual exclusivity, fast-mapping, and generalization from social cues.

Another way is to use the social context of an utterance to infer the intended referent of a word. Here we present a Bayesian model of cross-situational word learning, and an extension of this model that also learns which social cues are relevant to determining reference. We test our model on a small corpus of mother-infant interaction and find it performs better than competing models. Finally, we show that our model accounts for experimental phenomena including mutual exclusivity, fast-mapping, and generalization from social cues.

paragraphs: Early word learning involves two connected sources of evidence. A child can notice that a word repeatedly occurs alongside a particular object or referent, and can use the social circumstances of an utterance to interpret it. The difficulty is that neither word meanings nor the relevance of social cues is necessarily known in advance.

The paper develops a Bayesian model that combines evidence about words and referents across situations. An extension also learns which social cues help determine what a speaker means. This makes the relevance of social information something the model can infer through learning, alongside the word associations it is trying to establish.

On a small collection of mother-infant interactions, the model performs better than competing models. It also accounts for experimental phenomena involving mutual exclusivity, fast mapping, and generalization from social cues. These findings support the framework as an account of several aspects of word learning within one probabilistic approach; the reported comparison is specifically grounded in a small interaction corpus.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian model learns word meanings across situations and can also learn which social cues help identify intended referents.

title: A Bayesian Framework for Cross-Situational Word-Learning

abstract: This paper proposes a principled extension of the traditional single-layer flat sparse coding scheme, where a two-layer coding scheme is derived based on theoretical analysis of nonlinear functional approximation that extends recent results for local coordinate coding. The two-layer approach can be easily generalized to deeper structures in a hierarchical multiple-layer manner. Empirically, it is shown that the deep coding approach yields improved performance in benchmark datasets.
originalAbstract: This paper proposes a principled extension of the traditional single-layer flat sparse coding scheme, where a two-layer coding scheme is derived based on theoretical analysis of nonlinear functional approximation that extends recent results for local coordinate coding. The two-layer approach can be easily generalized to deeper structures in a hierarchical multiple-layer manner. Empirically, it is shown that the deep coding approach yields improved performance in benchmark datasets.

paragraphs: This paper extends a traditional sparse coding approach from a single flat layer to a two-layer representation. Its focus is how to organize coding hierarchically, so that a representation can have multiple levels. The proposed architecture begins with two layers and is designed to extend naturally to deeper structures.

The two-layer scheme is derived from a theoretical analysis of nonlinear function approximation. That analysis extends results for local coordinate coding and provides the basis for moving beyond the single-layer formulation. The role of theory here is to motivate the coding construction through its relationship to function approximation, giving the architectural extension an explicit mathematical foundation.

The authors also report improved performance on benchmark datasets using the deep coding approach. This empirical result accompanies the theoretical derivation, supporting the usefulness of the proposed representation in the evaluated settings. Together, the contributions connect a specific two-layer construction, a route to hierarchical multilayer coding, and observed improvements from using the resulting approach.
summary.tldr: A theoretically derived two-layer sparse coding scheme extends to deeper hierarchies and improves performance on benchmark datasets.

title: Deep Coding Network

abstract: Languages vary widely in many ways, including their canonical word order. A basic aspect of the observed variation is the fact that some word orders are much more common than others. Although this regularity has been recognized for some time, it has not been well-explained. In this paper we offer an information-theoretic explanation for the observed word-order distribution across languages, based on the concept of Uniform Information Density (UID). We suggest that object-first languages are particularly disfavored because they are highly non-optimal if the goal is to distribute information content approximately evenly throughout a sentence, and that the rest of the observed word-order distribution is at least partially explainable in terms of UID. We support our theoretical analysis with data from child-directed speech and experimental work.

paragraphs: Languages differ in their usual ordering of sentence elements, but the possible orders are not equally common. This paper seeks an information-theoretic explanation for that uneven distribution. It builds on Uniform Information Density, the idea that information content is distributed approximately evenly as a sentence unfolds.

The authors suggest that object-first languages are particularly disfavored because those orders distribute information poorly under this objective. The explanatory step is to evaluate word order in terms of how it spreads information through a sentence. They further argue that the frequency pattern among the remaining orders is at least partly explainable through the same principle, without claiming that it provides a complete account.

The paper supports its theoretical analysis with child-directed speech data and experimental work. These sources provide evidence for the proposed connection between information distribution and cross-language word-order patterns. The findings position uniform information density as a possible contributor to the observed preferences, especially the relative rarity of object-first orders.
summary.tldr: The paper argues that more even information distribution may partly explain word-order frequencies, especially the rarity of object-first languages.

title: Why are some word orders more common than others? A uniform information density account

abstract: Continuous Markov random fields are a general formalism to model joint probability distributions over events with continuous outcomes. We prove that marginal computation for constrained continuous MRFs is #P-hard in general and present a polynomial-time approximation scheme under mild assumptions on the structure of the random field. Moreover, we introduce a sampling algorithm to compute marginal distributions and develop novel techniques to increase its efficiency. Continuous MRFs are a general purpose probabilistic modeling tool and we demonstrate how they can be applied to statistical relational learning. On the problem of collective classification, we evaluate our algorithm and show that the standard deviation of marginals serves as a useful measure of confidence.

We prove that marginal computation for constrained continuous MRFs is #P-hard in general and present a polynomial-time approximation scheme under mild assumptions on the structure of the random field. Moreover, we introduce a sampling algorithm to compute marginal distributions and develop novel techniques to increase its efficiency. Continuous MRFs are a general purpose probabilistic modeling tool and we demonstrate how they can be applied to statistical relational learning. paragraphs: Continuous Markov random fields describe joint probability distributions over outcomes that vary continuously. To answer questions about particular outcomes, one often needs marginal distributions, which summarize selected variables while accounting for the others. This paper studies both the computational difficulty of obtaining those marginals and methods for approximating them.

The authors prove that marginal computation for constrained continuous Markov random fields is #P-hard in general. They also give a polynomial-time approximation scheme under assumptions about the field’s structure that they describe as mild. These results distinguish the difficult general problem from structured cases where approximation has a stronger computational guarantee. A sampling algorithm and additional efficiency techniques provide another part of the proposed inference toolkit.

The paper applies continuous Markov random fields to statistical relational learning and evaluates the algorithm on collective classification. In that setting, the standard deviation of marginal distributions proves useful as a confidence measure. The findings therefore concern both computing predictions and extracting useful uncertainty information from the resulting distributions.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes general marginal-inference hardness, develops approximation and sampling methods, and finds marginal spread useful for confidence in collective classification.

title: Computing Marginal Distributions over Continuous Markov Networks for Statistical Relational Learning

abstract: Many applications in computer vision measure the similarity between images or image patches based on some statistics such as oriented gradients. These are often modeled implicitly or explicitly with a Gaussian noise assumption, leading to the use of the Euclidean distance when comparing image descriptors. In this paper, we show that the statistics of gradient based image descriptors often follow a heavy-tailed distribution, which undermines any principled motivation for the use of Euclidean distances. We advocate for the use of a distance measure based on the likelihood ratio test with appropriate probabilistic models that fit the empirical data distribution. We instantiate this similarity measure with the Gamma-compound-Laplace distribution, and show significant improvement over existing distance measures in the application of SIFT feature matching, at relatively low computational cost.

These are often modeled implicitly or explicitly with a Gaussian noise assumption, leading to the use of the Euclidean distance when comparing image descriptors. In this paper, we show that the statistics of gradient based image descriptors often follow a heavy-tailed distribution, which undermines any principled motivation for the use of Euclidean distances. We advocate for the use of a distance measure based on the likelihood ratio test with appropriate probabilistic models that fit the empirical data distribution. We instantiate this similarity measure with the Gamma-compound-Laplace distribution, and show significant improvement over existing distance measures in the application of SIFT feature matching, at relatively low computational cost.

paragraphs: Image-matching systems often compare descriptors built from local gradient statistics, such as the directions of intensity changes. Euclidean distance is a common comparison rule, with a Gaussian noise model providing a familiar probabilistic justification. This paper examines that modeling choice and finds that gradient-based descriptors often have heavy-tailed statistics, making large deviations more prominent than a Gaussian model suggests.

The authors argue that the comparison rule should follow a probability model that fits the observed descriptor distribution. They construct a similarity measure from a likelihood-ratio test and instantiate it with a Gamma-compound-Laplace distribution. The essential change is to let the statistical behavior of the descriptors shape how differences between them are judged.

For SIFT feature matching, the proposed measure produces significant improvement over existing distances at relatively low computational cost. The empirical finding concerns this matching application. More broadly, the paper challenges the probabilistic rationale for routine Euclidean comparison when descriptor statistics are heavy-tailed, and demonstrates a practical alternative grounded in the measured distribution.
summary.tldr: A likelihood-based distance matched to heavy-tailed descriptor statistics improves SIFT feature matching at relatively low computational cost.

title: Heavy-tailed Distances for Gradient Based Image Descriptors

abstract: We describe how the pre-training algorithm for Deep Boltzmann Machines (DBMs) is related to the pre-training algorithm for Deep Belief Networks and we show that under certain conditions, the pre-training procedure improves the variational lower bound of a two-hidden-layer DBM. Based on this analysis, we develop a different method of pre-training DBMs that distributes the modelling work more evenly over the hidden layers. Our results on the MNIST and NORB datasets demonstrate that the new pre-training algorithm allows us to learn better generative models.
originalAbstract: We describe how the pre-training algorithm for Deep Boltzmann Machines (DBMs) is related to the pre-training algorithm for Deep Belief Networks and we show that under certain conditions, the pre-training procedure improves the variational lower bound of a two-hidden-layer DBM. Based on this analysis, we develop a different method of pre-training DBMs that distributes the modelling work more evenly over the hidden layers. Our results on the MNIST and NORB datasets demonstrate that the new pre-training algorithm allows us to learn better generative models.

paragraphs: The paper examines how to prepare a Deep Boltzmann Machine for learning through pretraining. Its central concern is how the hidden layers divide the work of modeling the data. The authors connect the pretraining procedure for these models to the corresponding procedure for Deep Belief Networks, using that relationship to understand what the initialization accomplishes.

For a Deep Boltzmann Machine with two hidden layers, they show that pretraining improves a variational lower bound under certain conditions. This bound provides a tractable way to assess the model's fit. The result gives a conditional theoretical justification for pretraining, while also motivating a different procedure that spreads the modeling work more evenly across hidden layers.

The authors evaluate the revised procedure on MNIST and NORB and report better generative models. The stated outcome concerns how well the learned models represent data distributions. Together, the analysis and experiments support changing the allocation of modeling work during pretraining as a way to improve these models.
summary.tldr: A revised pretraining method distributes modeling work more evenly across hidden layers and improves generative results on MNIST and NORB.

title: A Better Way to Pretrain Deep Boltzmann Machines

abstract: In this paper we propose a class of efficient Generalized Method-of-Moments(GMM) algorithms for computing parameters of the Plackett-Luce model, where the data consists of full rankings over alternatives. Our technique is based on breaking the full rankings into pairwise comparisons, and then computing parameters that satisfy a set of generalized moment conditions. We identify conditions for the output of GMM to be unique, and identify a general class of consistent and inconsistent breakings. We then show by theory and experiments that our algorithms run significantly faster than the classical Minorize-Maximization (MM) algorithm, while achieving competitive statistical efficiency.

Our technique is based on breaking the full rankings into pairwise comparisons, and then computing parameters that satisfy a set of generalized moment conditions. We identify conditions for the output of GMM to be unique, and identify a general class of consistent and inconsistent breakings. We then show by theory and experiments that our algorithms run significantly faster than the classical Minorize-Maximization (MM) algorithm, while achieving competitive statistical efficiency.

paragraphs: Rank aggregation seeks to learn about alternatives from the orderings people or systems assign to them. This paper studies parameter estimation for the Plackett-Luce model when each observation supplies a complete ranking. Its goal is to make that estimation computationally efficient while retaining competitive statistical performance.

The proposed algorithms break full rankings into pairwise comparisons and fit parameters through generalized moment conditions. These conditions provide equations that connect the comparisons to the model parameters. A central issue is how to perform the breaking: the authors identify a general class of choices that give consistent estimates, alongside choices that do not. They also establish conditions under which the resulting parameter estimate is unique.

Theory and experiments show substantially faster computation than the classical Minorize-Maximization algorithm, with competitive statistical efficiency. The contribution therefore includes both an efficient estimation strategy and guidance on when its simplification is statistically sound. Turning rankings into pairs is useful here, but the analysis makes clear that the choice of pairs matters to the validity of the resulting estimates.
summary.tldr: Moment-based algorithms fit Plackett-Luce ranking models faster by using carefully chosen pairwise comparisons.

title: Generalized Method-of-Moments for Rank Aggregation

abstract: Biclustering is the analog of clustering on a bipartite graph. Existent methods infer biclusters through local search strategies that find one cluster at a time; a common technique is to update the row memberships based on the current column memberships, and vice versa. We propose a biclustering algorithm that maximizes a global objective function using message passing. Our objective function closely approximates a general likelihood function, separating a cluster size penalty term into row- and column-count penalties. Because we use a global optimization framework, our approach excels at resolving the overlaps between biclusters, which are important features of biclusters in practice. Moreover, Expectation-Maximization can be used to learn the model parameters if they are unknown. In simulations, we find that our method outperforms two of the best existing biclustering algorithms, ISA and LAS, when the planted clusters overlap. Applied to three gene expression datasets, our method finds coregulated gene clusters that have high quality in terms of cluster size and density.

paragraphs: Biclustering finds related subsets on both sides of a bipartite dataset, such as groups of rows together with groups of columns. Existing methods often discover one cluster at a time by alternating row and column membership updates. This paper instead formulates biclustering around a global objective optimized using message passing.

The objective closely approximates a general likelihood, with the cluster-size penalty separated into row-count and column-count terms. Considering biclusters together helps resolve overlaps between them, a feature the authors emphasize as important in practice. When model parameters are unknown, expectation-maximization can estimate them as part of the modeling procedure.

In simulations with overlapping planted clusters, the method outperforms ISA and LAS, two strong existing biclustering algorithms. Applied to three gene-expression datasets, it finds coregulated gene clusters with high quality in size and density. These findings support the global formulation particularly for overlapping structure, where decisions about one bicluster interact with decisions about others. The empirical advantage is tied to the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: A message-passing biclustering method optimizes a global likelihood-based objective and handles overlapping clusters well in simulations and gene-expression data.

title: Biclustering Using Message Passing

abstract: Previous theoretical and experimental work on optimal decision-making was restricted to the artificial setting of a reliability of the momentary sensory evidence that remained constant within single trials. The work presented here describes the computation and characterization of optimal decision-making in the more realistic case of an evidence reliability that varies across time even within a trial. It shows that, in this case, the optimal behavior is determined by a bound in the decision maker's belief that depends only on the current, but not the past, reliability. We furthermore demonstrate that simpler heuristics fail to match the optimal performance for certain characteristics of the process that determines the time-course of this reliability, causing a drop in reward rate by more than 50%.

The work presented here describes the computation and characterization of optimal decision-making in the more realistic case of an evidence reliability that varies across time even within a trial. It shows that, in this case, the optimal behavior is determined by a bound in the decision maker's belief that depends only on the current, but not the past, reliability. We furthermore demonstrate that simpler heuristics fail to match the optimal performance for certain characteristics of the process that determines the time-course of this reliability, causing a drop in reward rate by more than 50%.

paragraphs: Sensory evidence need not remain equally reliable throughout a decision. This paper studies optimal decision-making when reliability changes even within a single trial. It moves beyond the constant-reliability setting used in the previous theoretical and experimental work described by the authors, asking how the decision rule should respond to changing evidence quality.

The authors compute and characterize optimal behavior using a boundary in the decision-maker’s belief. That boundary depends on the current reliability of the evidence, but not on its past reliability. This is a specific statement about what determines the optimal boundary; it distinguishes the present quality of incoming evidence from the history of how that quality changed.

The paper also compares optimal behavior with simpler heuristics. For certain characteristics of the process governing reliability over time, those heuristics fail to match optimal performance and reduce reward rate by more than 50%. This conditional result shows that changes in evidence quality can have substantial consequences for decision strategies, making the reliability process an important part of the optimization problem.
summary.tldr: With time-varying evidence reliability, the optimal belief boundary depends on current reliability, and simpler heuristics can suffer large reward-rate losses in certain settings.

title: Optimal decision-making with time-varying evidence reliability

abstract: In this paper, we study the problem of answering visual analogy questions. These questions take the form of image A is to image B as image C is to what. Answering these questions entails discovering the mapping from image A to image B and then extending the mapping to image C and searching for the image D such that the relation from A to B holds for C to D. We pose this problem as learning an embedding that encourages pairs of analogous images with similar transformations to be close together using convolutional neural networks with a quadruple Siamese architecture. We introduce a dataset of visual analogy questions in natural images, and show first results of its kind on solving analogy questions on natural images.

Answering these questions entails discovering the mapping from image A to image B and then extending the mapping to image C and searching for the image D such that the relation from A to B holds for C to D. We pose this problem as learning an embedding that encourages pairs of analogous images with similar transformations to be close together using convolutional neural networks with a quadruple Siamese architecture. We introduce a dataset of visual analogy questions in natural images, and show first results of its kind on solving analogy questions on natural images.

paragraphs: Visual analogy asks for an image that completes a relationship: image A relates to image B as image C relates to the missing image D. Solving it requires identifying the mapping between the first pair and finding a second pair that expresses a similar mapping. This paper formulates that task for natural images.

The authors learn an embedding using convolutional neural networks arranged in a quadruple Siamese architecture. The training objective encourages analogous image pairs with similar transformations to lie close together in the learned representation. The representation is therefore organized around relationships between images, which is the information needed to complete an analogy.

The paper also introduces a dataset of natural-image analogy questions and reports initial results on solving them. Its contribution combines a task formulation, a learning architecture, and data for evaluation. These first results establish an approach to the problem, showing how visual transformations can serve as the basis for searching for an image that completes a specified relationship.
summary.tldr: A quadruple Siamese convolutional network learns relationships between image pairs to answer natural-image analogy questions.

title: Visalogy: Answering Visual Analogy Questions

abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of jointly learning both the per-task model parameters and the inter-task relationships in a multi-task online learning setting. The proposed algorithm features probabilistic interpretation, efficient updating rules and flexible modulation on whether learners focus on their specific task or on jointly address all tasks. The paper also proves a sub-linear regret bound as compared to the best linear predictor in hindsight. Experiments over three multi-task learning benchmark datasets show advantageous performance of the proposed approach over several state-of-the-art online multi-task learning baselines.
originalAbstract: This paper addresses the challenge of jointly learning both the per-task model parameters and the inter-task relationships in a multi-task online learning setting. The proposed algorithm features probabilistic interpretation, efficient updating rules and flexible modulation on whether learners focus on their specific task or on jointly address all tasks. The paper also proves a sub-linear regret bound as compared to the best linear predictor in hindsight. Experiments over three multi-task learning benchmark datasets show advantageous performance of the proposed approach over several state-of-the-art online multi-task learning baselines.

paragraphs: Online multi-task learning must update several related prediction problems as observations arrive. The challenge here is twofold: learn a model for each task while also learning how the tasks relate to one another. The relationships matter because they determine how information from one task can contribute to learning another.

The proposed algorithm handles both parts jointly and gives the procedure a probabilistic interpretation. Its update rules are designed to be efficient, and it allows flexible control over how much learners emphasize their own task versus learning across all tasks. This makes the balance between specialization and shared learning an explicit part of the approach.

The authors prove a sublinear regret bound relative to the best linear predictor chosen in hindsight. In that comparison, the accumulated performance gap grows more slowly than the number of rounds, so its average contribution diminishes. Experiments on three multi-task benchmark datasets show advantages over several leading online multi-task baselines. These results support the combination of adaptive task relationships and efficient online updates in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: An online algorithm jointly learns task models and their relationships, with sublinear regret and favorable results on three benchmarks.

title: Adaptive Smoothed Online Multi-Task Learning

abstract: We show that there are no spurious local minima in the non-convex factorized parametrization of low-rank matrix recovery from incoherent linear measurements. With noisy measurements we show all local minima are very close to a global optimum. Together with a curvature bound at saddle points, this yields a polynomial time global convergence guarantee for stochastic gradient descent {\em from random initialization}.
originalAbstract: We show that there are no spurious local minima in the non-convex factorized parametrization of low-rank matrix recovery from incoherent linear measurements. With noisy measurements we show all local minima are very close to a global optimum. Together with a curvature bound at saddle points, this yields a polynomial time global convergence guarantee for stochastic gradient descent {\em from random initialization}.

paragraphs: The paper studies recovering a low-rank matrix from linear measurements using a factorized representation. In this formulation, optimization works with factors of the matrix, and the objective is nonconvex. The central question is whether local search can become trapped at a locally optimal solution that is worse than the best solution overall.

For the setting of incoherent linear measurements, the authors prove that no such spurious local minima exist. They also address noisy measurements, showing that every local minimum lies very close to a global optimum. These conclusions describe the optimization landscape under the stated measurement condition; the noisy result retains a closeness qualification rather than asserting exact optimality.

The analysis also bounds curvature at saddle points, which are distinct from local minima. Combining that result with the characterization of minima yields a polynomial-time global convergence guarantee for stochastic gradient descent starting from random initialization. The significance is that nonconvex factorization can still admit a rigorous global optimization guarantee in this matrix recovery setting.
summary.tldr: Under incoherent linear measurements, low-rank matrix recovery has no spurious local minima and admits a global convergence guarantee from random initialization.

title: Global Optimality of Local Search for Low Rank Matrix Recovery

abstract: Statistical performance bounds for reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms can be critical for high-stakes applications like healthcare. This paper introduces a new framework for theoretically measuring the performance of such algorithms called Uniform-PAC, which is a strengthening of the classical Probably Approximately Correct (PAC) framework. In contrast to the PAC framework, the uniform version may be used to derive high probability regret guarantees and so forms a bridge between the two setups that has been missing in the literature. We demonstrate the benefits of the new framework for finite-state episodic MDPs with a new algorithm that is Uniform-PAC and simultaneously achieves optimal regret and PAC guarantees except for a factor of the horizon.
originalAbstract: Statistical performance bounds for reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms can be critical for high-stakes applications like healthcare. This paper introduces a new framework for theoretically measuring the performance of such algorithms called Uniform-PAC, which is a strengthening of the classical Probably Approximately Correct (PAC) framework. In contrast to the PAC framework, the uniform version may be used to derive high probability regret guarantees and so forms a bridge between the two setups that has been missing in the literature. We demonstrate the benefits of the new framework for finite-state episodic MDPs with a new algorithm that is Uniform-PAC and simultaneously achieves optimal regret and PAC guarantees except for a factor of the horizon.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning guarantees can describe performance through probably approximately correct learning or through regret. These frameworks capture different aspects of how an algorithm learns, leaving a gap between their guarantees. This paper introduces Uniform-PAC, a stronger version of the classical PAC framework, to connect the two forms of analysis.

The key property is that Uniform-PAC guarantees can be used to derive high-probability regret guarantees, something the classical PAC framework does not provide in the same way. The framework therefore offers a shared theoretical basis for reasoning about approximate correctness and the performance cost accumulated while learning.

The authors demonstrate the framework for finite-state episodic Markov decision processes with a new algorithm. It is Uniform-PAC and simultaneously achieves regret and PAC guarantees that are optimal except for a factor depending on the horizon. The result makes the connection constructive: one algorithm supports both types of assurance, with the remaining horizon factor explicitly qualifying the optimality claim. This is relevant to settings where formal learning guarantees matter.
summary.tldr: Uniform-PAC links PAC and high-probability regret guarantees, with an episodic RL algorithm achieving both optimally up to a horizon factor.

title: Unifying PAC and Regret: Uniform PAC Bounds for Episodic Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Variational autoencoders (VAEs) learn representations of data by jointly training a probabilistic encoder and decoder network. Typically these models encode all features of the data into a single variable. Here we are interested in learning disentangled representations that encode distinct aspects of the data into separate variables. We propose to learn such representations using model architectures that generalise from standard VAEs, employing a general graphical model structure in the encoder and decoder. This allows us to train partially-specified models that make relatively strong assumptions about a subset of interpretable variables and rely on the flexibility of neural networks to learn representations for the remaining variables. We further define a general objective for semi-supervised learning in this model class, which can be approximated using an importance sampling procedure. We evaluate our framework's ability to learn disentangled representations, both by qualitative exploration of its generative capacity, and quantitative evaluation of its discriminative ability on a variety of models and datasets.

paragraphs: Variational autoencoders jointly learn an encoder and a decoder, but their representations typically collect the features of an observation into one variable. This paper instead seeks representations that place distinct aspects of the data into separate variables. The aim is to make some of the representation's structure correspond to interpretable aspects of the observations.

The proposed architecture generalizes standard VAEs by allowing a general graphical model structure in both encoder and decoder. This supports partially specified models: researchers can impose relatively strong assumptions on selected interpretable variables while leaving neural networks to learn representations for the remaining variables. The division combines explicit modeling choices with flexible learned components.

The authors also define a general semi-supervised learning objective for this model class and approximate it through importance sampling. They evaluate disentanglement through qualitative exploration of generated outputs and quantitative assessment of discriminative ability across models and datasets. These evaluations examine both what the representations can generate and how useful they are for discrimination, providing complementary views of the framework.
summary.tldr: Structured semi-supervised generative models combine explicit interpretable variables with neural representations to learn disentangled features.

title: Learning Disentangled Representations with Semi-Supervised Deep Generative Models

abstract: We study the problem of learning from group comparisons, with applications in predicting outcomes of sports and online games. Most of the previous works in this area focus on learning individual effects---they assume each player has an underlying score, and the ''ability'' of the team is modeled by the sum of team members' scores. Therefore, all the current approaches cannot model deeper interaction between team members: some players perform much better if they play together, and some players perform poorly together. In this paper, we propose a new model that takes the player-interaction effects into consideration. However, under certain circumstances, the total number of individuals can be very large, and number of player interactions grows quadratically, which makes learning intractable. In this case, we propose a latent factor model, and show that the sample complexity of our model is bounded under mild assumptions. Finally, we show that our proposed models have much better prediction power on several E-sports datasets, and furthermore can be used to reveal interesting patterns that cannot be discovered by previous methods.

paragraphs: Predicting team outcomes by adding individual player scores assumes that a player's contribution is independent of teammates. The paper addresses the missing interaction effects: some combinations perform unusually well together, while others perform poorly. It proposes models that learn from group comparisons while representing these dependencies between members.

Explicitly modeling player interactions creates a scaling challenge because the number of possible pairs grows quadratically with the player population. For large populations, the authors introduce a latent factor model to make the problem tractable. They also bound its sample complexity under mild assumptions, providing a theoretical account of the data needed for learning in that setting.

On several esports datasets, the proposed models have much stronger predictive performance than earlier approaches. They also reveal patterns that methods based only on individual effects cannot discover. These findings give interaction modeling two roles: improving predictions of group outcomes and exposing relationships among members. The results support treating a team's composition as more informative than the sum of independently estimated player strengths.
summary.tldr: Models of player interactions improve esports outcome predictions and use latent factors to address the growth in possible teammate relationships.

title: Learning from Group Comparisons: Exploiting Higher Order Interactions

abstract: We study the sample complexity of semi-supervised learning (SSL) and introduce new assumptions based on the mismatch between a mixture model learned from unlabeled data and the true mixture model induced by the (unknown) class conditional distributions. Under these assumptions, we establish an $\Omega(K\log K)$ labeled sample complexity bound without imposing parametric assumptions, where $K$ is the number of classes. Our results suggest that even in nonparametric settings it is possible to learn a near-optimal classifier using only a few labeled samples. Unlike previous theoretical work which focuses on binary classification, we consider general multiclass classification ($K>2$), which requires solving a difficult permutation learning problem. This permutation defines a classifier whose classification error is controlled by the Wasserstein distance between mixing measures, and we provide finite-sample results characterizing the behaviour of the excess risk of this classifier. Finally, we describe three algorithms for computing these estimators based on a connection to bipartite graph matching, and perform experiments to illustrate the superiority of the MLE over the majority vote estimator.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised learning seeks to use unlabeled data to reduce the need for labeled examples. This paper studies that possibility through mixture models without imposing parametric distributional assumptions. Its assumptions instead describe the mismatch between a mixture learned from unlabeled data and the true mixture associated with the unknown class-conditional distributions.

Under those assumptions, the authors establish a labeled-sample complexity lower bound of order K log K, where K is the number of classes. Their broader results suggest that near-optimal classification can be possible with few labels in nonparametric settings. For more than two classes, a central challenge is learning the permutation that associates mixture components with class identities.

The paper controls the resulting classifier’s error using Wasserstein distance between mixing measures and provides finite-sample results for excess risk. It also develops three estimation algorithms through a connection to bipartite graph matching. Experiments illustrate an advantage of maximum likelihood over majority vote. The work links mixture quality, component-to-class assignment, and labeled-data requirements within one analysis of multiclass semi-supervised learning.
summary.tldr: The paper relates multiclass semi-supervised learning’s label requirements to mixture mismatch and the challenge of assigning components to classes.

title: The Sample Complexity of Semi-Supervised Learning with Nonparametric Mixture Models

abstract: Gaussian processes (GPs) provide a powerful non-parametric framework for reasoning over functions. Despite appealing theory, its superlinear computational and memory complexities have presented a long-standing challenge. State-of-the-art sparse variational inference methods trade modeling accuracy against complexity. However, the complexities of these methods still scale superlinearly in the number of basis functions, implying that that sparse GP methods are able to learn from large datasets only when a small model is used. Recently, a decoupled approach was proposed that removes the unnecessary coupling between the complexities of modeling the mean and the covariance functions of a GP. It achieves a linear complexity in the number of mean parameters, so an expressive posterior mean function can be modeled. While promising, this approach suffers from optimization difficulties due to ill-conditioning and non-convexity. In this work, we propose an alternative decoupled parametrization. It adopts an orthogonal basis in the mean function to model the residues that cannot be learned by the standard coupled approach. Therefore, our method extends, rather than replaces, the coupled approach to achieve strictly better performance. This construction admits a straightforward natural gradient update rule, so the structure of the information manifold that is lost during decoupling can be leveraged to speed up learning. Empirically, our algorithm demonstrates significantly faster convergence in multiple experiments.

paragraphs: Gaussian processes model functions but can be expensive in computation and memory. Sparse variational methods reduce that cost by limiting the model's basis, creating an accuracy–complexity tradeoff. Earlier decoupled methods let the mean use more parameters efficiently, but their optimization can suffer from ill-conditioning and non-convexity.

This paper proposes a different decoupled parameterization. It retains the standard coupled construction and adds an orthogonal basis to the mean, representing residual behavior that the coupled part cannot learn. The resulting model extends the existing construction, giving it additional expressive capacity while preserving that starting point.

The parameterization also permits a straightforward natural-gradient update, allowing learning to use the information geometry that decoupling had otherwise lost. The authors describe the construction as achieving strictly better performance than the coupled approach and report significantly faster convergence across multiple experiments. Its practical contribution is to connect a more expressive mean representation with an optimization rule designed to train that representation efficiently.
summary.tldr: An orthogonal extension of sparse Gaussian processes expands the mean representation and enables natural-gradient learning with faster empirical convergence.

title: Orthogonally Decoupled Variational Gaussian Processes

abstract: Deep image translation methods have recently shown excellent results, outputting high-quality images covering multiple modes of the data distribution. There has also been increased interest in disentangling the internal representations learned by deep methods to further improve their performance and achieve a finer control. In this paper, we bridge these two objectives and introduce the concept of cross-domain disentanglement. We aim to separate the internal representation into three parts. The shared part contains information for both domains. The exclusive parts, on the other hand, contain only factors of variation that are particular to each domain. We achieve this through bidirectional image translation based on Generative Adversarial Networks and cross-domain autoencoders, a novel network component. Our model offers multiple advantages. We can output diverse samples covering multiple modes of the distributions of both domains, perform domain- specific image transfer and interpolation, and cross-domain retrieval without the need of labeled data, only paired images. We compare our model to the state-of-the-art in multi-modal image translation and achieve better results for translation on challenging datasets as well as for cross-domain retrieval on realistic datasets.

The shared part contains information for both domains. The exclusive parts, on the other hand, contain only factors of variation that are particular to each domain. paragraphs: This paper connects image translation with the goal of separating different sources of variation inside a learned representation. It introduces cross-domain disentanglement: one representation component holds information shared by two image domains, while two additional components capture factors specific to each domain. This separation is intended to give finer control over translation and related operations.

The method combines bidirectional translation through generative adversarial networks with a new component called a cross-domain autoencoder. Training requires paired images but does not require labels. That distinction matters because the model still receives correspondence information between the two domains, even though semantic annotations are unnecessary.

The resulting model can generate diverse outputs across both domains, perform domain-specific transfer and interpolation, and retrieve corresponding content across domains. Comparisons with state-of-the-art multimodal translation methods show better translation results on challenging datasets and better cross-domain retrieval on realistic datasets. These findings support the proposed separation as useful both for producing varied images and for identifying information shared across domains.
summary.tldr: A model trained on paired images separates shared and domain-specific information to improve diverse image translation and cross-domain retrieval.

title: Image-to-image translation for cross-domain disentanglement

abstract: Many state-of-the-art algorithms for solving Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes (POMDPs) rely on turning the problem into a “fully observable” problem—a belief MDP—and exploiting the piece-wise linearity and convexity (PWLC) of the optimal value function in this new state space (the belief simplex ∆). This approach has been extended to solving ρ-POMDPs—i.e., for information-oriented criteria—when the reward ρ is convex in ∆. General ρ-POMDPs can also be turned into “fully observable” problems, but with no means to exploit the PWLC property. In this paper, we focus on POMDPs and ρ-POMDPs with λ ρ -Lipschitz reward function, and demonstrate that, for finite horizons, the optimal value function is Lipschitz-continuous. Then, value function approximators are proposed for both upper- and lower-bounding the optimal value function, which are shown to provide uniformly improvable bounds. This allows proposing two algorithms derived from HSVI which are empirically evaluated on various benchmark problems.

paragraphs: In a partially observable decision problem, an agent acts using a belief about the hidden state. Many solution methods treat that belief as the state of a fully observable problem and exploit a piecewise-linear, convex value function. For general information-oriented rewards in rho-POMDPs, that useful structure is unavailable, creating a need for another way to approximate value.

The paper considers reward functions that satisfy a Lipschitz condition, meaning their variation is bounded relative to changes in belief. For finite horizons, the authors prove that the optimal value function is also Lipschitz-continuous. This supplies a different form of regularity that can guide approximation even when the usual piecewise-linear structure cannot be used.

Building on that result, the authors construct approximations that bound the optimal value from above and below. They show that these bounds can be improved uniformly, then use them to develop two algorithms derived from heuristic search value iteration. Empirical evaluations on benchmark problems accompany the theory, linking the continuity result to concrete planning procedures.
summary.tldr: For finite horizons and Lipschitz rewards, POMDP value functions are Lipschitz-continuous, enabling improvable bounds and two planning algorithms.

title: rho-POMDPs have Lipschitz-Continuous epsilon-Optimal Value Functions

abstract: We propose a novel nonparametric online predictor for discrete labels conditioned on multivariate continuous features. The predictor is based on a feature space discretization induced by a full-fledged k-d tree with randomly picked directions and a recursive Bayesian distribution, which allows to automatically learn the most relevant feature scales characterizing the conditional distribution. We prove its pointwise universality, i.e., it achieves a normalized log loss performance asymptotically as good as the true conditional entropy of the labels given the features. The time complexity to process the n-th sample point is O(log n) in probability with respect to the distribution generating the data points, whereas other exact nonparametric methods require to process all past observations. Experiments on challenging datasets show the computational and statistical efficiency of our algorithm in comparison to standard and state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: The paper proposes an online predictor for discrete labels given several continuous features. Its goal is to learn a flexible relationship between features and labels while keeping the work required for each new observation small. The predictor does not rely on a fixed parametric form for that relationship.

It partitions feature space with a k-d tree using randomly selected directions and combines this partition with a recursive Bayesian distribution. The construction automatically learns which feature scales are relevant to the conditional label distribution. This makes the choice of resolution part of learning, rather than requiring a single predetermined discretization.

The authors prove pointwise universality: asymptotically, normalized log loss becomes as good as the true conditional entropy of labels given features. They also show that processing the nth observation takes logarithmic time in probability under the data-generating distribution. This is a probabilistic complexity statement, not a worst-case bound for every observation. Experiments on challenging datasets support both computational and statistical efficiency relative to standard and state-of-the-art alternatives.
summary.tldr: A tree-based Bayesian online predictor combines asymptotically optimal normalized log loss with logarithmic per-sample processing time in probability.

title: Low-Complexity Nonparametric Bayesian Online Prediction with Universal Guarantees

abstract: We propose new methods for learning control policies and neural network Lyapunov functions for nonlinear control problems, with provable guarantee of stability. The framework consists of a learner that attempts to find the control and Lyapunov functions, and a falsifier that finds counterexamples to quickly guide the learner towards solutions. The procedure terminates when no counterexample is found by the falsifier, in which case the controlled nonlinear system is provably stable. The approach significantly simplifies the process of Lyapunov control design, provides end-to-end correctness guarantee, and can obtain much larger regions of attraction than existing methods such as LQR and SOS/SDP. We show experiments on how the new methods obtain high-quality solutions for challenging robot control problems such as path tracking for wheeled vehicles and humanoid robot balancing.

The framework consists of a learner that attempts to find the control and Lyapunov functions, and a falsifier that finds counterexamples to quickly guide the learner towards solutions. The procedure terminates when no counterexample is found by the falsifier, in which case the controlled nonlinear system is provably stable. paragraphs: Designing a controller for a nonlinear system involves more than finding behavior that looks successful in a simulation: stability must also be established. This paper learns both a control policy and a neural-network Lyapunov function. The Lyapunov function serves as a mathematical certificate supporting the stability of the resulting controlled system.

The framework pairs a learner with a falsifier. The learner searches for control and Lyapunov functions, while the falsifier finds counterexamples that direct further learning. The procedure terminates when the falsifier finds no counterexample; under this procedure, that outcome certifies stability. This creates a feedback loop between proposing a controller and checking the mathematical conditions supporting it.

The authors report that the approach simplifies Lyapunov control design and can obtain much larger regions of attraction than methods including LQR and SOS/SDP. These regions describe the scope of the controller's stabilizing behavior. Experiments demonstrate high-quality solutions for wheeled-vehicle path tracking and humanoid balancing, connecting the certification framework to challenging robot-control tasks.
summary.tldr: A learner–falsifier loop jointly learns controllers and Lyapunov certificates, providing provable stability when its verification procedure terminates.

title: Neural Lyapunov Control

abstract: In real-world machine learning applications, data subsets correspond to especially critical outcomes: vulnerable cyclist detections are safety-critical in an autonomous driving task, and "question" sentences might be important to a dialogue agent's language understanding for product purposes. While machine learning models can achieve quality performance on coarse-grained metrics like F1-score and overall accuracy, they may underperform on these critical subsets---we define these as slices, the key abstraction in our approach. To address slice-level performance, practitioners often train separate "expert" models on slice subsets or use multi-task hard parameter sharing. We propose Slice-based Learning, a new programming model in which the slicing function (SF), a programmer abstraction, is used to specify additional model capacity for each slice. Any model can leverage SFs to learn slice-specific representations, which are combined with an attention mechanism to make slice-aware predictions. We show that our approach improves over baselines in terms of computational complexity and slice-specific performance by up to 19.0 points, and overall performance by up to 4.6 F1 points on applications spanning natural language understanding and computer vision benchmarks as well as production-scale industrial systems.
