paragraphs: Strong overall accuracy can conceal poor performance on a subset of examples that matters especially much. The paper calls these subsets slices, such as cyclist detections in autonomous driving or question sentences in a dialogue system. It addresses how practitioners can explicitly direct model capacity toward such subsets while still producing a combined prediction.

Slice-based Learning introduces slicing functions as a programming abstraction for specifying additional capacity for individual slices. A model learns representations specific to those slices, and an attention mechanism combines them to make slice-aware predictions. This provides a shared approach to targeted learning, addressing a need otherwise handled through separate expert models or multi-task models with hard parameter sharing.

The authors report improvements over baselines in computational complexity and predictive performance across language, vision, and production-scale industrial applications. Gains reach 19.0 points for slice-specific performance and 4.6 F1 points overall. These are reported upper-end improvements, rather than gains promised for every slice. The findings show that explicitly representing critical subsets can improve both targeted outcomes and aggregate performance.
summary.tldr: Slice-based Learning uses programmer-defined data subsets and attention-combined representations to improve performance on critical slices and overall predictions.

title: Slice-based Learning: A Programming Model for Residual Learning in Critical Data Slices

abstract: We introduce the problem of model selection for contextual bandits, where a learner must adapt to the complexity of the optimal policy while balancing exploration and exploitation. Our main result is a new model selection guarantee for linear contextual bandits. We work in the stochastic realizable setting with a sequence of nested linear policy classes of dimension $d_1 < d_2 < \ldots$, where the $m^\star$-th class contains the optimal policy, and we design an algorithm that achieves $\tilde{O}l(T^{2/3}d^{1/3}_{m^\star})$ regret with no prior knowledge of the optimal dimension $d_{m^\star}$. The algorithm also achieves regret $\tilde{O}(T^{3/4} + \sqrt{Td_{m^\star}})$, which is optimal for $d_{m^{\star}}\geq{}\sqrt{T}$. This is the first model selection result for contextual bandits with non-vacuous regret for all values of $d_{m^\star}$, and to the best of our knowledge is the first positive result of this type for any online learning setting with partial information. The core of the algorithm is a new estimator for the gap in the best loss achievable by two linear policy classes, which we show admits a convergence rate faster than the rate required to learn the parameters for either class.

The core of the algorithm is a new estimator for the gap in the best loss achievable by two linear policy classes, which we show admits a convergence rate faster than the rate required to learn the parameters for either class.

paragraphs: A contextual bandit learner must choose actions while balancing information gathering with good immediate decisions. This paper adds model selection: adapting to the complexity needed to express the optimal policy. It studies a stochastic, realizable setting with nested linear policy classes, where some class of dimension d contains that policy but d is unknown to the learner.

The proposed algorithm achieves regret bounds of order T^(2/3)d^(1/3) and T^(3/4) + √(Td), with logarithmic factors suppressed. Here T is the learning horizon, and regret measures accumulated loss relative to the optimal policy. The second guarantee is optimal when d is at least √T. These bounds provide meaningful model-selection guarantees across all values of the optimal dimension in the stated setting.

The key ingredient estimates the difference between the best losses achievable by two policy classes. The authors show that this comparison can converge faster than learning either class's parameters. That distinction makes adaptation possible: the learner can obtain useful evidence about whether a richer class helps without first fully learning both candidate models.
summary.tldr: A contextual-bandit algorithm adapts to an unknown optimal linear-policy dimension by efficiently estimating performance gaps between nested classes.

title: Model Selection for Contextual Bandits

abstract: We present Point-Voxel CNN (PVCNN) for efficient, fast 3D deep learning. Previous work processes 3D data using either voxel-based or point-based NN models. However, both approaches are computationally inefficient. The computation cost and memory footprints of the voxel-based models grow cubically with the input resolution, making it memory-prohibitive to scale up the resolution. As for point-based networks, up to 80% of the time is wasted on dealing with the sparse data which have rather poor memory locality, not on the actual feature extraction. In this paper, we propose PVCNN that represents the 3D input data in points to reduce the memory consumption, while performing the convolutions in voxels to reduce the irregular, sparse data access and improve the locality. Our PVCNN model is both memory and computation efficient. Evaluated on semantic and part segmentation datasets, it achieves much higher accuracy than the voxel-based baseline with 10× GPU memory reduction; it also outperforms the state-of-the-art point-based models with 7× measured speedup on average. Remarkably, the narrower version of PVCNN achieves 2× speedup over PointNet (an extremely efficient model) on part and scene segmentation benchmarks with much higher accuracy. We validate the general effectiveness of PVCNN on 3D object detection: by replacing the primitives in Frustrum PointNet with PVConv, it outperforms Frustrum PointNet++ by 2.4% mAP on average with 1.5× measured speedup and GPU memory reduction.

paragraphs: Three-dimensional networks face different computational problems depending on their representation. Dense voxel grids become expensive as resolution increases because memory and computation grow cubically. Point-based networks avoid that dense representation, but irregular access to sparse data can consume much of their execution time instead of useful feature extraction.

Point-Voxel CNN combines the two representations. It stores the input as points to control memory consumption and performs convolutions in voxels to improve memory locality. The design connects representation choice to hardware efficiency: compact point storage and more regular convolutional access address separate sources of cost.

On semantic and part segmentation datasets, PVCNN reports higher accuracy than a voxel baseline with tenfold lower GPU memory use, and an average sevenfold measured speedup over leading point-based models while also improving accuracy. A narrower version achieves twice PointNet's speed with higher accuracy on the reported segmentation benchmarks. Replacing components in Frustrum PointNet with PVConv also improves detection over Frustrum PointNet++, with a reported 2.4% average mAP gain, 1.5-fold speedup, and reduced GPU memory use.
summary.tldr: PVCNN combines point storage with voxel convolutions to improve accuracy, speed, and memory efficiency in reported 3D learning benchmarks.

title: Point-Voxel CNN for Efficient 3D Deep Learning

abstract: We propose Generative Well-intentioned Networks (GWINs), a novel framework for increasing the accuracy of certainty-based, closed-world classifiers. A conditional generative network recovers the distribution of observations that the classifier labels correctly with high certainty. We introduce a reject option to the classifier during inference, allowing the classifier to reject an observation instance rather than predict an uncertain label. These rejected observations are translated by the generative network to high-certainty representations, which are then relabeled by the classifier. This architecture allows for any certainty-based classifier or rejection function and is not limited to multilayer perceptrons. The capability of this framework is assessed using benchmark classification datasets and shows that GWINs significantly improve the accuracy of uncertain observations.
originalAbstract: We propose Generative Well-intentioned Networks (GWINs), a novel framework for increasing the accuracy of certainty-based, closed-world classifiers. A conditional generative network recovers the distribution of observations that the classifier labels correctly with high certainty. We introduce a reject option to the classifier during inference, allowing the classifier to reject an observation instance rather than predict an uncertain label. These rejected observations are translated by the generative network to high-certainty representations, which are then relabeled by the classifier. This architecture allows for any certainty-based classifier or rejection function and is not limited to multilayer perceptrons. The capability of this framework is assessed using benchmark classification datasets and shows that GWINs significantly improve the accuracy of uncertain observations.

paragraphs: A classifier may encounter observations for which it cannot confidently choose among its available classes. Generative Well-intentioned Networks address these uncertain cases by adding a generative component to a certainty-based, closed-world classifier. The aim is to improve classification accuracy by transforming observations that the original classifier finds difficult.

A conditional generative network learns the distribution of observations that the classifier labels correctly with high certainty. At inference time, a rejection option identifies observations whose labels are uncertain. The generator translates these rejected inputs into high-certainty representations, which the classifier then labels again. Rejection therefore initiates a second prediction pathway within the overall architecture.

The framework allows different certainty-based classifiers and rejection functions, rather than requiring a multilayer perceptron. Benchmark evaluations show significant accuracy improvements on uncertain observations. This finding supports the use of a learned transformation for difficult inputs: the reported benefit concerns their classification accuracy, so the contribution goes beyond merely producing outputs that receive higher confidence scores from the classifier.
summary.tldr: GWINs transform rejected, uncertain inputs into high-certainty representations and improve their classification accuracy in benchmark evaluations.

title: Generative Well-intentioned Networks

abstract: Capsule networks have been shown to be powerful models for image classification, thanks to their ability to represent and capture viewpoint variations of an object. However, the high computational complexity of capsule networks that stems from the recurrent dynamic routing poses a major drawback making their use for large-scale image classification challenging. In this work, we propose Star-Caps a capsule-based network that exploits a straight-through attentive routing to address the drawbacks of capsule networks. By utilizing attention modules augmented by differentiable binary routers, the proposed mechanism estimates the routing coefficients between capsules without recurrence, as opposed to prior related work. Subsequently, the routers utilize straight-through estimators to make binary decisions to either connect or disconnect the route between capsules, allowing stable and faster performance. The experiments conducted on several image classification datasets, including MNIST, SmallNorb, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet show that Star-Caps outperforms the baseline capsule networks.

paragraphs: Capsule networks can represent changes in an object’s viewpoint, making them useful for image classification. Their recurrent dynamic routing, however, carries substantial computational cost and makes large-scale use challenging. STAR-Caps changes the routing mechanism to address that bottleneck while retaining a capsule-based network.

The method uses attention modules augmented with differentiable binary routers to estimate routing coefficients without recurrence. The routers use straight-through estimators to decide whether a connection between capsules is active or inactive. This replaces repeated routing calculations with an attentive mechanism that makes explicit connection decisions, supporting the stable and faster performance described by the authors.

Experiments evaluate the network on MNIST, SmallNorb, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet. STAR-Caps outperforms the baseline capsule networks in these evaluations. The contribution shows that changing how capsules communicate can improve their practical performance, with routing itself serving as the main design target. Its reported evidence spans both smaller image classification datasets and the larger-scale ImageNet setting.
summary.tldr: STAR-Caps replaces recurrent capsule routing with attentive binary connection decisions, delivering faster performance and better results than evaluated capsule baselines.

title: STAR-Caps: Capsule Networks with Straight-Through Attentive Routing

abstract: Various parallel actor-learner methods reduce long training times for deep reinforcement learning. Synchronous methods enjoy training stability while having lower data throughput. In contrast, asynchronous methods achieve high throughput but suffer from stability issues and lower sample efficiency due to ‘stale policies.’ To combine the advantages of both methods we propose High-Throughput Synchronous Deep Reinforcement Learning (HTS-RL). In HTS-RL, we perform learning and rollouts concurrently, devise a system design which avoids ‘stale policies’ and ensure that actors interact with environment replicas in an asynchronous manner while maintaining full determinism. We evaluate our approach on Atari games and the Google Research Football environment. Compared to synchronous baselines, HTS-RL is 2−6X faster. Compared to state-of-the-art asynchronous methods, HTS-RL has competitive throughput and consistently achieves higher average episode rewards.

In contrast, asynchronous methods achieve high throughput but suffer from stability issues and lower sample efficiency due to ‘stale policies.’ To combine the advantages of both methods we propose High-Throughput Synchronous Deep Reinforcement Learning (HTS-RL). In HTS-RL, we perform learning and rollouts concurrently, devise a system design which avoids ‘stale policies’ and ensure that actors interact with environment replicas in an asynchronous manner while maintaining full determinism. We evaluate our approach on Atari games and the Google Research Football environment. Compared to synchronous baselines, HTS-RL is 2−6X faster. Compared to state-of-the-art asynchronous methods, HTS-RL has competitive throughput and consistently achieves higher average episode rewards.

paragraphs: Parallel reinforcement learning systems divide work between actors that collect experience and learners that update the policy. Synchronous designs offer training stability but can limit throughput. Asynchronous designs process more data, yet actors may use outdated policies, creating the stale-policy problem associated with reduced stability and sample efficiency.

High-Throughput Synchronous Deep Reinforcement Learning, or HTS-RL, combines concurrent learning and rollout collection with a system design that avoids stale policies. Actors interact asynchronously with separate environment replicas while the overall system maintains full determinism. The approach therefore reorganizes how collection and learning overlap while retaining the coordination properties sought in synchronous training.

Evaluations use Atari games and the Google Research Football environment. HTS-RL is two to six times faster than synchronous baselines. Against state-of-the-art asynchronous methods, it achieves competitive throughput and consistently higher average episode rewards in the reported comparisons. These results support the system's central goal: improving processing speed while preserving the training benefits that motivate synchronous actor-learner methods.
summary.tldr: HTS-RL overlaps learning and experience collection to accelerate synchronous reinforcement learning while avoiding stale policies.

title: High-Throughput Synchronous Deep RL

abstract: It is notoriously difficult to control the behavior of artificial neural networks such as generative neural language models. We recast the problem of controlling natural language generation as that of learning to interface with a pretrained language model, just as Application Programming Interfaces (APIs) control the behavior of programs by altering hyperparameters. In this new paradigm, a specialized neural network (called a Neural Programming Interface or NPI) learns to interface with a pretrained language model by manipulating the hidden activations of the pretrained model to produce desired outputs. Importantly, no permanent changes are made to the weights of the original model, allowing us to re-purpose pretrained models for new tasks without overwriting any aspect of the language model. We also contribute a new data set construction algorithm and GAN-inspired loss function that allows us to train NPI models to control outputs of autoregressive transformers. In experiments against other state-of-the-art approaches, we demonstrate the efficacy of our methods using OpenAI’s GPT-2 model, successfully controlling noun selection, topic aversion, offensive speech filtering, and other aspects of language while largely maintaining the controlled model's fluency under deterministic settings.

paragraphs: The paper approaches control over language generation as a problem of learning an interface to an existing language model. Its Neural Programming Interface, or NPI, is a separate specialized neural network that adjusts the model’s hidden activations: the internal signals involved in producing text. These adjustments aim to steer the pretrained model toward desired outputs.

The distinction between changing activations and changing model weights is central to the approach. The NPI makes no permanent changes to the original model’s weights, allowing the pretrained model to be repurposed without overwriting its learned parameters. The authors also introduce an algorithm for constructing training data and a training objective inspired by generative adversarial networks. Together, these support training interfaces to control autoregressive transformers, which generate text sequentially.

Experiments with GPT-2 compare the approach with other methods described as state of the art. The authors report successful control over noun choice, avoidance of particular topics, filtering of offensive speech, and other language properties. They also report that fluency was largely preserved under deterministic settings. These findings support the usefulness of learned activation control for steering generation while retaining much of the model’s ability to produce fluent text.
summary.tldr: A learned neural interface steers GPT-2 through its hidden activations without permanently changing its weights, achieving several forms of output control while largely preserving fluency under deterministic settings.

title: Towards Neural Programming Interfaces

abstract: Score function-based natural language generation (NLG) approaches such as REINFORCE, in general, suffer from low sample efficiency and training instability problems. This is mainly due to the non-differentiable nature of the discrete space sampling and thus these methods have to treat the discriminator as a black box and ignore the gradient information. To improve the sample efficiency and reduce the variance of REINFORCE, we propose a novel approach, TaylorGAN, which augments the gradient estimation by off-policy update and the first-order Taylor expansion. This approach enables us to train NLG models from scratch with smaller batch size --- without maximum likelihood pre-training, and outperforms existing GAN-based methods on multiple metrics of quality and diversity.
originalAbstract: Score function-based natural language generation (NLG) approaches such as REINFORCE, in general, suffer from low sample efficiency and training instability problems. This is mainly due to the non-differentiable nature of the discrete space sampling and thus these methods have to treat the discriminator as a black box and ignore the gradient information. To improve the sample efficiency and reduce the variance of REINFORCE, we propose a novel approach, TaylorGAN, which augments the gradient estimation by off-policy update and the first-order Taylor expansion. This approach enables us to train NLG models from scratch with smaller batch size --- without maximum likelihood pre-training, and outperforms existing GAN-based methods on multiple metrics of quality and diversity.

paragraphs: Generating text requires sampling discrete choices, which prevents ordinary differentiation through the sampling operation. Score-function methods such as REINFORCE can work with those choices, but commonly suffer from inefficient sampling and unstable training. The paper attributes much of this difficulty to treating the discriminator as a black box and ignoring its gradient information.

TaylorGAN augments gradient estimation using off-policy updates and a first-order Taylor expansion. The purpose is to make better use of available information when updating the generation policy, improving sample efficiency and reducing the variance associated with REINFORCE. The Taylor expansion supplies a local approximation that contributes to the augmented update.

The authors report that this approach enables natural language generation models to be trained from scratch with smaller batches, without maximum-likelihood pretraining. They also report improvements over existing GAN-based methods on multiple measures of both quality and diversity. These findings connect the gradient-estimation change to practical training behavior: more informative policy updates support a training route that does not depend on the stated pretraining stage.
summary.tldr: TaylorGAN combines off-policy updates with Taylor-based gradient estimation to improve text-generation training efficiency and enable training without maximum-likelihood pretraining.

title: TaylorGAN: Neighbor-Augmented Policy Update Towards Sample-Efficient Natural Language Generation

abstract: We present Quantized Variational Inference, a new algorithm for Evidence Lower Bound minimization. We show how Optimal Voronoi Tesselation produces variance free gradients for Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO) optimization at the cost of introducing asymptotically decaying bias. Subsequently, we propose a Richardson extrapolation type method to improve this bound. We show that using the Quantized Variational Inference framework leads to fast convergence for both score function and the reparametrized gradient estimator at a comparable computational cost. Finally, we propose several experiments to assess the performance of our method and its limitations.

paragraphs: Quantized Variational Inference tackles optimization of the Evidence Lower Bound through a different treatment of gradient estimation. The paper’s central tradeoff is explicit: eliminate gradient variance while accepting bias that decays asymptotically. This separates randomness in the optimization signal from systematic approximation error, rather than treating them as the same obstacle.

The proposed construction uses optimal Voronoi tessellation to obtain the variance-free gradients. The authors then introduce a method resembling Richardson extrapolation to improve the bound associated with the approximation. These components work together: quantization changes the gradient estimator’s error profile, while the extrapolation-style step improves the resulting bound.

The authors show fast convergence within this framework for both score-function and reparameterized gradient estimators at comparable computational cost. This makes the approach relevant to two different routes for obtaining gradients in variational inference. They also propose experiments to assess performance and limitations. The stated contribution is a framework for managing a specific bias–variance tradeoff, with the decay of bias central to interpreting the variance-free claim.
summary.tldr: Quantized Variational Inference produces variance-free gradients with asymptotically decaying bias and supports fast convergence at comparable computational cost.

title: Quantized Variational Inference

abstract: Recent advances in machine learning have led to growing interest in Explainable AI (xAI) to enable humans to gain insight into the decision-making of machine learning models. Despite this recent interest, the utility of xAI techniques has not yet been characterized in human-machine teaming. Importantly, xAI offers the promise of enhancing team situational awareness (SA) and shared mental model development, which are the key characteristics of effective human-machine teams. Rapidly developing such mental models is especially critical in ad hoc human-machine teaming, where agents do not have a priori knowledge of others' decision-making strategies. In this paper, we present two novel human-subject experiments quantifying the benefits of deploying xAI techniques within a human-machine teaming scenario. First, we show that xAI techniques can support SA ($p<0.05)$. Second, we examine how different SA levels induced via a collaborative AI policy abstraction affect ad hoc human-machine teaming performance. Importantly, we find that the benefits of xAI are not universal, as there is a strong dependence on the composition of the human-machine team. Novices benefit from xAI providing increased SA ($p<0.05$) but are susceptible to cognitive overhead ($p<0.05$). On the other hand, expert performance degrades with the addition of xAI-based support ($p<0.05$), indicating that the cost of paying attention to the xAI outweighs the benefits obtained from being provided additional information to enhance SA. Our results demonstrate that researchers must deliberately design and deploy the right xAI techniques in the right scenario by carefully considering human-machine team composition and how the xAI method augments SA.

paragraphs: Explanations may help people understand an AI teammate, but understanding more does not automatically produce better teamwork. This paper studies ad hoc teams, where participants initially lack knowledge of one another's decision strategies. It focuses on situational awareness and shared mental models, which are especially valuable when teammates must coordinate quickly.

Two human-subject experiments examine these effects. The first shows that explainable AI can support situational awareness. The second investigates how different awareness levels, induced through an abstraction of the collaborative AI's policy, affect team performance. This links the information supplied by an explanation to its consequences for collaboration, including the attention needed to process it.

The results depend strongly on team composition. Novices benefit from increased awareness but are also vulnerable to cognitive overhead. Experts perform worse with the added explanation support, suggesting that its attention cost outweighs its informational benefit in the studied setting. These reported effects are statistically significant. The findings support choosing explanations with the user's expertise and collaborative situation in mind, rather than assuming additional explanation always helps.
summary.tldr: Human-subject experiments find that AI explanations can help novices yet impair experts, with benefits depending on awareness gains and cognitive overhead.

title: The Utility of Explainable AI in Ad Hoc Human-Machine Teaming

abstract: Using deep latent variable models in causal inference has attracted considerable interest recently, but an essential open question is their ability to yield consistent causal estimates. While they have demonstrated promising results and theory exists on some simple model formulations, we also know that causal effects are not even identifiable in general with latent variables. We investigate this gap between theory and empirical results with analytical considerations and extensive experiments under multiple synthetic and real-world data sets, using the causal effect variational autoencoder (CEVAE) as a case study. While CEVAE seems to work reliably under some simple scenarios, it does not estimate the causal effect correctly with a misspecified latent variable or a complex data distribution, as opposed to its original motivation. Hence, our results show that more attention should be paid to ensuring the correctness of causal estimates with deep latent variable models.

paragraphs: Deep latent variable models try to account for hidden factors when estimating causal effects. Their flexibility makes them appealing, but accurately modeling observations does not by itself establish that a causal estimate is correct. The paper examines this concern through the causal effect variational autoencoder, or CEVAE, asking whether its promising empirical behavior is supported beyond simple settings.

The authors combine analytical reasoning with extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets. Their central issue is consistency: whether an estimation approach can recover the correct causal effect as data accumulate. This question is especially important with hidden variables, because causal effects cannot generally be identified from observed data without additional structure.

CEVAE appears reliable in some simple scenarios, but the investigated cases reveal incorrect causal estimates when the latent variable is misspecified or the data distribution is complex. These findings challenge the expectation that a flexible deep model will automatically resolve hidden-variable difficulties. The paper therefore argues for closer attention to the conditions that make causal estimates correct.
summary.tldr: An analysis of CEVAE finds that promising performance in simple settings does not ensure correct causal estimates under latent-variable misspecification or complex data.

title: A Critical Look at the Consistency of Causal Estimation with Deep Latent Variable Models

abstract: Computational level explanations based on optimal feedback control with signal-dependent noise have been able to account for a vast array of phenomena in human sensorimotor behavior. However, commonly a cost function needs to be assumed for a task and the optimality of human behavior is evaluated by comparing observed and predicted trajectories. Here, we introduce inverse optimal control with signal-dependent noise, which allows inferring the cost function from observed behavior. To do so, we formalize the problem as a partially observable Markov decision process and distinguish between the agent’s and the experimenter’s inference problems. Specifically, we derive a probabilistic formulation of the evolution of states and belief states and an approximation to the propagation equation in the linear-quadratic Gaussian problem with signal-dependent noise. We extend the model to the case of partial observability of state variables from the point of view of the experimenter. We show the feasibility of the approach through validation on synthetic data and application to experimental data. Our approach enables recovering the costs and benefits implicit in human sequential sensorimotor behavior, thereby reconciling normative and descriptive approaches in a computational framework.

paragraphs: Optimal feedback control models can explain many aspects of human sensorimotor behavior when they include signal-dependent noise. Such analyses commonly assume a task's cost function and compare predicted movements with observed ones. This paper develops an inverse approach that infers the cost function from behavior while accounting for that noise structure.

The authors formulate the task as a partially observable Markov decision process and distinguish the acting person's inference problem from the experimenter's. They derive a probabilistic description of how states and belief states evolve, together with an approximate propagation equation for the linear-quadratic Gaussian case with signal-dependent noise. They also allow the experimenter to observe only part of the state.

Validation on synthetic data and application to experimental data demonstrate the approach's feasibility. The framework provides a way to recover costs and benefits implicit in sequential sensorimotor behavior. It thereby connects explanations based on optimal action selection with descriptions grounded in observed behavior, while explicitly accounting for uncertainty faced by both actor and observer.
summary.tldr: An inverse-control framework infers human sensorimotor costs while accounting for signal-dependent noise and partial observation.

title: Inverse Optimal Control Adapted to the Noise Characteristics of the Human Sensorimotor System

abstract: Many features of human and animal behavior can be understood in the framework of Bayesian inference and optimal decision making, but the biological substrate of such processes is not fully understood. Neural sampling provides a flexible code for probabilistic inference in high dimensions and explains key features of sensory responses under experimental manipulations of uncertainty. However, since it encodes uncertainty implicitly, across time and neurons, it remains unclear how such representations can be used for decision making. Here we propose a spiking network model that maps neural samples of a task-specific marginal distribution into an instantaneous representation of uncertainty via a procedure inspired by online kernel density estimation, so that its output can be readily used for decision making. Our model is consistent with experimental results at the level of single neurons and populations, and makes predictions for how neural responses and decisions could be modulated by uncertainty and prior biases. More generally, our work brings together conflicting perspectives on probabilistic brain computation.

paragraphs: A brain can represent uncertainty through samples: patterns of neural activity collectively express different possibilities over neurons and time. This offers a flexible account of probabilistic inference, but it raises a practical question. If uncertainty is spread across many samples, how can a decision-making circuit access it at a particular moment?

The paper proposes a spiking neural network that converts samples from a task-relevant marginal distribution into an immediately available representation of uncertainty. Its procedure is inspired by online kernel density estimation, which builds an estimate of a probability distribution as samples arrive. The circuit thus links a sample-based representation to an output that can support decisions.

The model agrees with experimental findings concerning individual neurons and neural populations. It also predicts how uncertainty and prior biases could change both neural responses and decisions. These results support a possible biological bridge between different accounts of probabilistic computation, while retaining the distinction between a proposed circuit consistent with observations and an established account of the brain's implementation.
summary.tldr: A proposed spiking circuit turns neural probability samples into an instantaneous uncertainty representation that can support decision making.

title: A sampling-based circuit for optimal decision making

abstract: Policy optimization is a widely-used method in reinforcement learning. Due to its local-search nature, however, theoretical guarantees on global optimality often rely on extra assumptions on the Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) that bypass the challenge of global exploration. To eliminate the need of such assumptions, in this work, we develop a general solution that adds dilated bonuses to the policy update to facilitate global exploration. To showcase the power and generality of this technique, we apply it to several episodic MDP settings with adversarial losses and bandit feedback, improving and generalizing the state-of-the-art. Specifically, in the tabular case, we obtain $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{T})$ regret where $T$ is the number of episodes, improving the $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}({T}^{\frac{2}{3}})$ regret bound by Shani et al. [2020]. When the number of states is infinite, under the assumption that the state-action values are linear in some low-dimensional features, we obtain $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}({T}^{\frac{2}{3}})$ regret with the help of a simulator, matching the result of Neu and Olkhovskaya [2020] while importantly removing the need of an exploratory policy that their algorithm requires. To our knowledge, this is the first algorithm with sublinear regret for linear function approximation with adversarial losses, bandit feedback, and no exploratory assumptions. Finally, we also discuss how to further improve the regret or remove the need of a simulator using dilated bonuses, when an exploratory policy is available.

paragraphs: Policy optimization improves a policy through local updates, which can leave global exploration unresolved. This paper introduces dilated bonuses into those updates to encourage exploration. It studies episodic decision processes with adversarial losses and bandit feedback, aiming to establish guarantees without assumptions that already supply the needed exploration.

For tabular problems, the method achieves regret of order square root of T, up to logarithmic factors, improving the previous T-to-the-two-thirds bound. For infinite state spaces, it assumes state-action values are linear in low-dimensional features and uses a simulator. In that setting it obtains T-to-the-two-thirds regret without requiring an exploratory policy.

These are sublinear regret guarantees, meaning cumulative regret grows more slowly than the number of episodes. The linear-function result retains its feature and simulator assumptions while removing the exploratory-policy requirement. The paper also discusses how an available exploratory policy can support better regret or eliminate the simulator. Dilated bonuses thus provide a shared exploration mechanism across several distinct theoretical settings.
summary.tldr: Dilated exploration bonuses improve policy-optimization regret bounds and remove exploratory-policy requirements in the studied adversarial settings.

title: Policy Optimization in Adversarial MDPs: Improved Exploration via Dilated Bonuses

abstract: Standard lossy image compression algorithms aim to preserve an image's appearance, while minimizing the number of bits needed to transmit it. However, the amount of information actually needed by the user for downstream tasks -- e.g., deciding which product to click on in a shopping website -- is likely much lower. To achieve this lower bitrate, we would ideally only transmit the visual features that drive user behavior, while discarding details irrelevant to the user's decisions. We approach this problem by training a compression model through human-in-the-loop learning as the user performs tasks with the compressed images. The key insight is to train the model to produce a compressed image that induces the user to take the same action that they would have taken had they seen the original image. To approximate the loss function for this model, we train a discriminator that tries to distinguish whether a user's action was taken in response to the compressed image or the original. We evaluate our method through experiments with human participants on four tasks: reading handwritten digits, verifying photos of faces, browsing an online shopping catalogue, and playing a car racing video game. The results show that our method learns to match the user's actions with and without compression at lower bitrates than baseline methods, and adapts the compression model to the user's behavior: it preserves the digit number and randomizes handwriting style in the digit reading task, preserves hats and eyeglasses while randomizing faces in the photo verification task, preserves the perceived price of an item while randomizing its color and background in the online shopping task, and preserves upcoming bends in the road in the car racing game.

paragraphs: An image may contain much more detail than a person needs to make a particular decision. This paper trains image compression around preserving the user's actions. Its objective is for a person viewing a compressed image to act as they would after viewing the original, while transmitting fewer bits.

Training includes humans performing tasks with compressed images. A discriminator learns to distinguish whether an action followed an original or compressed image, providing an approximation to the compression model's loss. This makes user behavior part of the training signal and allows the retained visual information to adapt to the task.

Its outputs preserve task-relevant properties: digit identity despite changed handwriting, hats and glasses despite randomized faces, perceived price despite changed colors and backgrounds, and upcoming road bends. These examples show how behavior-based compression can prioritize different information for different uses.
summary.tldr: Human-in-the-loop compression learns which visual information preserves users' decisions, matching actions at lower bitrates than baselines.

title: Pragmatic Image Compression for Human-in-the-Loop Decision-Making

abstract: We propose a novel technique for faster deep neural network training which systematically applies sample-based approximation to the constituent tensor operations, i.e., matrix multiplications and convolutions. We introduce new sampling techniques, study their theoretical properties, and prove that they provide the same convergence guarantees when applied to SGD training. We apply approximate tensor operations to single and multi-node training of MLP and CNN networks on MNIST, CIFAR-10 and ImageNet datasets. We demonstrate up to 66% reduction in the amount of computations and communication, and up to 1.37x faster training time while maintaining negligible or no impact on the final test accuracy.

paragraphs: Training neural networks involves repeated matrix multiplications and convolutions. This paper accelerates training by systematically replacing these tensor operations with sample-based approximations. The approach targets the computations making up training itself, allowing the authors to examine both the mathematical behavior of the approximations and their effect on training cost.

The authors introduce sampling techniques and analyze their theoretical properties. They prove that, when used in stochastic gradient descent training, the techniques preserve the same convergence guarantees. This provides a theoretical basis for reducing work inside individual tensor operations while retaining the analyzed convergence behavior of the overall training procedure.

Experiments cover multilayer perceptrons and convolutional networks, on single machines and multiple nodes, using MNIST, CIFAR-10, and ImageNet. The reported improvements reach up to 66% less computation and communication and up to 1.37 times faster training, with negligible or no effect on final test accuracy. These are reported maxima across the evaluated settings; together they show that savings in operations can translate into practical training speedups.
summary.tldr: Sample-based tensor approximations reduce neural-network training work while preserving SGD convergence guarantees and largely maintaining tested accuracy.

title: Faster Neural Network Training with Approximate Tensor Operations

abstract: Bilevel optimization problems involve two nested objectives, where an upper-level objective depends on a solution to a lower-level problem. When the latter is non-convex, multiple critical points may be present, leading to an ambiguous definition of the problem. In this paper, we introduce a key ingredient for resolving this ambiguity through the concept of a selection map which allows one to choose a particular solution to the lower-level problem. Using such maps, we define a class of hierarchical games between two agents that resolve the ambiguity in bilevel problems. This new class of games requires introducing new analytical tools in Morse theory to extend implicit differentiation, a technique used in bilevel optimization resulting from the implicit function theorem. In particular, we establish the validity of such a method even when the latter theorem is inapplicable due to degenerate critical points.Finally, we show that algorithms for solving bilevel problems based on unrolled optimization solve these games up to approximation errors due to finite computational power. A simple correction to these algorithms is then proposed for removing these errors.

paragraphs: Bilevel optimization nests one optimization problem inside another: the upper objective depends on a solution produced by the lower problem. If the lower problem is non-convex, it may have several critical points. Without specifying which one is selected, the upper problem can be ambiguous because different lower-level outcomes can lead to different decisions.

This paper introduces selection maps that specify a particular lower-level solution. Using these maps, the authors define hierarchical games between two agents. They develop analytical tools from Morse theory to extend implicit differentiation, establishing its validity even in the presence of degenerate critical points where the usual implicit function theorem cannot be applied.

The paper also connects this formulation to algorithms that differentiate through a finite sequence of optimization steps. It shows that such unrolled algorithms solve the proposed games up to approximation errors arising from finite computation. The authors then propose a simple correction to remove those errors. The contribution clarifies both which problem these algorithms address and how their approximate computations relate to it.
summary.tldr: Selection maps resolve ambiguity in non-convex bilevel problems and support extended differentiation theory and corrected unrolled algorithms.

title: Non-Convex Bilevel Games with Critical Point Selection Maps

abstract: Single-index models are a class of functions given by an unknown univariate ``link'' function applied to an unknown one-dimensional projection of the input. These models are particularly relevant in high dimension, when the data might present low-dimensional structure that learning algorithms should adapt to. While several statistical aspects of this model, such as the sample complexity of recovering the relevant (one-dimensional) subspace, are well-understood, they rely on tailored algorithms that exploit the specific structure of the target function. In this work, we introduce a natural class of shallow neural networks and study its ability to learn single-index models via gradient flow. More precisely, we consider shallow networks in which biases of the neurons are frozen at random initialization. We show that the corresponding optimization landscape is benign, which in turn leads to generalization guarantees that match the near-optimal sample complexity of dedicated semi-parametric methods.

paragraphs: A single-index model reduces a potentially high-dimensional input to one projection, then applies an unknown one-variable function to that projection. Both the relevant direction and the function must be learned. This captures situations where many measured variables conceal a much simpler predictive structure, making adaptation to that structure valuable.

Existing statistical understanding includes methods tailored specifically to single-index models. The paper instead studies whether a natural class of shallow neural networks can learn them through gradient flow. A defining feature of the analyzed networks is that neuron biases remain fixed at their random initial values. The result therefore concerns a particular network and training setup.

The authors show that this setup has a benign optimization landscape and derive generalization guarantees from that property. The guarantees match the near-optimal sample complexity of dedicated semi-parametric methods. This connects the behavior of neural-network training to statistical efficiency: in the studied setting, a shallow network can exploit the hidden one-dimensional structure with comparable data requirements.
summary.tldr: Shallow networks with randomly fixed biases can learn single-index models through gradient flow with near-optimal sample-complexity guarantees.

title: Learning single-index models with shallow neural networks

abstract: Modeling directed graphs with differentiable representations is a fundamental requirement for performing machine learning on graph-structured data. Geometric embedding models (e.g. hyperbolic, cone, and box embeddings) excel at this task, exhibiting useful inductive biases for directed graphs. However, modeling directed graphs that both contain cycles and some element of transitivity, two properties common in real-world settings, is challenging. Box embeddings, which can be thought of as representing the graph as an intersection over some learned super-graphs, have a natural inductive bias toward modeling transitivity, but (as we prove) cannot model cycles. To this end, we propose binary code box embeddings, where a learned binary code selects a subset of graphs for intersection. We explore several variants, including global binary codes (amounting to a union over intersections) and per-vertex binary codes (allowing greater flexibility) as well as methods of regularization. Theoretical and empirical results show that the proposed models not only preserve a useful inductive bias of transitivity but also have sufficient representational capacity to model arbitrary graphs, including graphs with cycles.

paragraphs: Directed graphs can contain both transitive relationships and cycles. Transitivity means that relationships can carry through intermediate vertices, while cycles create paths that return to their starting point. Learning representations that accommodate both is challenging. The paper shows that standard box embeddings have a useful bias toward transitivity but cannot model cycles.

The authors interpret box embeddings as representing a graph through intersections of learned super-graphs. Their extension adds learned binary codes that select which graphs participate in an intersection. They explore global codes, which produce a union of intersections, and codes assigned to individual vertices, which provide greater flexibility. They also investigate regularization methods.

Theoretical and empirical results show that binary code box embeddings preserve a useful transitivity bias while having enough representational capacity to model arbitrary graphs, including cyclic ones. This addresses the conflict between a helpful structural preference and an overly restrictive representation. The capacity result concerns what the model can express; the empirical results also examine the proposed constructions in practice.
summary.tldr: Learned binary codes extend box embeddings to represent cyclic graphs while retaining a useful bias toward transitivity.

title: Modeling Transitivity and Cyclicity in Directed Graphs via Binary Code Box Embeddings

abstract: Existing pipelines of semantic correspondence commonly include extracting high-level semantic features for the invariance against intra-class variations and background clutters. This architecture, however, inevitably results in a low-resolution matching field that additionally requires an ad-hoc interpolation process as a post-processing for converting it into a high-resolution one, certainly limiting the overall performance of matching results. To overcome this, inspired by recent success of implicit neural representation, we present a novel method for semantic correspondence, called Neural Matching Field (NeMF). However, complicacy and high-dimensionality of a 4D matching field are the major hindrances, which we propose a cost embedding network to process a coarse cost volume to use as a guidance for establishing high-precision matching field through the following fully-connected network. Nevertheless, learning a high-dimensional matching field remains challenging mainly due to computational complexity, since a na\"ive exhaustive inference would require querying from all pixels in the 4D space to infer pixel-wise correspondences. To overcome this, we propose adequate training and inference procedures, which in the training phase, we randomly sample matching candidates and in the inference phase, we iteratively performs PatchMatch-based inference and coordinate optimization at test time. With these combined, competitive results are attained on several standard benchmarks for semantic correspondence. Code and pre-trained weights are available at~\url{https://ku-cvlab.github.io/NeMF/}.

paragraphs: Semantic correspondence matches related locations across images despite differences in appearance and background. Existing pipelines extract high-level features, but these often produce coarse matching fields that must be interpolated afterward. Neural Matching Fields, or NeMF, aims to represent more precise correspondences directly through an implicit neural representation.

The matching field is four-dimensional because it relates positions in two images. To manage its complexity, a cost-embedding network processes a coarse cost volume and guides a fully connected network that represents the finer matching field. This preserves coarse matching evidence while using a neural representation to establish higher-precision relationships.

Evaluating every possible pair of pixels would still be computationally expensive. NeMF therefore samples matching candidates randomly during training and combines iterative PatchMatch-based inference with coordinate optimization at test time. The authors report competitive results on several standard semantic-correspondence benchmarks. The contribution pairs a continuous matching representation with procedures that make training and querying the high-dimensional field more manageable.
summary.tldr: NeMF represents visual correspondences implicitly and uses targeted training and inference to handle a high-dimensional matching field.

title: Neural Matching Fields: Implicit Representation of Matching Fields for Visual Correspondence

abstract: Massive amounts of data are naturally dispersed over different clients in many real-world applications, collaborative learning has been a promising paradigm that allows to learn models through collaboration among the clients. However, leveraging these dispersed data to learn good models is still challenging since data over different clients are heterogeneous. Previous works mainly focus on learning the centralized model for all clients or learning a personalized model for each client. When there are numerous clients, the centralized model performs badly on some clients, while learning a personalized model for each client costs unaffordable computational resources. In this paper, we propose the collaborative learning method to detect collaboration partners and adaptively learn $K$ models for numerous heterogeneous clients. We theoretically prove that the model learned for each client is a good approximation of its personalized model. Experimental results on real-world datasets verify the effectiveness of our method.

paragraphs: Collaborative learning draws on data held by different clients, but those clients may have substantially different data distributions. A single shared model can consequently serve some clients poorly. Training a separate personalized model for every client addresses a different objective, but the computational burden can become unaffordable when the client population is large.

This paper proposes detecting suitable collaboration partners and adaptively learning K models for the clients. The important choice is therefore not simply whether clients collaborate, but which clients should learn together. Maintaining a collection of models gives the method a way to accommodate heterogeneity without requiring a distinct model for every individual client.

The authors theoretically establish that the model learned for each client is a good approximation to that client's personalized model. Experiments on real-world datasets also support the method's effectiveness. Together, these findings motivate selecting collaboration partners as a way to balance individualized learning needs against the resources required to train many models.
summary.tldr: Detecting collaboration partners lets heterogeneous clients share K models while theoretically approximating their individual personalized models.

title: Collaborative Learning by Detecting Collaboration Partners

abstract: Large sequence models (SM) such as GPT series and BERT have displayed outstanding performance and generalization capabilities in natural language process, vision and recently reinforcement learning. A natural follow-up question is how to abstract multi-agent decision making also as an sequence modeling problem and benefit from the prosperous development of the SMs. In this paper, we introduce a novel architecture named Multi-Agent Transformer (MAT) that effectively casts cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) into SM problems wherein the objective is to map agents' observation sequences to agents' optimal action sequences. Our goal is to build the bridge between MARL and SMs so that the modeling power of modern sequence models can be unleashed for MARL. Central to our MAT is an encoder-decoder architecture which leverages the multi-agent advantage decomposition theorem to transform the joint policy search problem into a sequential decision making process; this renders only linear time complexity for multi-agent problems and, most importantly, endows MAT with monotonic performance improvement guarantee. Unlike prior arts such as Decision Transformer fit only pre-collected offline data, MAT is trained by online trial and error from the environment in an on-policy fashion. To validate MAT, we conduct extensive experiments on StarCraftII, Multi-Agent MuJoCo, Dexterous Hands Manipulation, and Google Research Football benchmarks. Results demonstrate that MAT achieves superior performance and data efficiency compared to strong baselines including MAPPO and HAPPO. Furthermore, we demonstrate that MAT is an excellent few-short learner on unseen tasks regardless of changes in the number of agents.See our project page at https://sites.google.com/view/multi-agent-transformer.

paragraphs: Cooperative multi-agent learning requires choosing actions that work well together across several agents. Multi-Agent Transformer, or MAT, reformulates this problem as mapping a sequence of agents' observations to a sequence of actions. This makes sequence-modeling machinery directly applicable to coordinated decision making.

MAT uses an encoder-decoder architecture and a multi-agent advantage decomposition theorem to turn joint policy search into a sequential decision process. The paper attributes linear time complexity and a monotonic performance-improvement guarantee to this construction. Training takes place through online interaction with the environment using the current policy, rather than fitting only a previously collected offline dataset.

Experiments span StarCraftII, Multi-Agent MuJoCo, Dexterous Hands Manipulation, and Google Research Football. The authors report better performance and data efficiency than strong baselines, including MAPPO and HAPPO. They also report strong few-shot learning on unseen tasks with changed agent counts. These results support the usefulness of the sequence formulation for both coordination and transfer in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: MAT casts cooperative multi-agent learning as sequence prediction, combining a performance-improvement guarantee with strong reported coordination and transfer results.

title: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning is a Sequence Modeling Problem

abstract: Many classification problems consider classes that form a hierarchy. Classifiers that are aware of this hierarchy may be able to make confident predictions at a coarse level despite being uncertain at the fine-grained level. While it is generally possible to vary the granularity of predictions using a threshold at inference time, most contemporary work considers only leaf-node prediction, and almost no prior work has compared methods at multiple operating points. We present an efficient algorithm to produce operating characteristic curves for any method that assigns a score to every class in the hierarchy. Applying this technique to evaluate existing methods reveals that top-down classifiers are dominated by a naive flat softmax classifier across the entire operating range. We further propose two novel loss functions and show that a soft variant of the structured hinge loss is able to significantly outperform the flat baseline. Finally, we investigate the poor accuracy of top-down classifiers and demonstrate that they perform relatively well on unseen classes.

paragraphs: In hierarchical classification, labels range from broad categories to fine-grained classes. A classifier may be uncertain about a specific class while still confident about a broader category containing it. The paper studies how methods behave as the prediction threshold changes, allowing predictions at different levels of specificity.

The authors introduce an efficient algorithm for producing operating characteristic curves for any method that scores every class in the hierarchy. This enables comparison across multiple operating points instead of concentrating only on predictions at leaf nodes. In their evaluation, a simple flat softmax classifier dominates top-down classifiers throughout the operating range.

The paper also proposes two loss functions. A soft version of the structured hinge loss significantly improves on the flat baseline, showing that the training objective can improve performance beyond that simple reference method. Further analysis finds that top-down classifiers perform relatively well on unseen classes despite their poor accuracy in the main comparison. Together, the findings make evaluation across granularity levels central to judging hierarchical classifiers and reveal a distinct strength of top-down methods.
summary.tldr: Evaluating hierarchical classifiers across prediction granularities reveals weaknesses in top-down methods and supports a stronger soft structured-hinge training objective.

title: Hierarchical classification at multiple operating points

abstract: The deployment constraints in practical applications necessitate the pruning of large-scale deep learning models, i.e., promoting their weight sparsity. As illustrated by the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH), pruning also has the potential of improving their generalization ability. At the core of LTH, iterative magnitude pruning (IMP) is the predominant pruning method to successfully find ‘winning tickets’. Yet, the computation cost of IMP grows prohibitively as the targeted pruning ratio increases. To reduce the computation overhead, various efficient ‘one-shot’ pruning methods have been developed, but these schemes are usually unable to find winning tickets as good as IMP. This raises the question of how to close the gap between pruning accuracy and pruning efficiency? To tackle it, we pursue the algorithmic advancement of model pruning. Specifically, we formulate the pruning problem from a fresh and novel viewpoint, bi-level optimization (BLO). We show that the BLO interpretation provides a technically-grounded optimization base for an efficient implementation of the pruning-retraining learning paradigm used in IMP. We also show that the proposed bi-level optimization-oriented pruning method (termed BiP) is a special class of BLO problems with a bi-linear problem structure. By leveraging such bi-linearity, we theoretically show that BiP can be solved as easily as first-order optimization, thus inheriting the computation efficiency. Through extensive experiments on both structured and unstructured pruning with 5 model architectures and 4 data sets, we demonstrate that BiP can find better winning tickets than IMP in most cases, and is computationally as efficient as the one-shot pruning schemes, demonstrating $2-7\times$ speedup over IMP for the same level of model accuracy and sparsity.

paragraphs: Model pruning removes weights to make large neural networks easier to deploy. Iterative magnitude pruning repeatedly prunes and retrains a model to find effective sparse subnetworks, often called winning tickets. Its computational cost grows as more weights are removed. Faster one-shot methods address that cost, but typically produce weaker winning tickets, creating a trade-off between efficiency and accuracy.

This paper formulates pruning as bi-level optimization, giving the pruning and retraining process a joint mathematical foundation. The proposed method, BiP, has a particular bi-linear structure. The authors use that structure to show that solving the resulting problem can be as straightforward as first-order optimization, providing a route to efficient pruning without abandoning the pruning–retraining relationship.

Experiments cover structured and unstructured pruning across five architectures and four datasets. BiP finds better winning tickets than iterative magnitude pruning in most tested cases while achieving efficiency comparable to one-shot methods. At matched accuracy and sparsity, the reported speedup over iterative magnitude pruning is two to seven times.
summary.tldr: BiP uses bi-level optimization to find strong sparse subnetworks with reported two- to seven-fold speedups over iterative magnitude pruning.

title: Advancing Model Pruning via Bi-level Optimization

abstract: Incremental or continual learning has been extensively studied for image classification tasks to alleviate catastrophic forgetting, a phenomenon in which earlier learned knowledge is forgotten when learning new concepts. For class incremental semantic segmentation, such a phenomenon often becomes much worse due to the semantic shift of the background class, \ie, some concepts learned at previous stages are assigned to the background class at the current training stage, therefore, significantly reducing the performance of these old concepts. To address this issue, we propose a simple yet effective method in this paper, named Mining unseen Classes via Regional Objectness (MicroSeg). Our MicroSeg is based on the assumption that \emph{background regions with strong objectness possibly belong to those concepts in the historical or future stages}. Therefore, to avoid forgetting old knowledge at the current training stage, our MicroSeg first splits the given image into hundreds of segment proposals with a proposal generator. Those segment proposals with strong objectness from the background are then clustered and assigned new defined labels during the optimization. In this way, the distribution characterizes of old concepts in the feature space could be better perceived, relieving the catastrophic forgetting caused by the semantic shift of the background class accordingly. We conduct extensive experiments on Pascal VOC and ADE20K, and competitive results well demonstrate the effectiveness of our MicroSeg. Code is available at \href{https://github.com/zkzhang98/MicroSeg}{\textcolor{orange}{\texttt{https://github.com/zkzhang98/MicroSeg}}}.

paragraphs: In incremental semantic segmentation, a model learns new classes over successive training stages. Forgetting becomes particularly difficult when the meaning of background changes: objects learned previously can be labeled as background in the current stage. Training on those labels can weaken the model's knowledge of old concepts even though the corresponding objects remain visible.

MicroSeg starts from the assumption that background regions with strong objectness may represent concepts from earlier or future stages. A proposal generator first divides an image into hundreds of candidate segments. Background proposals with strong objectness are then clustered and assigned newly defined labels during optimization, giving these regions a more differentiated training role.

The intention is to preserve information about how old concepts are distributed in feature space, reducing forgetting caused by changing background semantics. The assumption is deliberately about possible membership in other-stage concepts, not certainty that every object-like region belongs to an old class. Competitive results on Pascal VOC and ADE20K support the effectiveness of this strategy for incremental segmentation.
summary.tldr: MicroSeg clusters object-like background regions into additional labels to reduce forgetting caused by shifting background meanings in incremental segmentation.

title: Mining Unseen Classes via Regional Objectness: A Simple Baseline for Incremental Segmentation

abstract: We prove new lower bounds for statistical estimation tasks under the constraint of $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-differential privacy. First, we provide tight lower bounds for private covariance estimation of Gaussian distributions. We show that estimating the covariance matrix in Frobenius norm requires $\Omega(d^2)$ samples, and in spectral norm requires $\Omega(d^{3/2})$ samples, both matching upper bounds up to logarithmic factors. We prove these bounds via our main technical contribution, a broad generalization of the fingerprinting method to exponential families. Additionally, using the private Assouad method of Acharya, Sun, and Zhang, we show a tight $\Omega(d/(\alpha^2 \varepsilon))$ lower bound for estimating the mean of a distribution with bounded covariance to $\alpha$-error in $\ell_2$-distance. Prior known lower bounds for all these problems were either polynomially weaker or held under the stricter condition of $(\varepsilon,0)$-differential privacy.

paragraphs: This paper establishes limits on statistical estimation under approximate differential privacy, expressed through epsilon and delta. A lower bound specifies how many samples a private method must have to achieve the relevant estimation objective. Such results help distinguish shortcomings of particular algorithms from sample requirements imposed by privacy and the statistical problem itself.

For Gaussian covariance estimation, the authors prove dimension-dependent lower bounds of order d squared under Frobenius-norm error and d to the three-halves under spectral-norm error. These match upper bounds up to logarithmic factors. The main technical contribution is a broad extension of the fingerprinting method to exponential families, which supplies the tool for proving these covariance bounds.

The paper also uses a private Assouad method to prove a tight lower bound of order d divided by alpha squared times epsilon for mean estimation with bounded covariance and alpha error in Euclidean distance. Earlier lower bounds were polynomially weaker or required pure differential privacy. The results therefore sharpen known sample requirements while covering the less restrictive approximate-privacy setting.
summary.tldr: The paper proves tight or nearly tight sample lower bounds for private covariance and mean estimation using an expanded fingerprinting technique.

title: New Lower Bounds for Private Estimation and a Generalized Fingerprinting Lemma

abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) have been studied over decades to incorporate their biological plausibility and leverage their promising energy efficiency. Throughout existing SNNs, the leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) model is commonly adopted to formulate the spiking neuron and evolves into numerous variants with different biological features. However, most LIF-based neurons support only single biological feature in different neuronal behaviors, limiting their expressiveness and neuronal dynamic diversity. In this paper, we propose GLIF, a unified spiking neuron, to fuse different bio-features in different neuronal behaviors, enlarging the representation space of spiking neurons. In GLIF, gating factors, which are exploited to determine the proportion of the fused bio-features, are learnable during training. Combining all learnable membrane-related parameters, our method can make spiking neurons different and constantly changing, thus increasing the heterogeneity and adaptivity of spiking neurons. Extensive experiments on a variety of datasets demonstrate that our method obtains superior performance compared with other SNNs by simply changing their neuronal formulations to GLIF. In particular, we train a spiking ResNet-19 with GLIF and achieve $77.35\%$ top-1 accuracy with six time steps on CIFAR-100, which has advanced the state-of-the-art. Codes are available at https://github.com/Ikarosy/Gated-LIF.

paragraphs: Spiking neural networks use neuron models that accumulate inputs and produce spikes. The widely used leaky integrate-and-fire formulation has many variants, but the paper argues that most support only one biological feature within a given neuronal behavior. That restriction limits the range of dynamics the neurons can express.

GLIF combines multiple biological features within a unified neuron formulation. Learnable gates determine the proportions in which those features contribute. Together with other trainable membrane-related parameters, these gates let neurons develop different behaviors and adapt during training. The architectural change therefore expands the representation available at the level of the individual spiking neuron.

Across several datasets, the authors report improved performance over other spiking networks by replacing their neuron formulations with GLIF. A spiking ResNet-19 using GLIF reaches 77.35% top-1 accuracy on CIFAR-100 with six time steps, reported as advancing the state of the art. These results support the value of richer, learnable neuronal dynamics; the abstract's energy-efficiency motivation is separate from these reported accuracy findings.
summary.tldr: GLIF uses learnable gates to combine biological neuron features, increasing spiking-network flexibility and improving reported classification performance.

title: GLIF: A Unified Gated Leaky Integrate-and-Fire Neuron for Spiking Neural Networks

abstract: Analyzing the distribution shift of data is a growing research direction in nowadays Machine Learning (ML), leading to emerging new benchmarks that focus on providing a suitable scenario for studying the generalization properties of ML models. The existing benchmarks are focused on supervised learning, and to the best of our knowledge, there is none for unsupervised learning. Therefore, we introduce an unsupervised anomaly detection benchmark with data that shifts over time, built over Kyoto-2006+, a traffic dataset for network intrusion detection. This type of data meets the premise of shifting the input distribution: it covers a large time span (10 years), with naturally occurring changes over time (e.g. users modifying their behavior patterns, and software updates). We first highlight the non-stationary nature of the data, using a basic per-feature analysis, t-SNE, and an Optimal Transport approach for measuring the overall distribution distances between years. Next, we propose AnoShift, a protocol splitting the data in IID, NEAR, and FAR testing splits. We validate the performance degradation over time with diverse models, ranging from classical approaches to deep learning. Finally, we show that by acknowledging the distribution shift problem and properly addressing it, the performance can be improved compared to the classical training which assumes independent and identically distributed data (on average, by up to 3% for our approach). Dataset and code are available at https://github.com/bit-ml/AnoShift/.

paragraphs: An anomaly detector can face different data after deployment than it encountered during training. AnoShift makes this problem measurable for unsupervised anomaly detection using Kyoto-2006+, a network traffic dataset spanning ten years. Changes in user behavior and software provide naturally occurring shifts, giving the benchmark a temporal basis for evaluating generalization.

The authors examine those changes through individual features, t-SNE visualizations, and Optimal Transport measurements of distribution differences between years. They then define a testing protocol with IID, NEAR, and FAR splits. These divisions let researchers assess performance under different degrees of separation from the training distribution within one organized benchmark.

Tests involving both classical and deep learning models show performance deteriorating over time. The authors also demonstrate that addressing distribution shift can improve results relative to training that assumes independently drawn data from one unchanged distribution, reporting average improvements of up to 3% for their approach. The benchmark therefore exposes a practical weakness while providing a setting for measuring attempts to address it.
summary.tldr: AnoShift benchmarks how unsupervised anomaly detectors handle naturally changing network traffic over time.

title: AnoShift: A Distribution Shift Benchmark for Unsupervised Anomaly Detection

abstract: As the model size grows rapidly, fine-tuning the large pre-trained language model has become increasingly difficult due to its extensive memory usage. Previous works usually focus on reducing the number of trainable parameters in the network. While the model parameters do contribute to memory usage, the primary memory bottleneck during training arises from storing feature maps, also known as activations, as they are crucial for gradient calculation. Notably, machine learning models are typically trained using stochastic gradient descent.We argue that in stochastic optimization, models can handle noisy gradients as long as the gradient estimator is unbiased with reasonable variance.Following this motivation, we propose a new family of unbiased estimators called \sas, for matrix production with reduced variance, which only requires storing the sub-sampled activations for calculating the gradient.Our work provides both theoretical and experimental evidence that, in the context of tuning transformers, our proposed estimators exhibit lower variance compared to existing ones.By replacing the linear operation with our approximated one in transformers, we can achieve up to 2.7X peak memory reduction with almost no accuracy drop and enables up to $6.4\times$ larger batch size.Under the same hardware, \sas enables better down-streaming task performance by applying larger models and/or faster training speed with larger batch sizes.The code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/WTACRS-A5C5/.
