Previous works usually focus on reducing the number of trainable parameters in the network. While the model parameters do contribute to memory usage, the primary memory bottleneck during training arises from storing feature maps, also known as activations, as they are crucial for gradient calculation. Notably, machine learning models are typically trained using stochastic gradient descent.We argue that in stochastic optimization, models can handle noisy gradients as long as the gradient estimator is unbiased with reasonable variance.Following this motivation, we propose a new family of unbiased estimators called \sas, for matrix production with reduced variance, which only requires storing the sub-sampled activations for calculating the gradient.Our work provides both theoretical and experimental evidence that, in the context of tuning transformers, our proposed estimators exhibit lower variance compared to existing ones.By replacing the linear operation with our approximated one in transformers, we can achieve up to 2.7X peak memory reduction with almost no accuracy drop and enables up to $6.4\times$ larger batch size.Under the same hardware, \sas enables better down-streaming task performance by applying larger models and/or faster training speed with larger batch sizes.The code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/WTACRS-A5C5/.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning large language models requires memory for more than their trainable weights. The authors identify stored activations, which are needed for gradient calculations, as the primary training-memory bottleneck. Their approach reduces how much activation information must be retained by accepting carefully controlled noise in the gradient calculation.

The paper introduces unbiased estimators for matrix multiplication that require only sampled activations. Its motivation is that stochastic optimization can tolerate noisy gradients when estimates remain unbiased and their variance is reasonable. Both theoretical analysis and transformer-tuning experiments indicate lower estimator variance than existing alternatives.

Replacing transformer linear operations with the proposed approximation yields up to a 2.7-fold reduction in peak memory use with almost no accuracy loss, and permits batches up to 6.4 times larger. Under the same hardware constraints, the authors report improved downstream performance through larger models or faster training through larger batches. The contribution targets activation storage directly while using estimator design to control the optimization noise introduced by sampling.
summary.tldr: Unbiased, lower-variance sampling estimators reduce activation storage during transformer tuning, enabling substantial memory savings with little reported accuracy loss.

title: Winner-Take-All Column Row Sampling for Memory Efficient Adaptation of Language Model

abstract: We study the problem of Federated Learning (FL) under client subsampling and data heterogeneity with an objective function that has potentially unbounded smoothness. This problem is motivated by empirical evidence that the class of relaxed smooth functions, where the Lipschitz constant of the gradient scales linearly with the gradient norm, closely resembles the loss functions of certain neural networks such as recurrent neural networks (RNNs) with possibly exploding gradient. We introduce EPISODE++, the first algorithm to solve this problem. It maintains historical statistics for each client to construct control variates and decide clipping behavior for sampled clients in the current round. We prove that EPISODE++ achieves linear speedup in the number of participating clients, reduced communication rounds, and resilience to data heterogeneity. Our upper bound proof relies on novel techniques of recursively bounding the client updates under unbounded smoothness and client subsampling, together with a refined high probability analysis. In addition, we prove a lower bound showing that the convergence rate of a special case of clipped minibatch SGD (without randomness in the stochastic gradient and with randomness in client subsampling) suffers from an explicit dependence on the maximum gradient norm of the objective in a sublevel set, which may be large. This effectively demonstrates that applying gradient clipping to minibatch SGD in our setting does not eliminate the problem of exploding gradients. Our lower bound is based on new constructions of hard instances tailored to client subsampling and a novel analysis of the trajectory of the algorithm in the presence of clipping. Lastly, we provide an experimental evaluation of EPISODE++ when training RNNs on federated text classification tasks, demonstrating that EPISODE++ outperforms strong baselines in FL. The code is available at https://github.com/MingruiLiu-ML-Lab/episode_plusplus.

paragraphs: Federated training becomes harder when only some clients participate in each round, their data differs, and gradients can grow sharply. This paper studies these issues together under relaxed smoothness: the gradient’s rate of change can scale with its magnitude. The setting is motivated by loss functions of certain neural networks, including recurrent networks with potentially exploding gradients.

The proposed algorithm, EPISODE++, keeps historical statistics for each client. It uses them to construct correction terms called control variates and to decide how to clip updates from currently sampled clients. The analysis proves linear speedup with the number of participating clients, fewer communication rounds, and resilience to heterogeneous data within the studied setting.

summary.tldr: EPISODE++ uses client history to stabilize federated training with partial participation, heterogeneous data, and potentially unbounded smoothness.

title: Federated Learning with Client Subsampling, Data Heterogeneity, and Unbounded Smoothness: A New Algorithm and Lower Bounds

abstract: We propose a robust and reliable evaluation metric for generative models called Topological Precision and Recall (TopP&R, pronounced “topper”), which systematically estimates supports by retaining only topologically and statistically significant features with a certain level of confidence. Existing metrics, such as Inception Score (IS), Frechet Inception Distance (FID), and various Precision and Recall (P&R) variants, rely heavily on support estimates derived from sample features. However, the reliability of these estimates has been overlooked, even though the quality of the evaluation hinges entirely on their accuracy. In this paper, we demonstrate that current methods not only fail to accurately assess sample quality when support estimation is unreliable, but also yield inconsistent results. In contrast, TopP&R reliably evaluates the sample quality and ensures statistical consistency in its results. Our theoretical and experimental findings reveal that TopP&R provides a robust evaluation, accurately capturing the true trend of change in samples, even in the presence of outliers and non-independent and identically distributed (Non-IID) perturbations where other methods result in inaccurate support estimations. To our knowledge, TopP&R is the first evaluation metric specifically focused on the robust estimation of supports, offering statistical consistency under noise conditions.

paragraphs: Evaluating a generative model requires judging both sample quality and the range of outputs it produces. Many metrics depend on estimating the support of sample features: the regions occupied by the underlying distributions. This paper argues that unreliable support estimates can undermine the evaluation itself, causing existing metrics to misjudge quality or produce inconsistent results.

Topological Precision and Recall, or TopP&R, makes support estimation the central design concern. It retains features that are significant both topologically and statistically at a specified confidence level. The aim is to base fidelity and diversity assessment on supported structure in the samples, reducing the influence of unreliable features in the estimated distributions.

The authors provide theoretical and experimental findings supporting robust evaluation and statistical consistency under noise conditions. Their results show that TopP&R captures the direction of changes in sample quality in the presence of outliers and non-IID perturbations, where compared methods produce inaccurate support estimates. This connects the reliability of a generative-model score to the quality of the distributional structure used to calculate it.
summary.tldr: TopP&R improves generative-model evaluation by estimating distribution supports robustly using topological and statistical significance.

title: TopP&R: Robust Support Estimation Approach for Evaluating Fidelity and Diversity in Generative Models

abstract: Learning to navigate to an image-specified goal is an important but challenging task for autonomous systems like household robots. The agent is required to well understand and reason the location of the navigation goal from a picture shot in the goal position. Existing methods try to solve this problem by learning a navigation policy, which captures semantic features of the goal image and observation image independently and lastly fuses them for predicting a sequence of navigation actions. However, these methods suffer from two major limitations. 1) They may miss detailed information in the goal image, and thus fail to reason the goal location. 2) More critically, it is hard to focus on the goal-relevant regions in the observation image, because they attempt to understand observation without goal conditioning. In this paper, we aim to overcome these limitations by designing a Fine-grained Goal Prompting (\sexyname) method for image-goal navigation. In particular, we leverage fine-grained and high-resolution feature maps in the goal image as prompts to perform conditioned embedding, which preserves detailed information in the goal image and guides the observation encoder to pay attention to goal-relevant regions. Compared with existing methods on the image-goal navigation benchmark, our method brings significant performance improvement on 3 benchmark datasets (\textit{i.e.,} Gibson, MP3D, and HM3D). Especially on Gibson, we surpass the state-of-the-art success rate by 8\% with only 1/50 model size.

paragraphs: Image-goal navigation asks an agent to reach a location specified by a picture taken there. The agent must connect details in that target picture with its current observations. Existing methods often encode the goal and observation separately, combining their features only when predicting navigation actions.

FGPrompt addresses two weaknesses of that arrangement: losing detailed goal information and interpreting the current view without knowing which regions matter for the goal. It uses high-resolution, fine-grained feature maps from the goal image as prompts that condition observation encoding. Goal information therefore influences how the current scene is represented, preserving details and directing attention toward relevant regions.

The authors report significant improvements on Gibson, MP3D, and HM3D. On Gibson, they report an 8% improvement over the state-of-the-art success rate while using a model one-fiftieth the size. These results support the value of introducing detailed goal information into observation processing itself. In the evaluated settings, this design improves navigation performance while also enabling a much smaller model.
summary.tldr: FGPrompt conditions visual observation encoding on detailed goal-image features, improving image-goal navigation with a substantially smaller model on Gibson.

title: FGPrompt: Fine-grained Goal Prompting for Image-goal Navigation

abstract: We consider the problem of idempotent learned image compression (LIC).The idempotence of codec refers to the stability of codec to re-compression.To achieve idempotence, previous codecs adopt invertible transforms such as DCT and normalizing flow.In this paper, we first identify that invertibility of transform is sufficient but not necessary for idempotence. Instead, it can be relaxed into right-invertibility. And such relaxation allows wider family of transforms.Based on this identification, we implement an idempotent codec using our proposed blocked convolution and null-space enhancement.Empirical results show that we achieve state-of-the-art rate-distortion performance among idempotent codecs. Furthermore, our codec can be extended into near-idempotent codec by relaxing the right-invertibility. And this near-idempotent codec has significantly less quality decay after $50$ rounds of re-compression compared with other near-idempotent codecs.

paragraphs: Repeated image compression can progressively change an image. An idempotent codec is designed to remain stable when its output is compressed again. Earlier approaches achieved this using invertible transforms, but this paper shows that full invertibility is a sufficient condition rather than a necessary requirement for that stability.

The authors identify right-invertibility as a weaker condition that can support idempotence. Relaxing the requirement makes a wider family of transforms available for codec design. They build a learned codec around this observation using blocked convolution and null-space enhancement, turning the mathematical distinction into a concrete compression method.

Experiments report state-of-the-art rate-distortion performance among idempotent codecs, meaning a favorable balance between compressed size and reconstruction quality. The authors also relax right-invertibility to create a near-idempotent version. After 50 recompression rounds, that version shows substantially less quality decay than the other near-idempotent codecs compared. These results distinguish exact recompression stability from an approximate variant that empirically limits accumulated degradation.
summary.tldr: Right-invertible transforms enable a broader class of recompression-stable learned codecs with strong reported rate-distortion performance.

title: Idempotent Learned Image Compression with Right-Inverse

abstract: Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) is a sub-domain of classification problems with positive and negative labels and a "bag" of inputs, where the label is positive if and only if a positive element is contained within the bag, and otherwise is negative. Training in this context requires associating the bag-wide label to instance-level information, and implicitly contains a causal assumption and asymmetry to the task (i.e., you can't swap the labels without changing the semantics). MIL problems occur in healthcare (one malignant cell indicates cancer), cyber security (one malicious executable makes an infected computer), and many other tasks. In this work, we examine five of the most prominent deep-MIL models and find that none of them respects the standard MIL assumption. They are able to learn anti-correlated instances, i.e., defaulting to "positive" labels until seeing a negative counter-example, which should not be possible for a correct MIL model. We suspect that enhancements and other works derived from these models will share the same issue. In any context in which these models are being used, this creates the potential for learning incorrect models, which creates risk of operational failure. We identify and demonstrate this problem via a proposed ``algorithmic unit test'', where we create synthetic datasets that can be solved by a MIL respecting model, and which clearly reveal learning that violates MIL assumptions. The five evaluated methods each fail one or more of these tests. This provides a model-agnostic way to identify violations of modeling assumptions, which we hope will be useful for future development and evaluation of MIL models.

paragraphs: In standard multiple instance learning, an example is a bag of items. A bag is positive exactly when it contains at least one positive item. This rule creates an asymmetry: evidence for a positive item determines the bag’s label, and swapping the meaning of positive and negative changes the task. The paper examines whether prominent deep-learning models respect that assumption.

The authors evaluate five deep multiple instance learning models and find that none consistently adheres to the standard rule. The models can learn the opposite pattern, treating bags as positive until a negative counterexample appears. Such behavior can fit correlations while violating the intended relationship between individual items and the bag label.

To reveal this problem, the authors propose algorithmic unit tests using synthetic datasets solvable by models that respect the assumption. Each evaluated method fails at least one test. The tests offer a model-agnostic way to check semantic behavior beyond predictive performance. The authors suspect related models may share the issue, while their demonstrated findings concern the five examined methods.
summary.tldr: Synthetic algorithmic unit tests show that five prominent deep multiple instance learning models can violate the task’s defining label assumption.

title: Reproducibility in Multiple Instance Learning: A Case For Algorithmic Unit Tests

abstract: Learning to control unknown nonlinear dynamical systems is a fundamental problem in reinforcement learning and control theory. A commonly applied approach is to first explore the environment (exploration), learn an accurate model of it (system identification), and then compute an optimal controller with the minimum cost on this estimated system (policy optimization). While existing work has shown that it is possible to learn a uniformly good model of the system (Mania et al., 2020), in practice, if we aim to learn a good controller with a low cost on the actual system, certain system parameters may be significantly more critical than others, and we therefore ought to focus our exploration on learning such parameters.In this work, we consider the setting of nonlinear dynamical systems and seek to formally quantify, in such settings, (a) which parameters are most relevant to learning a good controller, and (b) how we can best explore so as to minimize uncertainty in such parameters. Inspired by recent work in linear systems (Wagenmaker et al., 2021), we show that minimizing the controller loss in nonlinear systems translates to estimating the system parameters in a particular, task-dependent metric. Motivated by this, we develop an algorithm able to efficiently explore the system to reduce uncertainty in this metric, and prove a lower bound showing that our approach learns a controller at a near-instance-optimal rate. Our algorithm relies on a general reduction from policy optimization to optimal experiment design in arbitrary systems, and may be of independent interest. We conclude with experiments demonstrating the effectiveness of our method in realistic nonlinear robotic systems.

paragraphs: Learning a model of an unknown dynamical system is useful for control, but some modeling errors matter more to the eventual controller than others. This paper studies how exploration should prioritize those consequential uncertainties in nonlinear systems. Its objective is to learn a controller with low cost on the actual system.

The authors show that minimizing controller loss corresponds to estimating system parameters under a task-dependent metric. This metric expresses which parameter errors are important for the control objective. They then develop an exploration algorithm that reduces uncertainty in that metric, connecting data collection directly to the quality of the controller that will be learned.

A lower-bound analysis establishes that the method learns a controller at a near-instance-optimal rate, relating its efficiency to the difficulty of the particular system. The algorithm uses a general reduction from policy optimization to optimal experiment design in arbitrary systems. Experiments on realistic nonlinear robotic systems demonstrate its effectiveness. Together, the theory and experiments support directing exploration toward control-relevant information instead of treating every parameter as equally important.
summary.tldr: Task-dependent exploration targets the system parameters most relevant to control and achieves a near-instance-optimal learning rate.

title: Optimal Exploration for Model-Based RL in Nonlinear Systems

abstract: Recent work has demonstrated the effectiveness of formulating decision making as supervised learning on offline-collected trajectories. Powerful sequence models, such as GPT or BERT, are often employed to encode the trajectories. However, the benefits of performing sequence modeling on trajectory data remain unclear. In this work, we investigate whether sequence modeling has the ability to condense trajectories into useful representations that enhance policy learning. We adopt a two-stage framework that first leverages sequence models to encode trajectory-level representations, and then learns a goal-conditioned policy employing the encoded representations as its input. This formulation allows us to consider many existing supervised offline RL methods as specific instances of our framework. Within this framework, we introduce Goal-Conditioned Predictive Coding (GCPC), a sequence modeling objective that yields powerful trajectory representations and leads to performant policies. Through extensive empirical evaluations on AntMaze, FrankaKitchen and Locomotion environments, we observe that sequence modeling can have a significant impact on challenging decision making tasks. Furthermore, we demonstrate that GCPC learns a goal-conditioned latent representation encoding the future trajectory, which enables competitive performance on all three benchmarks.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning can treat decision-making as supervised learning from previously collected trajectories. Sequence models are often used to process those trajectories, but their specific contribution is not always clear. This paper asks whether they compress experience into representations that are useful for learning policies, separating the representation-learning question from the subsequent task of choosing actions.

The authors use a two-stage framework. First, a sequence model encodes trajectory-level representations. Second, a goal-conditioned policy learns with those representations as inputs. Several existing supervised approaches to offline reinforcement learning fit within this formulation. The paper introduces Goal-Conditioned Predictive Coding, or GCPC, as an objective for learning representations that encode future trajectories in relation to a goal.

Evaluations on AntMaze, FrankaKitchen, and Locomotion show that sequence modeling can substantially affect performance on challenging decision-making tasks. GCPC achieves competitive performance on all three benchmarks. The findings support the usefulness of goal-related future information in a learned representation, while the two-stage organization helps identify how sequence modeling contributes to policy learning.
summary.tldr: GCPC learns goal-conditioned representations of future trajectories that support competitive offline reinforcement learning across three benchmarks.

title: Goal-Conditioned Predictive Coding for Offline Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We introduce a novel grid-independent model for learning partial differential equations (PDEs) from noisy and partial observations on irregular spatiotemporal grids. We propose a space-time continuous latent neural PDE model with an efficient probabilistic framework and a novel encoder design for improved data efficiency and grid independence. The latent state dynamics are governed by a PDE model that combines the collocation method and the method of lines. We employ amortized variational inference for approximate posterior estimation and utilize a multiple shooting technique for enhanced training speed and stability. Our model demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on complex synthetic and real-world datasets, overcoming limitations of previous approaches and effectively handling partially-observed data. The proposed model outperforms recent methods, showing its potential to advance data-driven PDE modeling and enabling robust, grid-independent modeling of complex partially-observed dynamic processes across various domains.

paragraphs: Learning a dynamic process from observations is difficult when measurements are noisy, incomplete, and scattered irregularly across space and time. This paper introduces a neural partial differential equation model that operates independently of a fixed observation grid. It represents the underlying state continuously in space and time, allowing the model to address partially observed processes.

The approach combines a probabilistic framework with an encoder designed for data efficiency and grid independence. A PDE governs the latent state’s evolution, using a combination of collocation and the method of lines. Amortized variational inference estimates an approximate posterior, while multiple shooting is used to improve training speed and stability.

These components connect uncertain observations with a continuously evolving hidden representation. On complex synthetic and real-world datasets, the authors report state-of-the-art performance and improvements over recent methods, including effective handling of partial observations. The findings support the potential of this formulation for learning dynamic processes when the available measurements do not fit a complete, regular space-time grid.
summary.tldr: A continuous latent neural PDE model learns dynamic processes from noisy, partial observations on irregular space-time grids.

title: Learning Space-Time Continuous Latent Neural PDEs from Partially Observed States

abstract: The ability to collect a large dataset of human preferences from text-to-image users is usually limited to companies, making such datasets inaccessible to the public. To address this issue, we create a web app that enables text-to-image users to generate images and specify their preferences. Using this web app we build Pick-a-Pic, a large, open dataset of text-to-image prompts and real users’ preferences over generated images. We leverage this dataset to train a CLIP-based scoring function, PickScore, which exhibits superhuman performance on the task of predicting human preferences. Then, we test PickScore’s ability to perform model evaluation and observe that it correlates better with human rankings than other automatic evaluation metrics. Therefore, we recommend using PickScore for evaluating future text-to-image generation models, and using Pick-a-Pic prompts as a more relevant dataset than MS-COCO. Finally, we demonstrate how PickScore can enhance existing text-to-image models via ranking.

paragraphs: Large collections of user preferences for generated images are often held by companies and unavailable to other researchers. This paper introduces a web application where people generate images from text and indicate their preferences. The resulting open dataset, Pick-a-Pic, contains prompts and real users' judgments about generated images.

The authors use these data to train PickScore, a CLIP-based function that scores images according to predicted human preference. On the evaluated preference-prediction task, it achieves performance described as superhuman. That finding concerns predicting preference judgments, giving the scoring function a specific role in assessing how people are likely to respond to generated images.

When used to evaluate generation models, PickScore correlates more closely with human rankings than the other automatic metrics tested. The authors consequently recommend it for model evaluation and recommend Pick-a-Pic prompts as more relevant than MS-COCO prompts for this purpose. They also demonstrate that ranking generated outputs with PickScore can enhance existing text-to-image systems.
summary.tldr: Pick-a-Pic collects open user-preference data that enables PickScore to evaluate and rank generated images in closer agreement with human judgments.

title: Pick-a-Pic: An Open Dataset of User Preferences for Text-to-Image Generation

abstract: Finite-difference methods are a class of algorithms designed to solve black-box optimization problems by approximating a gradient of the target function on a set of directions. In black-box optimization, the non-smooth setting is particularly relevant since, in practice, differentiability and smoothness assumptions cannot be verified. To cope with nonsmoothness, several authors use a smooth approximation of the target function and show that finite difference methods approximate its gradient. Recently, it has been proved that imposing a structure in the directions allows improving performance. However, only the smooth setting was considered. To close this gap, we introduce and analyze O-ZD, the first structured finite-difference algorithm for non-smooth black-box optimization. Our method exploits a smooth approximation of the target function and we prove that it approximates its gradient on a subset of random {\em orthogonal} directions. We analyze the convergence of O-ZD under different assumptions. For non-smooth convex functions, we obtain the optimal complexity. In the non-smooth non-convex setting, we characterize the number of iterations needed to bound the expected norm of the smoothed gradient. For smooth functions, our analysis recovers existing results for structured zeroth-order methods for the convex case and extends them to the non-convex setting. We conclude with numerical simulations where assumptions are satisfied, observing that our algorithm has very good practical performances.

paragraphs: Black-box optimization searches for good solutions using function evaluations when gradients are unavailable. Finite-difference methods estimate gradients by comparing evaluations along selected directions. Nonsmooth functions complicate this strategy because a conventional gradient may not exist, and practical black-box settings may offer no way to verify smoothness assumptions.

The paper introduces O-ZD, which combines a smooth approximation of the objective with a structured choice of probing directions. Specifically, it uses a subset of random orthogonal directions and proves that the resulting estimates approximate the gradient of the smoothed function. The contribution extends the analysis of structured finite differences beyond the previously studied smooth setting.

The guarantees depend on the objective class. For nonsmooth convex functions, O-ZD achieves optimal complexity. For nonsmooth nonconvex functions, the analysis bounds the iterations required to control the expected size of the smoothed gradient. It also recovers smooth convex results and extends them to smooth nonconvex problems. Numerical simulations satisfying the assumptions show strong practical performance.
summary.tldr: O-ZD uses random orthogonal finite-difference directions to optimize nonsmooth black-box functions, achieving optimal complexity in the convex setting.

title: An Optimal Structured Zeroth-order Algorithm for Non-smooth Optimization

abstract: The projection operation is a critical component in a wide range of optimization algorithms, such as online gradient descent (OGD), for enforcing constraints and achieving optimal regret bounds. However, it suffers from computational complexity limitations in high-dimensional settings or when dealing with ill-conditioned constraint sets. Projection-free algorithms address this issue by replacing the projection oracle with more efficient optimization subroutines. But to date, these methods have been developed primarily in the Euclidean setting, and while there has been growing interest in optimization on Riemannian manifolds, there has been essentially no work in trying to utilize projection-free tools here. An apparent issue is that non-trivial affine functions are generally non-convex in such domains. In this paper, we present methods for obtaining sub-linear regret guarantees in online geodesically convex optimization on curved spaces for two scenarios: when we have access to (a) a separation oracle or (b) a linear optimization oracle. For geodesically convex losses, and when a separation oracle is available, our algorithms achieve $O(T^{\frac{1}{2}})$, $O(T^{\frac{3}{4}})$ and $O(T^{\frac{1}{2}})$ adaptive regret guarantees in the full information setting, the bandit setting with one-point feedback and the bandit setting with two-point feedback, respectively. When a linear optimization oracle is available, we obtain regret rates of $O(T^{\frac{3}{4}})$ for geodesically convex losses and $O(T^{\frac{2}{3}}\log T)$ for strongly geodesically convex losses.

paragraphs: Constrained online optimization often uses projection to keep decisions inside an allowed set, but that operation can be expensive. Projection-free methods replace it with other optimization tools. This paper extends that idea to curved Riemannian spaces, where familiar Euclidean arguments become difficult because nontrivial affine functions are generally non-convex.

The authors develop methods for geodesically convex losses under two kinds of oracle access: separation and linear optimization. With a separation oracle, they obtain adaptive regret of O(T^(1/2)) with full information, O(T^(3/4)) with one-point bandit feedback, and O(T^(1/2)) with two-point bandit feedback. The guarantees therefore distinguish how much feedback the learner receives.

With a linear optimization oracle, the regret rates are O(T^(3/4)) for geodesically convex losses and O(T^(2/3) log T) for strongly geodesically convex losses. These sublinear guarantees mean accumulated regret grows more slowly than the number of rounds. The contribution establishes projection-free online learning guarantees on curved spaces under the specified loss and oracle conditions.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes sublinear-regret projection-free online optimization on Riemannian spaces under specified oracle and geodesic-convexity conditions.

title: Riemannian Projection-free Online Learning

abstract: Segmenting untrimmed videos into chapters enables users to quickly navigate to the information of their interest. This important topic has been understudied due to the lack of publicly released datasets. To address this issue, we present VidChapters-7M, a dataset of 817K user-chaptered videos including 7M chapters in total. VidChapters-7M is automatically created from videos online in a scalable manner by scraping user-annotated chapters and hence without any additional manual annotation. We introduce the following three tasks based on this data. First, the video chapter generation task consists of temporally segmenting the video and generating a chapter title for each segment. To further dissect the problem, we also define two variants of this task: video chapter generation given ground-truth boundaries, which requires generating a chapter title given an annotated video segment, and video chapter grounding, which requires temporally localizing a chapter given its annotated title. We benchmark both simple baselines as well as state-of-the-art video-language models on these three tasks. We also show that pretraining on VidChapters-7M transfers well to dense video captioning tasks, largely improving the state of the art on the YouCook2 and ViTT benchmarks. Finally, our experiments reveal that downstream performance scales well with the size of the pretraining dataset.

paragraphs: Video chapters help viewers jump to information within long, untrimmed videos. Research on automatically producing them has been limited by a lack of public datasets. VidChapters-7M addresses this gap with 817,000 videos containing seven million chapters, collected from existing user annotations without additional manual labeling.

The paper defines three tasks that separate different parts of chapter creation. Full chapter generation requires finding segment boundaries and writing titles. A second task supplies the annotated boundaries and asks only for titles. Chapter grounding reverses that relationship: given an annotated title, the model must locate the corresponding interval in the video.

The authors evaluate simple baselines and state-of-the-art video-language models on all three tasks. They also show that pretraining on the dataset transfers well to dense video captioning, substantially improving the state of the art on YouCook2 and ViTT. Downstream performance improves with larger pretraining datasets in their experiments, supporting the value of scalable chapter collection for related video-understanding tasks.
summary.tldr: VidChapters-7M supplies seven million user-created video chapters, three evaluation tasks, and evidence that chapter pretraining benefits dense video captioning.

title: VidChapters-7M: Video Chapters at Scale

abstract: The remarkable capabilities of pretrained image diffusion models have been utilized not only for generating fixed-size images but also for creating panoramas. However, naive stitching of multiple images often results in visible seams. Recent techniques have attempted to address this issue by performing joint diffusions in multiple windows and averaging latent features in overlapping regions. However, these approaches, which focus on seamless montage generation, often yield incoherent outputs by blending different scenes within a single image. To overcome this limitation, we propose SyncDiffusion, a plug-and-play module that synchronizes multiple diffusions through gradient descent from a perceptual similarity loss. Specifically, we compute the gradient of the perceptual loss using the predicted denoised images at each denoising step, providing meaningful guidance for achieving coherent montages. Our experimental results demonstrate that our method produces significantly more coherent outputs compared to previous methods (66.35% vs. 33.65% in our user study) while still maintaining fidelity (as assessed by GIQA) and compatibility with the input prompt (as measured by CLIP score). We further demonstrate the versatility of our method across three plug-and-play applications: layout-guided image generation, conditional image generation and 360-degree panorama generation. Our project page is at https://syncdiffusion.github.io.

paragraphs: Generating a panorama from multiple diffusion windows requires more than hiding the seams between images. Even when overlapping latent features are averaged, the result can combine incompatible scenes into one montage. SyncDiffusion addresses this broader coherence problem by synchronizing the diffusion processes through a perceptual similarity objective.

At each denoising step, the method uses predicted denoised images to compute a perceptual loss and its gradient. Gradient descent then provides guidance for coordinating the multiple diffusions. The authors present this as a plug-and-play module, allowing coherence guidance to be added to a generation process. Using predicted clean images gives the similarity objective meaningful visual content throughout denoising.

The reported user study favors SyncDiffusion’s coherence over previous methods by 66.35% to 33.65%. The authors also report maintaining image fidelity and compatibility with the input prompt, assessed using GIQA and CLIP score. Demonstrations cover layout-guided generation, conditional generation, and 360-degree panoramas. These results support perceptual synchronization as a way to improve agreement across generated regions while preserving other evaluated aspects of image quality.
summary.tldr: SyncDiffusion coordinates multiple diffusion windows through perceptual gradients to produce more coherent panoramas and image montages.

title: SyncDiffusion: Coherent Montage via Synchronized Joint Diffusions

abstract: Reconstructing the 3D articulated shape of an animal from a single in-the-wild image is a challenging task. We propose LEPARD, a learning-based framework that discovers semantically meaningful 3D parts and reconstructs 3D shapes in a part-based manner. This is advantageous as 3D parts are robust to pose variations due to articulations and their shape is typically simpler than the overall shape of the object. In our framework, the parts are explicitly represented as parameterized primitive surfaces with global and local deformations in 3D that deform to match the image evidence. We propose a kinematics-inspired optimization to guide each transformation of the primitive deformation given 2D evidence. Similar to recent approaches, LEPARD is only trained using off-the-shelf deep features from DINO and does not require any form of 2D or 3D annotations. Experiments on 3D animal shape reconstruction, demonstrate significant improvement over existing alternatives in terms of both the overall reconstruction performance as well as the ability to discover semantically meaningful and consistent parts.

paragraphs: LEPARD reconstructs an animal’s articulated 3D shape from a single image taken in an uncontrolled setting. It approaches the animal as a collection of meaningful parts. This decomposition is useful because individual parts usually have simpler shapes than the entire animal and remain useful units of representation as articulation changes the overall pose.

The framework represents parts explicitly as parameterized primitive surfaces in three dimensions. Global and local deformations adjust these surfaces to match evidence in the image. An optimization procedure inspired by kinematics guides the transformations using two-dimensional evidence, connecting the reconstruction process to the movement and arrangement of the component parts.

Training uses existing DINO deep features and requires no 2D or 3D annotations. In animal reconstruction experiments, the authors report significant improvements over existing alternatives in both overall reconstruction and discovery of consistent, semantically meaningful parts. The findings support explicit part representations as a way to address shape and articulation together while avoiding the need for manually annotated training targets.
summary.tldr: LEPARD reconstructs articulated 3D animals through explicit deformable parts, learning from DINO features without 2D or 3D annotations.

title: LEPARD: Learning Explicit Part Discovery for 3D Articulated Shape Reconstruction

abstract: Contrastive representation learning is crucial in medical time series analysis as it alleviates dependency on labor-intensive, domain-specific, and scarce expert annotations. However, existing contrastive learning methods primarily focus on one single data level, which fails to fully exploit the intricate nature of medical time series. To address this issue, we present COMET, an innovative hierarchical framework that leverages data consistencies at all inherent levels in medical time series. Our meticulously designed model systematically captures data consistency from four potential levels: observation, sample, trial, and patient levels. By developing contrastive loss at multiple levels, we can learn effective representations that preserve comprehensive data consistency, maximizing information utilization in a self-supervised manner. We conduct experiments in the challenging patient-independent setting. We compare COMET against six baselines using three diverse datasets, which include ECG signals for myocardial infarction and EEG signals for Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s diseases. The results demonstrate that COMET consistently outperforms all baselines, particularly in setup with 10% and 1% labeled data fractions across all datasets. These results underscore the significant impact of our framework in advancing contrastive representation learning techniques for medical time series. The source code is available at https://github.com/DL4mHealth/COMET.

paragraphs: Medical time-series analysis often depends on scarce annotations that require specialist effort. Contrastive learning can reduce that dependence by learning representations from relationships within data. This paper argues that focusing on a single data level leaves useful structure unused, because medical recordings contain consistencies at several levels of organization.

COMET introduces a hierarchical framework with contrastive losses at four potential levels: observation, sample, trial, and patient. The approach aims to preserve these different forms of consistency within the learned representation. Its purpose is to make fuller use of the available data through self-supervision, so that subsequent learning can benefit even when only a small fraction has labels.

The evaluation uses a patient-independent setting and compares COMET with six baselines on three datasets. These include ECG data for myocardial infarction and EEG data for Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases. COMET outperforms all baselines across the datasets, with particularly strong results when labeled fractions are 10% or 1%. The findings support learning from multiple organizational levels when expert annotations are limited.
summary.tldr: COMET learns medical time-series representations through contrastive objectives at four levels, improving results especially when labels are scarce.

title: Contrast Everything: A Hierarchical Contrastive Framework for Medical Time-Series

abstract: We present a novel multi-agent RL approach, Selective Multi-Agent Prioritized Experience Relay, in which agents share with other agents a limited number of transitions they observe during training. The intuition behind this is that even a small number of relevant experiences from other agents could help each agent learn. Unlike many other multi-agent RL algorithms, this approach allows for largely decentralized training, requiring only a limited communication channel between agents. We show that our approach outperforms baseline no-sharing decentralized training and state-of-the art multi-agent RL algorithms. Further, sharing only a small number of highly relevant experiences outperforms sharing all experiences between agents, and the performance uplift from selective experience sharing is robust across a range of hyperparameters and DQN variants.

paragraphs: Agents learning separately may encounter experiences that would help one another. Sharing everything, however, is not the only way to benefit from that information. This paper introduces Selective Multi-Agent Prioritized Experience Relay, in which agents pass along a limited number of observed training transitions. Its guiding idea is that a small set of relevant experiences can improve another agent’s learning.

The approach supports largely decentralized training and requires only a limited communication channel between agents. Experience selection is therefore central to both the communication arrangement and the learning method. Each agent can benefit from observations gathered elsewhere without making unrestricted exchange of all experience the basis of training.

The reported experiments outperform both decentralized training without sharing and state-of-the-art multi-agent reinforcement learning algorithms. Selectively sharing a small number of highly relevant transitions also performs better than sharing every experience. The gains persist across a range of hyperparameters and DQN variants, supporting the usefulness of selective exchange across the tested configurations rather than only one narrowly chosen setup.
summary.tldr: Sharing a small set of relevant experiences improves the reported multi-agent learning results, outperforming both no sharing and sharing all experiences.

title: Selectively Sharing Experiences Improves Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

abstract: How neuronal circuits achieve credit assignment remains a central unsolved question in systems neuroscience. Various studies have suggested plausible solutions for back-propagating error signals through multi-layer networks. These purely functionally motivated models assume distinct neuronal compartments to represent local error signals that determine the sign of synaptic plasticity. However, this explicit error modulation is inconsistent with phenomenological plasticity models in which the sign depends primarily on postsynaptic activity. Here we show how a plausible microcircuit model and Hebbian learning rule derived within an adaptive control theory framework can resolve this discrepancy. Assuming errors are encoded in top-down dis-inhibitory synaptic afferents, we show that error-modulated learning emerges naturally at the circuit level when recurrent inhibition explicitly influences Hebbian plasticity. The same learning rule accounts for experimentally observed plasticity in the absence of inhibition and performs comparably to back-propagation of error (BP) on several non-linearly separable benchmarks. Our findings bridge the gap between functional and experimentally observed plasticity rules and make concrete predictions on inhibitory modulation of excitatory plasticity.

paragraphs: Neural credit assignment asks how individual connections receive information about their contribution to an error. Some proposed biological learning models assign local error signals to separate neuronal compartments, using those signals to determine whether a synapse strengthens or weakens. That account conflicts with phenomenological plasticity models in which the direction of change primarily depends on postsynaptic activity.

The paper develops a plausible microcircuit and a Hebbian learning rule within an adaptive control framework. Its key assumption is that errors are carried by top-down dis-inhibitory inputs. When recurrent inhibition explicitly affects Hebbian plasticity, error-dependent learning emerges through the circuit's behavior. This offers a mechanism connecting activity-dependent synaptic changes with error-based learning.

The same rule accounts for experimentally observed plasticity when inhibition is absent. It also performs comparably to backpropagation on several benchmarks requiring nonlinear separation. These findings support a bridge between functionally motivated learning models and observed plasticity rules under the proposed circuit assumptions. The model additionally produces concrete predictions about how inhibition modulates changes at excitatory synapses.
summary.tldr: A proposed inhibitory microcircuit makes error-modulated Hebbian learning emerge under an explicit assumption about how top-down inputs encode errors.

title: Dis-inhibitory neuronal circuits can control the sign of synaptic plasticity

abstract: Since its inception in 1982, Oja's algorithm has become an established method for streaming principle component analysis (PCA). We study the problem of streaming PCA, where the data-points are sampled from an irreducible, aperiodic, and reversible Markov chain starting in stationarity. Our goal is to estimate the top eigenvector of the unknown covariance matrix of the stationary distribution. This setting has implications in scenarios where data can solely be sampled from a Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) type algorithm, and the objective is to perform inference on parameters of the stationary distribution. Most convergence guarantees for Oja's algorithm in the literature assume that the data-points are sampled IID. For data streams with Markovian dependence, one typically downsamples the data to get a "nearly" independent data stream. In this paper, we obtain the first near-optimal rate for Oja's algorithm on the entire data, where we remove the logarithmic dependence on the sample size, $n$, resulting from throwing data away in downsampling strategies.

paragraphs: Streaming principal component analysis estimates a leading direction of variation while processing observations sequentially. Oja’s algorithm is an established method for this task, but much of its convergence theory assumes independent samples. This paper analyzes the more dependent setting in which observations are generated by a Markov chain.

The target is the top eigenvector of the covariance matrix of the chain’s stationary distribution. The analysis assumes an irreducible, aperiodic, reversible chain that starts in stationarity. Such a setting is relevant when observations can only be obtained through a Markov Chain Monte Carlo procedure and the desired inference concerns its stationary distribution.

A common response to dependence is to discard observations until the retained stream is nearly independent. The authors instead establish a near-optimal convergence rate for Oja’s algorithm using the entire stream. Their result removes the logarithmic dependence on sample size associated with those downsampling strategies. Under the stated chain assumptions, this provides theoretical support for retaining dependent observations when estimating the principal direction.
summary.tldr: For specified stationary Markov chains, Oja’s algorithm achieves a near-optimal streaming PCA rate without discarding observations to approximate independence.

title: Streaming PCA for Markovian Data

abstract: A major challenge in reinforcement learning is to develop practical, sample-efficient algorithms for exploration in high-dimensional domains where generalization and function approximation is required. Low-Rank Markov Decision Processes---where transition probabilities admit a low-rank factorization based on an unknown feature embedding---offer a simple, yet expressive framework for RL with function approximation, yet existing algorithms either (1) are computationally intractable, or (2) require restrictive statistical assumptions such as latent variable structure or access to model-based function approximation. In this work, we propose the first provably sample-efficient algorithm for exploration in Low-Rank MDPs that is both computationally efficient and model-free, allowing for general function approximation while requiring no structural assumptions beyond a reachability condition that we show is substantially weaker than that assumed in prior work. Our algorithm, SpanRL, uses the notion of a barycentric spanner for the feature embedding as an efficiently computable basis for exploration, performing efficient spanner computation by interleaving representation learning and policy optimization subroutines. Our analysis---which is appealingly simple and modular---carefully combines several techniques, including a new approach to error-tolerant barycentric spanner computation, and a new analysis of a certain minimax representation learning objective found in prior work.

paragraphs: Exploration becomes difficult when reinforcement learning must generalize across high-dimensional observations. This paper studies low-rank Markov decision processes, whose transition probabilities admit a compact factorization through an unknown feature representation. Earlier approaches in this setting face either computational obstacles or restrictive statistical requirements, motivating a method that is efficient in both computation and data use.

The proposed algorithm, SpanRL, uses a barycentric spanner as a basis for exploration in the learned feature space. It constructs this basis by alternating representation learning and policy optimization. The analysis includes a procedure for computing the spanner despite errors and a new treatment of a minimax representation-learning objective.

The authors establish sample and computational efficiency for a model-free algorithm that permits general function approximation. Beyond the low-rank setting, its structural requirement is a reachability condition that they show is substantially weaker than earlier assumptions. The contribution is therefore a conditional theoretical advance: efficient exploration becomes possible in this expressive setting without the additional structures required by prior approaches.
summary.tldr: SpanRL provides computationally and sample-efficient model-free exploration in low-rank decision processes under a comparatively weak reachability condition.

title: Efficient Model-Free Exploration in Low-Rank MDPs

abstract: While the general machine learning (ML) community has benefited from public datasets, tasks, and models, the progress of ML in healthcare has been hampered by a lack of such shared assets. The success of foundation models creates new challenges for healthcare ML by requiring access to shared pretrained models to validate performance benefits. We help address these challenges through three contributions. First, we publish a new dataset, EHRSHOT, which contains de-identified structured data from the electronic health records (EHRs) of 6,739 patients from Stanford Medicine. Unlike MIMIC-III/IV and other popular EHR datasets, EHRSHOT is longitudinal and not restricted to ICU/ED patients. Second, we publish the weights of CLMBR-T-base, a 141M parameter clinical foundation model pretrained on the structured EHR data of 2.57M patients. We are one of the first to fully release such a model for coded EHR data; in contrast, most prior models released for clinical data (e.g. GatorTron, ClinicalBERT) only work with unstructured text and cannot process the rich, structured data within an EHR. Third, we define 15 few-shot clinical prediction tasks, enabling evaluation of foundation models on benefits such as sample efficiency and task adaptation. Our model and dataset are available via a research data use agreement from here: https://stanfordaimi.azurewebsites.net/. Code to reproduce our results is available here: https://github.com/som-shahlab/ehrshot-benchmark.

title: EHRSHOT: An EHR Benchmark for Few-Shot Evaluation of Foundation Models

abstract: Learning to solve tasks from a sparse reward signal is a major challenge for standard reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms. However, in the real world, agents rarely need to solve sparse reward tasks entirely from scratch. More often, we might possess prior experience to draw on that provides considerable guidance about which actions and outcomes are possible in the world, which we can use to explore more effectively for new tasks. In this work, we study how prior data without reward labels may be used to guide and accelerate exploration for an agent solving a new sparse reward task. We propose a simple approach that learns a reward model from online experience, labels the unlabeled prior data with optimistic rewards, and then uses it concurrently alongside the online data for downstream policy and critic optimization. This general formula leads to rapid exploration in several challenging sparse-reward domains where tabula rasa exploration is insufficient, including the AntMaze domain, Adroit hand manipulation domain, and a visual simulated robotic manipulation domain. Our results highlight the ease of incorporating unlabeled prior data into existing online RL algorithms, and the (perhaps surprising) effectiveness of doing so.

paragraphs: When rewards are rare, a reinforcement learning agent may struggle to discover which actions lead toward its goal. Yet previously collected experience can already reveal useful actions and possible outcomes, even if nobody labeled that experience with rewards. This paper studies how such unlabeled data can help an agent explore a new task.

The proposed method learns a reward model from the agent's ongoing interactions. It then assigns optimistic reward estimates to the prior data and trains using both that relabeled experience and newly collected experience. Both the policy, which chooses actions, and the critic, which evaluates them, benefit from this combined training data.

The authors report rapid exploration in challenging sparse-reward settings involving AntMaze, dexterous hand manipulation, and visual simulated robotic manipulation, where exploration from scratch is insufficient. The findings suggest that prior data can guide learning without arriving with task-specific reward labels. The contribution is also practical: this recipe can be incorporated into existing online reinforcement learning algorithms.
summary.tldr: Assigning optimistic learned rewards to unlabeled prior experience accelerates exploration on several difficult sparse-reward tasks.

title: Accelerating Exploration with Unlabeled Prior Data

abstract: Sharpness-aware minimization (SAM) was proposed to reduce sharpness of minima and has been shown to enhance generalization performance in various settings. In this work we show that perturbing only the affine normalization parameters (typically comprising 0.1% of the total parameters) in the adversarial step of SAM can outperform perturbing all of the parameters. This finding generalizesto different SAM variants and both ResNet (Batch Normalization) and Vision Transformer (Layer Normalization) architectures. We consider alternative sparse perturbation approaches and find that these do not achieve similar performance enhancement at such extreme sparsity levels, showing that this behaviour is unique to the normalization layers. Although our findings reaffirm the effectivenessof SAM in improving generalization performance, they cast doubt on whether this is solely caused by reduced sharpness.

paragraphs: Sharpness-aware minimization, or SAM, is a training method intended to reduce the sharpness of learned minima and improve generalization. Its adversarial step perturbs model parameters. This paper asks how much of that perturbation is actually needed and finds that concentrating it on a very small, specific subset can improve performance.

The subset consists of the affine parameters in normalization layers, typically about 0.1% of all parameters. Perturbing only these parameters can outperform perturbing the entire model. The authors observe this behavior across different SAM variants and in both ResNets with Batch Normalization and Vision Transformers with Layer Normalization. The finding concerns which parameters receive the adversarial perturbation, rather than a claim that the rest of the network can be discarded.

Alternative sparse perturbation strategies do not achieve similar gains at such extreme sparsity in the comparisons reported. This points to a special role for normalization parameters in the observed effect. The results reaffirm SAM's generalization benefits while questioning whether reduced sharpness alone explains them; they do not establish that sharpness has no role.
summary.tldr: Perturbing only normalization parameters during SAM can outperform full-parameter perturbation, challenging a sharpness-only explanation of its benefits.

title: Normalization Layers Are All That Sharpness-Aware Minimization Needs

abstract: We consider the problem of variational Bayesian inference in a latent variable model where a (possibly complex) observed stochastic process is governed by the unobserved solution of a latent stochastic differential equation (SDE). Motivated by the challenges that arise when trying to learn a latent SDE in $\mathbb{R}^n$ from large-scale data, such as efficient gradient computation, we take a step back and study a specific subclass instead. In our case, the SDE evolves inside a homogeneous latent space and is induced by stochastic dynamics of the corresponding (matrix) Lie group. In the context of learning problems, SDEs on the $n$-dimensional unit sphere are arguably the most relevant incarnation of this setup. For variational inference, the sphere not only facilitates using a uniform prior on the initial state of the SDE, but we also obtain a particularly simple and intuitive expression for the KL divergence between the approximate posterior and prior process in the evidence lower bound. We provide empirical evidence that a latent SDE of the proposed type can be learned efficiently by means of an existing one-step geometric Euler-Maruyama scheme. Despite restricting ourselves to a less diverse class of SDEs, we achieve competitive or even state-of-the-art performance on a collection of time series interpolation and classification benchmarks.

paragraphs: The paper studies models in which an observed random process is governed by an unobserved stochastic differential equation, or SDE. Learning general latent SDEs from large datasets can create computational difficulties, including efficient gradient calculation. The authors investigate a more structured family whose hidden dynamics evolve on homogeneous spaces and arise from corresponding matrix Lie groups.

A central example places the latent SDE on a unit sphere. For variational Bayesian inference, this geometry supports a uniform prior over the initial state. It also yields a particularly simple expression for the divergence between the approximate posterior process and the prior process within the training objective. The restricted geometry therefore changes both the possible latent dynamics and the computations needed to learn them.

The authors provide empirical evidence that an existing geometric Euler-Maruyama scheme can learn these models efficiently. Despite using a less diverse class of SDEs, the models achieve competitive or state-of-the-art results on time-series interpolation and classification benchmarks. The findings show that the studied structural restriction can retain useful modeling capacity while making inference more manageable.
summary.tldr: Restricting latent stochastic dynamics to structured spaces simplifies inference and delivers competitive time-series results despite reduced model diversity.

title: Latent SDEs on Homogeneous Spaces

abstract: Deep neural networks are known to be vulnerable to small adversarial perturbations in test data. To defend against adversarial attacks, probabilistic classifiers have been proposed as an alternative to deterministic ones. However, literature has conflicting findings on the effectiveness of probabilistic classifiers in comparison to deterministic ones. In this paper, we clarify the role of randomization in building adversarially robust classifiers.Given a base hypothesis set of deterministic classifiers, we show the conditions under which a randomized ensemble outperforms the hypothesis set in adversarial risk, extending previous results.Additionally, we show that for any probabilistic binary classifier (including randomized ensembles), there exists a deterministic classifier that outperforms it. Finally, we give an explicit description of the deterministic hypothesis set that contains such a deterministic classifier for many types of commonly used probabilistic classifiers, *i.e.* randomized ensembles and parametric/input noise injection.

paragraphs: Randomized classifiers have been proposed as defenses against small adversarial changes to test inputs, but findings about their effectiveness have conflicted. This paper clarifies the comparison by distinguishing between a fixed family of deterministic classifiers and the broader collection of deterministic classifiers that might be considered.

For a given base hypothesis set, the authors establish conditions under which a randomized ensemble achieves lower adversarial risk than that set. Randomization can therefore improve on the available base classifiers under those conditions. Separately, they prove that every probabilistic binary classifier has a deterministic classifier that outperforms it, including when the probabilistic classifier is a randomized ensemble.

These statements concern different comparison sets, which explains how both can hold. Beating the original family does not establish an advantage over all deterministic classifiers. The paper also explicitly describes a deterministic hypothesis set containing such a better classifier for common randomization schemes, including ensembles and parameter or input noise. The result sharpens what a claimed robustness benefit from randomization actually establishes.
summary.tldr: Randomization can beat a fixed base family under stated conditions, yet every probabilistic binary classifier has a better deterministic counterpart.

title: On the Role of Randomization in Adversarially Robust Classification

abstract: Large Reconstruction Models have made significant strides in the realm of automated 3D content generation from single or multiple input images. Despite their success, these models often produce 3D meshes with geometric inaccuracies, stemming from the inherent challenges of deducing 3D shapes solely from image data. In this work, we introduce a novel framework, the Large Image and Point Cloud Alignment Model (LAM3D), which utilizes 3D point cloud data to enhance the fidelity of generated 3D meshes. Our methodology begins with the development of a point-cloud-based network that effectively generates precise and meaningful latent tri-planes, laying the groundwork for accurate 3D mesh reconstruction. Building upon this, our Image-Point-Cloud Feature Alignment technique processes a single input image, aligning to the latent tri-planes to imbue image features with robust 3D information. This process not only enriches the image features but also facilitates the production of high-fidelity 3D meshes without the need for multi-view input, significantly reducing geometric distortions. Our approach achieves state-of-the-art high-fidelity 3D mesh reconstruction from a single image in just 6 seconds, and experiments on various datasets demonstrate its effectiveness.

paragraphs: LAM3D reconstructs a three-dimensional mesh from a single image. The paper targets geometric inaccuracies that arise when reconstruction models must infer shape from image information alone. Its approach uses three-dimensional point clouds to develop a stronger geometric representation that can subsequently guide reconstruction from an image.

The first component is a point-cloud network that produces latent tri-planes, an internal representation used for mesh reconstruction. The second component aligns features from a single image with those point-cloud-derived representations. Through this alignment, image features gain access to information about three-dimensional structure, helping the reconstruction process retain more accurate geometry.

The resulting system does not require multiple input views when reconstructing a mesh. The authors report reduced geometric distortions, state-of-the-art reconstruction fidelity, and a reconstruction time of six seconds, with effectiveness demonstrated on several datasets. The central idea is to transfer geometric information from point-cloud representations into image processing, making a single image a more useful starting point for producing a detailed three-dimensional mesh.
summary.tldr: LAM3D aligns image features with point-cloud-derived representations to reconstruct more accurate 3D meshes from a single image.

title: LAM3D: Large Image-Point Clouds Alignment Model for 3D Reconstruction from Single Image

abstract: Recently, Anil et al. (2024) show that many-shot (up to hundreds of) demonstrations can jailbreak state-of-the-art LLMs by exploiting their long-context capability. Nevertheless, is it possible to use few-shot demonstrations to efficiently jailbreak LLMs within limited context sizes? While the vanilla few-shot jailbreaking may be inefficient, we propose improved techniques such as injecting special system tokens like [/INST] and employing demo-level random search from a collected demo pool. These simple techniques result in surprisingly effective jailbreaking against aligned LLMs (even with advanced defenses). For example, our method achieves >80% (mostly >95%) ASRs on Llama-2-7B and Llama-3-8B without multiple restarts, even if the models are enhanced by strong defenses such as perplexity detection and/or SmoothLLM, which is challenging for suffix-based jailbreaking. In addition, we conduct comprehensive and elaborate (e.g., making sure to use correct system prompts) evaluations against other aligned LLMs and advanced defenses, where our method consistently achieves nearly 100% ASRs. Our code is available at https://github.com/sail-sg/I-FSJ.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether a small number of demonstrations can bypass language-model alignment within limited context windows. Earlier many-shot attacks relied on up to hundreds of examples. The authors examine whether improvements to demonstration-based prompting can make few-shot attacks substantially more effective, including against models equipped with additional defenses.

The proposed changes involve special system-token injection and randomized selection of demonstrations from a collected pool. The contribution is an empirical study of how these relatively simple changes affect attack success. Evaluations also attend to details such as using the correct system prompts, which helps ensure that the tested setup reflects the intended model configuration.

For Llama-2-7B and Llama-3-8B, the paper reports attack success rates above 80%, and mostly above 95%, without multiple restarts, including under perplexity detection or SmoothLLM defenses. Additional evaluations against other aligned models and defenses report rates near 100%. These results show substantial weaknesses in the evaluated protections and indicate that limited context size alone does not prevent effective demonstration-based jailbreaking.
summary.tldr: Improved few-shot demonstration attacks achieve high jailbreak success against the aligned models and defenses evaluated in the paper.

title: Improved Few-Shot Jailbreaking Can Circumvent Aligned Language Models and Their Defenses

abstract: Persistent homology is a popular computational tool for analyzing the topology of point clouds, such as the presence of loops or voids. However, many real-world datasets with low intrinsic dimensionality reside in an ambient space of much higher dimensionality. We show that in this case traditional persistent homology becomes very sensitive to noise and fails to detect the correct topology. The same holds true for existing refinements of persistent homology. As a remedy, we find that spectral distances on the k-nearest-neighbor graph of the data, such as diffusion distance and effective resistance, allow to detect the correct topology even in the presence of high-dimensional noise. Moreover, we derive a novel closed-form formula for effective resistance, and describe its relation to diffusion distances. Finally, we apply these methods to high-dimensional single-cell RNA-sequencing data and show that spectral distances allow robust detection of cell cycle loops.

paragraphs: Persistent homology analyzes the shape of a point cloud, including loops and voids. This paper studies a difficult case: the underlying data have few intrinsic dimensions but are represented in a much larger ambient space. The authors show that high-dimensional noise can make traditional persistent homology, including existing refinements, fail to recover the correct topology.

Their remedy changes how distances between data points are measured. They build a graph connecting each point to its nearest neighbors and use spectral distances on that graph, including diffusion distance and effective resistance. The authors find that these distances allow recovery of the correct topology in the presence of high-dimensional noise. They also derive a new closed-form expression for effective resistance and explain its relationship to diffusion distances.

An application to single-cell RNA-sequencing data demonstrates robust detection of cell-cycle loops. The findings show that the distance used to construct a topological analysis can be decisive when many observed dimensions contain noise, even when the underlying structure is comparatively low-dimensional.
summary.tldr: Graph-based spectral distances improve recovery of topological structure obscured by high-dimensional noise.

title: Persistent Homology for High-dimensional Data Based on Spectral Methods

abstract: In this work, we study the experts problem in the distributed setting where an expert's cost needs to be aggregated across multiple servers. Our study considers various communication models such as the message-passing model and the broadcast model, along with multiple aggregation functions, such as summing and taking the $\ell_p$ norm of an expert's cost across servers. We propose the first communication-efficient protocols that achieve near-optimal regret in these settings, even against a strong adversary who can choose the inputs adaptively. Additionally, we give a conditional lower bound showing that the communication of our protocols is nearly optimal. Finally, we implement our protocols and demonstrate empirical savings on the HPO-B benchmarks.

paragraphs: The distributed experts problem concerns making repeated choices when the information needed to evaluate each expert is spread across servers. An expert’s overall cost must be assembled from these separate contributions. The paper studies how to make good choices while limiting the communication required to combine that information, connecting prediction quality with the cost of distributed coordination.

The authors consider both message-passing and broadcast communication, as well as different ways to aggregate costs, including sums and ℓp norms. They introduce communication-efficient protocols with near-optimal regret, a measure of the accumulated disadvantage relative to a comparison choice. Their guarantees also cover a strong adversary that adaptively chooses inputs.

A conditional lower bound indicates that the protocols’ communication requirements are nearly optimal under the condition supporting that bound. This places the efficiency claim alongside evidence about how much communication may be unavoidable. Implementations on HPO-B benchmarks also show empirical savings, giving practical support to the theoretical treatment across the studied settings.
summary.tldr: The paper develops communication-efficient distributed expert-selection protocols with near-optimal regret and a conditional near-optimality bound on communication.

title: Communication Bounds for the Distributed Experts Problem

abstract: One of the urgent tasks of artificial intelligence is to assess the safety and alignment of large language models (LLMs) with human behavior. Conventional verification only in pure natural language processing benchmarks can be insufficient. Since emotions often influence human decisions, this paper examines LLM alignment in complex strategic and ethical environments, providing an in-depth analysis of the drawbacks of our psychology and the emotional impact on decision-making in humans and LLMs. We introduce the novel EAI framework for integrating emotion modeling into LLMs to examine the emotional impact on ethics and LLM-based decision-making in various strategic games, including bargaining and repeated games. Our experimental study with various LLMs demonstrated that emotions can significantly alter the ethical decision-making landscape of LLMs, highlighting the need for robust mechanisms to ensure consistent ethical standards. Our game-theoretic analysis revealed that LLMs are susceptible to emotional biases influenced by model size, alignment strategies, and primary pretraining language. Notably, these biases often diverge from typical human emotional responses, occasionally leading to unexpected drops in cooperation rates, even under positive emotional influence. Such behavior complicates the alignment of multiagent systems, emphasizing the need for benchmarks that can rigorously evaluate the degree of emotional alignment. Our framework provides a foundational basis for developing such benchmarks.
