paragraphs: Selecting diverse language-model training data requires deciding which examples are similar. Common practice uses embeddings from models trained for tasks such as retrieval, but similarity useful for retrieval may not reflect similarity useful for pretraining. This paper develops a framework for evaluating that fit directly.

The framework examines three aspects of an embedding model. First, it tests whether distances between examples reflect how pretraining loss generalizes between them. Second, it uses the embeddings in a standard diversity-based selection procedure, then trains a language model on the selected data and measures downstream performance. Third, it checks whether embeddings distinguish examples originating from different data sources.

Experiments use the Pile and pretrain a 1.7-billion-parameter language model on 200 billion tokens. In this setting, standard off-the-shelf embeddings perform worse for data curation than even simple embeddings extracted from models trained on the same corpus. The findings motivate assessing similarity through its consequences for pretraining, and provide concrete criteria for designing embeddings suited to that purpose.
summary.tldr: A pretraining-focused evaluation finds that common embedding models select data less effectively than simple embeddings from models trained on the same corpus.

title: Analyzing Similarity Metrics for Data Selection for Language Model Pretraining

abstract: Plug-and-play (PnP) methods with deep denoisers have shown impressive results in imaging problems. They typically require strong convexity or smoothness of the fidelity term and a (residual) non-expansive denoiser for convergence. These assumptions, however, are violated in Poisson inverse problems, and non-expansiveness can hinder denoising performance. To address these challenges, we propose a cocoercive conservative (CoCo) denoiser, which may be (residual) expansive, leading to improved denoising performance. By leveraging the generalized Helmholtz decomposition, we introduce a novel training strategy that combines Hamiltonian regularization to promote conservativeness and spectral regularization to ensure cocoerciveness. We prove that CoCo denoiser is a proximal operator of a weakly convex function, enabling a restoration model with an implicit weakly convex prior. The global convergence of PnP methods to a stationary point of this restoration model is established. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that our approach outperforms closely related methods in both visual quality and quantitative metrics.

paragraphs: Plug-and-play image restoration inserts a learned denoiser into an iterative reconstruction method. Standard convergence arguments often require properties of both the data-fitting term and denoiser that fail in Poisson imaging problems. Requiring a denoiser to be non-expansive can also restrict its denoising performance.

The paper proposes a cocoercive conservative denoiser, called CoCo, that may be expansive while supporting a convergence analysis. Its training strategy draws on generalized Helmholtz decomposition. Hamiltonian regularization promotes conservativeness, while spectral regularization ensures cocoerciveness. These conditions provide a different route to controlling the denoiser’s behavior without imposing the usual non-expansiveness requirement.

The authors prove that CoCo corresponds to a proximal operator of a weakly convex function, giving the restoration procedure an implicit weakly convex prior. They establish global convergence of the plug-and-play methods to a stationary point of that restoration model; this is not a claim of reaching a global optimum. Experiments report improvements over closely related methods in both visual quality and quantitative measures.
summary.tldr: CoCo denoisers improve Poisson image restoration while enabling convergence to a stationary point under a weakly convex restoration model.

title: Learning Cocoercive Conservative Denoisers via Helmholtz Decomposition for Poisson Imaging Inverse Problems

abstract: The rapid advancements in large language models (LLMs), particularly in their reasoning capabilities, hold transformative potential for addressing complex challenges and boosting scientific discovery in atmospheric science. However, leveraging LLMs effectively in this domain requires a robust and comprehensive evaluation benchmark. Toward this end, we present AtmosSci-Bench, a novel benchmark designed to systematically assess LLM performance across five core categories of atmospheric science problems: hydrology, atmospheric dynamics, atmospheric physics, geophysics, and physical oceanography.AtmosSci-Bench features a dual-format design comprising both multiple-choice questions (MCQs) and open-ended questions (OEQs), enabling scalable automated evaluation alongside deeper analysis of conceptual understanding. We employ a template-based MCQ generation framework to create diverse, graduate-level problems with symbolic perturbation, while OEQs are used to probe open-ended reasoning.We conduct a comprehensive evaluation of representative LLMs, categorized into four groups: instruction-tuned models, advanced reasoning models, math-augmented models, and domain-specific climate models. Our analysis provides some interesting insights into the reasoning and problem-solving capabilities of LLMs in atmospheric science. We believe AtmosSci-Bench can serve as a critical step toward advancing LLM applications in climate services by offering a standard and rigorous evaluation framework. The source code of AtmosSci-Bench is available at https://github.com/Relaxed-System-Lab/AtmosSci-Bench.

paragraphs: AtmosSci-Bench provides a structured way to evaluate language models on atmospheric science problems. It covers hydrology, atmospheric dynamics, atmospheric physics, geophysics, and physical oceanography. The motivation is that applying models to scientific work requires a domain-specific assessment of their reasoning and problem solving, beyond general impressions of language fluency.

The benchmark combines multiple-choice and open-ended questions. Multiple-choice questions support automated evaluation at scale, while open-ended responses allow closer examination of conceptual understanding and reasoning. A template-based process creates graduate-level multiple-choice problems using symbolic perturbations, producing variations within the problem-generation framework. The two formats therefore examine complementary aspects of model capability.

The authors evaluate instruction-tuned, advanced reasoning, math-augmented, and climate-specific models. This comparison is designed to examine how different kinds of model development translate into atmospheric science performance. The abstract reports insights from the evaluation without identifying a winning group or specific performance gaps. The stated contribution is a common, rigorous evaluation framework that could support further development of language-model applications in climate services.
summary.tldr: AtmosSci-Bench evaluates language-model reasoning across five atmospheric science fields using multiple-choice and open-ended problems.

title: AtmosSci-Bench: Evaluating the Recent Advance of Large Language Model for Atmospheric Science

abstract: We propose a smooth regularization technique that instills a strong temporal inductive bias in video recognition models, particularly benefiting lightweight architectures. Our method encourages smoothness in the intermediate-layer embeddings of consecutive frames by modeling their changes as a Gaussian Random Walk (GRW). This penalizes abrupt representational shifts, thereby promoting low- acceleration solutions that better align with the natural temporal coherence inherent in videos. By leveraging this enforced smoothness, lightweight models can more effectively capture complex temporal dynamics. Applied to such models, our technique yields a 3.8%–6.4% accuracy improvement on Kinetics-600. Notably, the MoViNets model family trained with our smooth regularization improves the current state-of-the-art by 3.8%–6.1% within their respective FLOP constraints, while MobileNetV3 and the MoViNets-Stream family achieve gains of 4.9%–6.4% over prior state-of-the-art models with comparable memory footprints. Our code and models are available at https://github.com/gilgoldm/grw-smoothing.

paragraphs: This paper improves video recognition by encouraging a model's internal representations to change smoothly between consecutive frames. The motivation is that videos contain temporal coherence, yet a lightweight network may not capture that structure effectively on its own. The proposed regularizer builds this expectation into training, helping limited-capacity models use the relationships between nearby frames.

The method models changes in intermediate-layer embeddings using a Gaussian Random Walk. It penalizes abrupt shifts in those representations and promotes low-acceleration solutions that align with the temporal continuity of video. Applying the constraint inside the network makes temporal structure part of representation learning, supporting the model's ability to capture complex dynamics without relying only on independent frame content.

On Kinetics-600, the technique produces reported accuracy improvements of 3.8%–6.4% for lightweight models. MoViNets improves the state of the art by 3.8%–6.1% within the corresponding FLOP budgets. MobileNetV3 and MoViNets-Stream achieve gains of 4.9%–6.4% over prior leading models with comparable memory footprints. These results connect temporal regularization to stronger recognition under concrete computation and memory constraints.
summary.tldr: Regularizing frame-to-frame feature changes improves lightweight video recognition within comparable computation and memory budgets.

title: Smooth Regularization for Efficient Video Recognition

abstract: The simple linear threshold units used in many artificial neural networks have a limited computational capacity. Famously, a single unit cannot handle non-linearly separable problems like XOR. In contrast, real neurons exhibit complex morphologies as well as active dendritic integration, suggesting that their computational capacities outperform those of simple linear units. Considering specific families of Boolean functions, we empirically examine the computational limits of single units that incorporate more complex dendritic structures. For random Boolean functions, we show that there is a phase transition in learnability as a function of the input dimension, with most random functions below a certain critical dimension being learnable and those above not. This critical dimension is best predicted by the overall size of the dendritic arbor. This demonstrates that real neurons have a far higher computational complexity than is usually considered in neural models, whether in machine learning or computational neuroscience. Furthermore, using architectures that are, respectively, more "apical" or "basal" we show that there are non-trivially disjoint sets of learnable functions by each type of neuron. Importantly, these two types of architectures differ in the robustness and generality of the computations they can perform. The basal-like architecture shows a higher probability of function realization, while the apical-like architecture shows an advantage with fast retraining for different functions. Given the cell-type specificity of morphological characteristics, these results suggest both that different components of the dendritic arbor as well as distinct cell types may have distinct computational roles. In single neurons, morphology sculpts computation, shaping not only what neurons do, but how they learn and adapt. Our analysis offers new directions for neuron-level inductive biases in NeuroAI models using scalable models for neuronal cell-type specific computation.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how the branching structure of a neuron's dendrites changes the computations a single unit can learn. Simple linear threshold units cannot solve some basic Boolean problems, including XOR. The authors empirically examine richer units with dendritic structures to understand how their computational abilities depend on morphology.

For random Boolean functions, the experiments reveal a transition as the number of inputs increases: most functions below a critical input dimension are learnable, while those above it are not. Their learnable function sets differ in nontrivial ways. These findings suggest that dendritic components and neuron types may support distinct computational roles, motivating neural models that incorporate cell-type-specific structure.
summary.tldr: Experiments link dendritic size and structure to a single neuron's learnable functions, reliability, and ability to adapt.

title: Bounds on the computational complexity of neurons due to dendritic morphology

abstract: While recent advancements in generative modeling have significantly improved text-image alignment, some residual misalignment between text and image representations still remains. Some approaches address this issue by fine-tuning models in terms of preference optimization, etc., which require tailored datasets. Orthogonal to these methods, we revisit the challenge from the perspective of representation alignment—an approach that has gained popularity with the success of REPresentation Alignment (REPA). We first argue that conventional text-to-image (T2I) diffusion models, typically trained on paired image and text data (i.e., positive pairs) by minimizing score matching or flow matching losses, is suboptimal from the standpoint of representation alignment. Instead, a better alignment can be achieved through contrastive learning that leverages existing dataset as both positive and negative pairs. To enable efficient alignment with pretrained models, we propose SoftREPA—a lightweight contrastive fine-tuning strategy that leverages soft text tokens for representation alignment. This approach improves alignment with minimal computational overhead by adding fewer than 1M trainable parameters to the pretrained model. Our theoretical analysis demonstrates that our method explicitly increases the mutual information between text and image representations, leading to enhanced semantic consistency. Experimental results across text-to-image generation and text-guided image editing tasks validate the effectiveness of our approach in improving the semantic consistency of T2I generative models.

paragraphs: A generated image can look convincing while still failing to match its text description. This paper approaches that problem through the alignment of internal text and image representations. The authors argue that standard diffusion training on matching image-text pairs, using score-matching or flow-matching objectives, is suboptimal for this particular alignment goal.

Their proposed method, SoftREPA, adds contrastive fine-tuning to a pretrained model. It uses the existing dataset to supply both matching and nonmatching pairs, giving training a way to distinguish compatible representations from incompatible ones. Soft text tokens provide the adjustable representation mechanism, requiring fewer than one million additional trainable parameters and minimal computational overhead.

The theoretical analysis shows that the method explicitly increases mutual information between text and image representations, supporting stronger semantic consistency. Experiments on both text-to-image generation and text-guided editing report improved alignment. The contribution is a lightweight way to address representation mismatch using existing paired data, alongside approaches such as preference optimization that require specially prepared datasets.
summary.tldr: SoftREPA improves text-image semantic alignment through lightweight contrastive fine-tuning with soft text tokens and existing paired data.

title: Aligning Text to Image in Diffusion Models is Easier Than You Think

abstract: Reliably predicting the behavior of language models---such as whether their outputs are correct or have been adversarially manipulated---is a fundamentally challenging task. This is often made even more difficult as frontier language models are offered only through closed-source APIs, providing only black-box access. In this paper, we predict the behavior of black-box language models by asking follow-up questions and taking the probabilities of responses _as_ representations to train reliable predictors. We first demonstrate that training a linear model on these responses reliably and accurately predicts model correctness on question-answering and reasoning benchmarks. Surprisingly, this can _even outperform white-box linear predictors_ that operate over model internals or activations. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these follow-up question responses can reliably distinguish between a clean version of an LLM and one that has been adversarially influenced via a system prompt to answer questions incorrectly or to introduce bugs into generated code. Finally, we show that they can also be used to differentiate between black-box LLMs, enabling the detection of misrepresented models provided through an API. Overall, our work shows promise in monitoring black-box language model behavior, supporting their deployment in larger, autonomous systems.

paragraphs: Assessing a language model’s answer is difficult when an API hides its internal representations. This paper uses follow-up questions to obtain an alternative representation of model behavior. The probabilities of responses to those questions become features for a predictor, allowing assessment through observable interactions rather than requiring access to hidden activations.

A linear model trained on these features predicts correctness on question-answering and reasoning benchmarks. The authors report that it can even outperform linear predictors with white-box access to model internals. This finding suggests that carefully elicited responses can expose useful behavioral information in a form that a simple predictor can use effectively.

The same approach also distinguishes clean models from versions influenced by adversarial system prompts to give incorrect answers or introduce code bugs. In another application, it differentiates between black-box models, supporting detection of misrepresented models behind an API. These results point to follow-up interactions as a promising monitoring tool across correctness assessment, behavioral manipulation detection, and model identification.
summary.tldr: Response probabilities from follow-up questions provide features for predicting black-box model correctness, detecting manipulation, and distinguishing model identities.

title: Predicting the Performance of Black-box Language Models with Follow-up Queries

abstract: Multi-domain task incremental learning (MTIL) demands models to master domain-specific expertise while preserving generalization capabilities. Inspired by human lifelong learning, which relies on revisiting, aligning, and integrating past experiences, we propose a Learning and Ensembling Bridge Adapters (LEBA) framework. To facilitate cohesive knowledge transfer across domains, specifically, we propose a continuous-domain bridge adaptation module, leveraging the distribution transfer capabilities of Schrödinger bridge for stable progressive learning. To strengthen memory consolidation, we further propose a progressive knowledge ensemble strategy that revisits past task representations via a diffusion model and dynamically integrates historical adapters. For efficiency, LEBA maintains a compact adapter pool through similarity-based selection and employs learnable weights to align replayed samples with current task semantics. Together, these components effectively mitigate catastrophic forgetting and enhance generalization across tasks. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks validate the effectiveness and superiority of LEBA over state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Learning tasks across changing domains requires a model to gain specialized knowledge without losing earlier capabilities or weakening generalization. LEBA approaches this problem by connecting new learning to previous task representations and adapters. Its design combines progressive adaptation across domains with a mechanism for revisiting and integrating historical knowledge.

The adaptation module uses a Schrödinger bridge to transfer between distributions and support stable learning as domains change. A separate knowledge-ensemble strategy uses a diffusion model to revisit representations from past tasks, then dynamically combines historical adapters. Together, these components address both the transition into a new domain and the consolidation of what the model learned before.

To keep the adapter collection compact, LEBA selects adapters based on similarity. Learnable weights align replayed samples with the meaning of the current task, helping historical information contribute appropriately. Experiments across multiple benchmarks report reduced catastrophic forgetting, better generalization, and stronger performance than existing methods. The findings support coordinating domain adaptation, replay, and adapter selection within one continual-learning framework.
summary.tldr: LEBA combines bridge-based domain adaptation, diffusion replay, and compact adapter ensembles to reduce forgetting across sequential tasks.

title: Learn and Ensemble Bridge Adapters for Multi-domain Task Incremental Learning

abstract: Reconstruction-based methods are competitive choices for multivariate time series anomaly detection (MTS AD). However, one challenge these methods may suffer is over generalization, where abnormal inputs are also well reconstructed. In addition, balancing robustness and sensitivity is also important for final performance, as robustness ensures accurate detection in potentially noisy data, while sensitivity enables early detection of subtle anomalies. To address these problems, inspired by idempotent generative network, we take the view from the manifold and propose a novel module named **I**dempotent **G**eneration for **A**nomaly **D**etection (IGAD) which can be flexibly combined with a reconstruction-based method without introducing additional trainable parameters. We modify the manifold to make sure that normal time points can be mapped onto it while tightening it to drop out abnormal time points simultaneously. Regarding the latest findings of AD metrics, we evaluated IGAD on various methods with four real-world datasets, and they achieve visible improvements in VUS-PR than their predecessors, demonstrating the effective potential of IGAD for further improvements in MTS AD tasks. Our instructions on integrating IGAD into customized models and example codes are available at https://github.com/ProEcho1/Idempotent-Generation-for-Anomaly-Detection-IGAD.

However, one challenge these methods may suffer is over generalization, where abnormal inputs are also well reconstructed. In addition, balancing robustness and sensitivity is also important for final performance, as robustness ensures accurate detection in potentially noisy data, while sensitivity enables early detection of subtle anomalies. To address these problems, inspired by idempotent generative network, we take the view from the manifold and propose a novel module named **I**dempotent **G**eneration for **A**nomaly **D**etection (IGAD) which can be flexibly combined with a reconstruction-based method without introducing additional trainable parameters. We modify the manifold to make sure that normal time points can be mapped onto it while tightening it to drop out abnormal time points simultaneously. Regarding the latest findings of AD metrics, we evaluated IGAD on various methods with four real-world datasets, and they achieve visible improvements in VUS-PR than their predecessors, demonstrating the effective potential of IGAD for further improvements in MTS AD tasks. paragraphs: Reconstruction-based anomaly detection relies on a model representing normal time-series behavior well while struggling with abnormal inputs. A problem arises when the model reconstructs anomalies well too, making them harder to distinguish. The paper also emphasizes the need to tolerate noise while remaining sensitive enough to detect subtle abnormalities early.

The proposed Idempotent Generation for Anomaly Detection module, IGAD, approaches this through the geometry of the learned representation. It modifies the manifold representing acceptable reconstructed behavior so normal time points can map onto it while abnormal points are excluded by tightening that manifold. IGAD can be combined with reconstruction-based methods without adding trainable parameters.

The authors integrate IGAD with several methods and evaluate them on four real-world datasets. The resulting systems improve over their predecessors on VUS-PR. These findings support the module's potential to improve existing detectors by changing what their reconstruction process accepts as normal. Its significance lies in addressing excessive generalization within reconstruction itself, while keeping the parameter count of the underlying model unchanged.
summary.tldr: IGAD improves reconstruction-based time-series anomaly detectors by tightening their representation of normal behavior without adding trainable parameters.

title: Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Detection with Idempotent Reconstruction

abstract: We introduce LoRAShop, the first framework for multi-concept image generation and editing with LoRA models. LoRAShop builds on a key observation about the feature interaction patterns inside Flux-style diffusion transformers: concept-specific transformer features activate spatially coherent regions early in the denoising process. We harness this observation to derive a disentangled latent mask for each concept in a prior forward pass and blend the corresponding LoRA weights only within regions bounding the concepts to be personalized. The resulting edits seamlessly integrate multiple subjects or styles into the original scene while preserving global context, lighting, and fine details. Our experiments demonstrate that LoRAShop delivers better identity preservation compared to baselines. By eliminating retraining and external constraints, LoRAShop turns personalized diffusion models into a practical `photoshop-with-LoRAs' tool and opens new avenues for compositional visual storytelling and rapid creative iteration.

paragraphs: LoRAShop combines multiple personalized concepts in image generation and editing using existing LoRA models. Its goal is to integrate several subjects or styles into a scene while retaining the surrounding context, lighting, and small details. The framework performs this composition without retraining or adding external constraints.

The approach builds on an observation inside Flux-style diffusion transformers: features associated with particular concepts activate spatially coherent regions early in denoising. LoRAShop uses an initial forward pass to derive a separate latent mask for each concept. It then blends the corresponding LoRA weights only within regions enclosing the concepts being personalized, giving each concept a localized area of influence.

Experiments show better identity preservation than the compared baselines. The stated preservation of global context and visual details makes this relevant to editing as well as new image generation. The contribution is a way to use spatial structure already present in transformer features to coordinate multiple personalized models, making repeated combinations of subjects and styles more practical.
summary.tldr: LoRAShop uses concept-specific spatial masks to combine existing LoRA models for multi-concept image generation and editing without retraining.

title: LoRAShop: Training-Free Multi-Concept Image Generation and Editing with Rectified Flow Transformers

abstract: Learning discrete linear functions is a notoriously difficult challenge. In this paper, the learning task is cast as combinatorial optimization problem: given a set of positive and negative feature vectors in the Euclidean space, the goal is to find a discrete linear function that minimizes the cumulative hinge loss of this training set. Since this problem is NP-hard, we propose two simple rounding algorithms that discretize the fractional solution of the problem. Generalization bounds are derived for two important classes of binary-weighted linear functions, by establishing the Rademacher complexity of these classes and proving approximation bounds for rounding methods. These methods are compared on both synthetic and real-world data.

Since this problem is NP-hard, we propose two simple rounding algorithms that discretize the fractional solution of the problem. Generalization bounds are derived for two important classes of binary-weighted linear functions, by establishing the Rademacher complexity of these classes and proving approximation bounds for rounding methods. These methods are compared on both synthetic and real-world data.

paragraphs: This paper studies linear classification when the learned function must be discrete. Given positively and negatively labeled feature vectors, the training objective is to minimize their cumulative hinge loss. The discrete restriction makes this a combinatorial optimization problem, and the paper identifies the resulting task as NP-hard.

The authors propose two simple rounding algorithms that convert a fractional solution into a discrete one. This separates the search for a fractional solution from the step that enforces discreteness. Approximation bounds for the rounding methods help characterize the consequences of that conversion, connecting a practical procedure to a theoretical account of its quality.

The paper also derives generalization bounds for two important classes of linear functions with binary weights. It does so by establishing their Rademacher complexity and combining that analysis with rounding guarantees. Comparisons on synthetic and real-world data complement the theory. The contribution thus addresses both how to construct discrete classifiers and how to analyze their behavior beyond training examples.
summary.tldr: Two rounding algorithms turn fractional solutions into discrete linear classifiers, supported by approximation and generalization bounds.

title: Rounding Methods for Discrete Linear Classification

abstract: We define the beta diffusion tree, a random tree structure with a set of leaves that defines a collection of overlapping subsets of objects, known as a feature allocation. The generative process for the tree is defined in terms of particles (representing the objects) diffusing in some continuous space, analogously to the Dirichlet and Pitman-Yor diffusion trees (Neal, 2003b; Knowles & Ghahramani, 2011), both of which define tree structures over clusters of the particles. With the beta diffusion tree, however, multiple copies of a particle may exist and diffuse to multiple locations in the continuous space, resulting in (a random number of) possibly overlapping clusters of the objects. We demonstrate how to build a hierarchically-clustered factor analysis model with the beta diffusion tree and how to perform inference over the random tree structures with a Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm. We conclude with several numerical experiments on missing data problems with data sets of gene expression arrays, international development statistics, and intranational socioeconomic measurements.

With the beta diffusion tree, however, multiple copies of a particle may exist and diffuse to multiple locations in the continuous space, resulting in (a random number of) possibly overlapping clusters of the objects. paragraphs: This paper introduces the beta diffusion tree, a probabilistic tree structure for organizing objects into overlapping subsets. Such a collection is called a feature allocation: an object can belong to several subsets instead of being assigned to just one cluster. The tree adds a hierarchical organization to these potentially overlapping memberships.

The construction represents objects as particles moving through a continuous space. Its key distinction from the related clustering trees discussed in the abstract is that a particle can have multiple copies. Those copies can move to different locations, allowing one object to contribute to multiple groups. The process produces a random number of groups, with overlap arising directly from its generative mechanism.

The authors use this structure to build a factor analysis model with hierarchically clustered factors and develop Markov chain Monte Carlo inference over the possible trees. They demonstrate the approach through missing-data experiments involving gene expression, international development, and intranational socioeconomic measurements. These experiments illustrate applications of the model without establishing a specific comparative performance advantage in the abstract.
summary.tldr: Beta diffusion trees model hierarchical, overlapping groups by allowing copies of object-representing particles to follow different paths.

title: Beta Diffusion Trees

abstract: We study parametric unsupervised mixture learning. We measure the loss of intrinsic information from the observations to complex mixture models, and then to simple mixture models. We present a geometric picture, where all these representations are regarded as free points in the space of probability distributions. Based on minimum description length, we derive a simple geometric principle to learn all these models together. We present a new learning machine with theories, algorithms, and simulations.
originalAbstract: We study parametric unsupervised mixture learning. We measure the loss of intrinsic information from the observations to complex mixture models, and then to simple mixture models. We present a geometric picture, where all these representations are regarded as free points in the space of probability distributions. Based on minimum description length, we derive a simple geometric principle to learn all these models together. We present a new learning machine with theories, algorithms, and simulations.

paragraphs: The paper studies unsupervised learning with parametric mixture models, which represent a distribution through a combination of component distributions. It considers a sequence of representations: the observations, a complex mixture model, and a simpler mixture model. The central question is how much intrinsic information is lost as the representation moves through these stages.

The authors place all of these representations in a common geometric setting, treating them as points in the space of probability distributions. This makes observations and models of different complexity part of one picture. The geometry provides a language for relating the representations and the information lost between them, rather than considering each model in isolation.

Using minimum description length, the paper derives a geometric principle for learning the models together. This connects model learning to the goal of describing information compactly while accounting for what the representation retains. The authors present a learning machine supported by theory, algorithms, and simulations. The contribution is a unified formulation of joint mixture learning through information loss, geometry, and description length.
summary.tldr: The paper uses information geometry and minimum description length to learn complex and simple mixture models together.

title: Information Geometry and Minimum Description Length Networks

abstract: Low-rank matrix approximation is a fundamental tool in data analysis for processing large datasets, reducing noise, and finding important signals. In this work, we present a novel truncated LU factorization called Spectrum-Revealing LU (SRLU) for effective low-rank matrix approximation, and develop a fast algorithm to compute an SRLU factorization. We provide both matrix and singular value approximation error bounds for the SRLU approximation computed by our algorithm. Our analysis suggests that SRLU is competitive with the best low-rank matrix approximation methods, deterministic or randomized, in both computational complexity and approximation quality. Numeric experiments illustrate that SRLU preserves sparsity, highlights important data features and variables, can be efficiently updated, and calculates data approximations nearly as accurately as the best possible. To the best of our knowledge this is the first practical variant of the LU factorization for effective and efficient low-rank matrix approximation.

We provide both matrix and singular value approximation error bounds for the SRLU approximation computed by our algorithm. Our analysis suggests that SRLU is competitive with the best low-rank matrix approximation methods, deterministic or randomized, in both computational complexity and approximation quality. Numeric experiments illustrate that SRLU preserves sparsity, highlights important data features and variables, can be efficiently updated, and calculates data approximations nearly as accurately as the best possible. To the best of our knowledge this is the first practical variant of the LU factorization for effective and efficient low-rank matrix approximation.

paragraphs: Low-rank approximation represents a large matrix through a smaller structure that retains important information. It is useful for reducing noise and identifying signals in data. This paper introduces Spectrum-Revealing LU, or SRLU, a truncated LU factorization designed for this purpose, together with a fast algorithm for computing it.

The authors derive error bounds for both the matrix approximation and its singular values. Their analysis suggests that SRLU is competitive with leading deterministic and randomized low-rank methods in computational cost and approximation quality. This gives theoretical support for using an LU-based construction as an effective approach to low-rank approximation.

Numerical experiments show that SRLU preserves sparsity, exposes important features and variables, and supports efficient updates. They also find approximation accuracy close to the best possible. These observations address several practical needs together: maintaining sparse structure, retaining useful information, and revising an approximation efficiently. The authors describe it, to their knowledge, as the first practical LU variant to deliver effective and efficient low-rank approximation.
summary.tldr: SRLU uses a truncated LU factorization for accurate, efficiently updatable low-rank approximations that preserve sparsity in experiments.

title: An Efficient, Sparsity-Preserving, Online Algorithm for Low-Rank Approximation

abstract: Deep learning models are often successfully trained using gradient descent, despite the worst case hardness of the underlying non-convex optimization problem. The key question is then under what conditions can one prove that optimization will succeed. Here we provide a strong result of this kind. We consider a neural net with one hidden layer and a convolutional structure with no overlap and a ReLU activation function. For this architecture we show that learning is NP-complete in the general case, but that when the input distribution is Gaussian, gradient descent converges to the global optimum in polynomial time. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first global optimality guarantee of gradient descent on a convolutional neural network with ReLU activations.

The key question is then under what conditions can one prove that optimization will succeed. Here we provide a strong result of this kind. We consider a neural net with one hidden layer and a convolutional structure with no overlap and a ReLU activation function. For this architecture we show that learning is NP-complete in the general case, but that when the input distribution is Gaussian, gradient descent converges to the global optimum in polynomial time. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first global optimality guarantee of gradient descent on a convolutional neural network with ReLU activations.

paragraphs: Gradient descent often trains neural networks successfully even though their optimization problems are non-convex. This paper asks when that success can be proved, rather than only observed. It studies a specific architecture: a network with one hidden layer, non-overlapping convolutional structure, and ReLU activation.

For this architecture, the authors establish a sharp distinction between general inputs and a particular input distribution. Learning is NP-complete in the general case. When inputs follow a Gaussian distribution, however, they prove that gradient descent converges to a global optimum in polynomial time. The distributional assumption is therefore central to the positive result.

The finding shows how a restricted statistical setting can make optimization provably tractable despite worst-case hardness for the same architecture. Its guarantee concerns reaching the global optimum, which is stronger than merely reaching a point with a small gradient. The stated architecture and Gaussian-input condition define the scope of that conclusion; the result does not assert the same behavior for arbitrary convolutional networks.
summary.tldr: Gradient descent provably reaches a global optimum in polynomial time for a specific non-overlapping ReLU ConvNet with Gaussian inputs.

title: Globally Optimal Gradient Descent for a ConvNet with Gaussian Inputs

abstract: We propose a new neural network architecture and use it for the task of statement-by-statement alignment of source code and its compiled object code. Our architecture learns the alignment between the two sequences – one being the translation of the other – by mapping each statement to a context-dependent representation vector and aligning such vectors using a grid of the two sequence domains. Our experiments include short C functions, both artificial and human-written, and show that our neural network architecture is able to predict the alignment with high accuracy, outperforming known baselines. We also demonstrate that our model is general and can learn to solve graph problems such as the Traveling Salesman Problem.

Our architecture learns the alignment between the two sequences – one being the translation of the other – by mapping each statement to a context-dependent representation vector and aligning such vectors using a grid of the two sequence domains. Our experiments include short C functions, both artificial and human-written, and show that our neural network architecture is able to predict the alignment with high accuracy, outperforming known baselines. We also demonstrate that our model is general and can learn to solve graph problems such as the Traveling Salesman Problem.

paragraphs: Source code and its compiled object code express related computations in different sequences of statements. This paper proposes a neural architecture for learning the correspondence between those sequences at the statement level. Its target is an alignment that links the two representations of the program.

The architecture maps each statement to a representation that depends on its context. It then aligns those vectors through a grid spanning both sequence domains. This combines contextual information about individual statements with an explicit representation of possible cross-sequence correspondences, giving the network a structure for learning how one sequence translates into the other.

Experiments use short C functions, including both artificial examples and human-written code. The model predicts alignments with high accuracy and outperforms the known baselines in those tests. The authors also demonstrate that the architecture can learn graph problems such as the Traveling Salesman Problem. That additional result indicates applicability beyond code alignment, while the code experiments specifically establish performance on short functions.
summary.tldr: A neural architecture aligns source and compiled statements using contextual vectors and a cross-sequence grid, outperforming baselines on short C functions.

title: Learning to Align the Source Code to the Compiled Object Code

abstract: Non-interactive Local Differential Privacy (LDP) requires data analysts to collect data from users through noisy channel at once. In this paper, we extend the frontiers of Non-interactive LDP learning and estimation from several aspects. For learning with smooth generalized linear losses, we propose an approximate stochastic gradient oracle estimated from non-interactive LDP channel using Chebyshev expansion, which is combined with inexact gradient methods to obtain an efficient algorithm with quasi-polynomial sample complexity bound. For the high-dimensional world, we discover that under $\ell_2$-norm assumption on data points, high-dimensional sparse linear regression and mean estimation can be achieved with logarithmic dependence on dimension, using random projection and approximate recovery. We also extend our methods to Kernel Ridge Regression. Our work is the first one that makes learning and estimation possible for a broad range of learning tasks under non-interactive LDP model.

paragraphs: Non-interactive local differential privacy requires collecting users' data through a noisy channel in a single round. This creates a learning problem in which the analyst must make effective use of already collected private information. The paper develops methods that expand the range of learning and estimation tasks possible under this restriction.

For smooth generalized linear losses, the authors use a Chebyshev expansion to construct an approximate stochastic gradient oracle from the private channel. They combine this oracle with optimization methods that tolerate inaccurate gradients. The resulting algorithm has a quasi-polynomial sample-complexity bound, establishing a route from noisy one-time collection to iterative learning.

For high-dimensional sparse linear regression and mean estimation, the paper obtains logarithmic dependence on dimension under an assumption on the data points' l2 norms. Random projection and approximate recovery are central to these results. The methods also extend to kernel ridge regression. Together, these contributions establish several distinct possibilities for non-interactive private learning, with the favorable high-dimensional dependence tied to the stated norm assumption.
summary.tldr: Approximate gradients and random projections enable several learning tasks from one-time locally private data collection, with stated complexity guarantees.

title: Collect at Once, Use Effectively: Making Non-interactive Locally Private Learning Possible

abstract: Exogenous state variables and rewards can slow down reinforcement learning by injecting uncontrolled variation into the reward signal. We formalize exogenous state variables and rewards and identify conditions under which an MDP with exogenous state can be decomposed into an exogenous Markov Reward Process involving only the exogenous state+reward and an endogenous Markov Decision Process defined with respect to only the endogenous rewards. We also derive a variance-covariance condition under which Monte Carlo policy evaluation on the endogenous MDP is accelerated compared to using the full MDP. Similar speedups are likely to carry over to all RL algorithms. We develop two algorithms for discovering the exogenous variables and test them on several MDPs. Results show that the algorithms are practical and can significantly speed up reinforcement learning.
originalAbstract: Exogenous state variables and rewards can slow down reinforcement learning by injecting uncontrolled variation into the reward signal. We formalize exogenous state variables and rewards and identify conditions under which an MDP with exogenous state can be decomposed into an exogenous Markov Reward Process involving only the exogenous state+reward and an endogenous Markov Decision Process defined with respect to only the endogenous rewards. We also derive a variance-covariance condition under which Monte Carlo policy evaluation on the endogenous MDP is accelerated compared to using the full MDP. Similar speedups are likely to carry over to all RL algorithms. We develop two algorithms for discovering the exogenous variables and test them on several MDPs. Results show that the algorithms are practical and can significantly speed up reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: A reinforcement learning agent can observe reward changes caused by factors outside its control. Such exogenous variation can obscure the effects of its decisions and slow learning. This paper asks when those factors can be separated from the part of the problem that depends on the agent's actions.

The authors formalize exogenous state variables and rewards, then give conditions for decomposing the original decision process. One component is an exogenous Markov reward process, containing the external state and reward. The other is an endogenous decision process defined using only endogenous rewards. This provides a principled basis for separating the two sources of variation.

They also derive a variance-covariance condition under which Monte Carlo policy evaluation becomes faster on the endogenous process. Broader speedups across reinforcement learning algorithms are presented as likely, rather than established universally. Two algorithms discover exogenous variables, and experiments on several decision processes find them practical and capable of substantial acceleration. The theoretical speedup remains tied to the stated condition.
summary.tldr: The paper identifies when uncontrollable state and reward variation can be separated out to accelerate reinforcement learning.

title: Discovering and Removing Exogenous State Variables and Rewards for Reinforcement Learning

abstract: The optimization of submodular functions on the integer lattice has received much attention recently, but the objective functions of many applications are non-submodular. We provide two approximation algorithms for maximizing a non-submodular function on the integer lattice subject to a cardinality constraint; these are the first algorithms for this purpose that have polynomial query complexity. We propose a general framework for influence maximization on the integer lattice that generalizes prior works on this topic, and we demonstrate the efficiency of our algorithms in this context.
originalAbstract: The optimization of submodular functions on the integer lattice has received much attention recently, but the objective functions of many applications are non-submodular. We provide two approximation algorithms for maximizing a non-submodular function on the integer lattice subject to a cardinality constraint; these are the first algorithms for this purpose that have polynomial query complexity. We propose a general framework for influence maximization on the integer lattice that generalizes prior works on this topic, and we demonstrate the efficiency of our algorithms in this context.

paragraphs: Optimization on the integer lattice chooses integer-valued quantities rather than only deciding whether individual elements are included. Many studied methods rely on submodularity, a form of diminishing returns. The paper addresses monotonic objectives that need not have that property, broadening the optimization setting to accommodate applications outside the usual submodular framework.

The authors provide two approximation algorithms for maximizing such objectives under a cardinality constraint, which limits the total amount selected. They identify these as the first algorithms for this purpose with polynomial query complexity. This guarantee concerns how many queries the algorithms make to the objective, while the solutions they return are approximate rather than asserted to be exact optima.

The paper also introduces an integer-lattice framework for influence maximization that generalizes earlier work. Within that application, the authors demonstrate the efficiency of their algorithms. The contribution thus combines algorithmic guarantees with an application framework, showing how optimization beyond submodularity can support a broader formulation of influence allocation.
summary.tldr: Two approximation algorithms achieve polynomial query complexity for cardinality-constrained maximization of non-submodular monotonic integer-lattice objectives.

title: Fast Maximization of Non-Submodular, Monotonic Functions on the Integer Lattice

abstract: Recently, the decentralized optimization problem is attracting growing attention. Most existing methods are deterministic with high per-iteration cost and have a convergence rate quadratically depending on the problem condition number. Besides, the dense communication is necessary to ensure the convergence even if the dataset is sparse. In this paper, we generalize the decentralized optimization problem to a monotone operator root finding problem, and propose a stochastic algorithm named DSBA that (1) converges geometrically with a rate linearly depending on the problem condition number, and (2) can be implemented using sparse communication only. Additionally, DSBA handles important learning problems like AUC-maximization which can not be tackled efficiently in the previous problem setting. Experiments on convex minimization and AUC-maximization validate the efficiency of our method.

Most existing methods are deterministic with high per-iteration cost and have a convergence rate quadratically depending on the problem condition number. Besides, the dense communication is necessary to ensure the convergence even if the dataset is sparse. In this paper, we generalize the decentralized optimization problem to a monotone operator root finding problem, and propose a stochastic algorithm named DSBA that (1) converges geometrically with a rate linearly depending on the problem condition number, and (2) can be implemented using sparse communication only. Additionally, DSBA handles important learning problems like AUC-maximization which can not be tackled efficiently in the previous problem setting. Experiments on convex minimization and AUC-maximization validate the efficiency of our method.

paragraphs: Decentralized learning must manage both local computation and communication. The paper identifies two obstacles in existing methods: expensive deterministic iterations with quadratic dependence on the condition number, and a need for dense communication even when data are sparse. It develops a stochastic method intended to improve both aspects of the learning process.

The authors broaden decentralized optimization into a monotone operator root-finding problem and introduce DSBA within that formulation. DSBA converges geometrically, with a rate depending linearly on the condition number, and can be implemented using sparse communication only. These properties connect improved convergence behavior with a communication pattern suited to sparse information.

The broader formulation also accommodates learning objectives such as AUC maximization that were not handled efficiently in the previous setting. Experiments on convex minimization and AUC maximization validate the method’s efficiency. The contribution combines a more general mathematical problem formulation with an algorithm that offers both convergence and communication benefits in the setting studied.
summary.tldr: DSBA enables stochastic decentralized learning with geometric convergence, linear condition-number dependence, and sparse communication.

title: Towards More Efficient Stochastic Decentralized Learning: Faster Convergence and Sparse Communication

abstract: Many sequence prediction tasks admit multiple correct outputs and so, it is often useful to decode a set of outputs that maximize some task-specific set-level metric. However, retooling standard sequence prediction procedures tailored towards predicting the single best output leads to the decoding of sets containing very similar sequences; failing to capture the variation in the output space. To address this, we propose $\nabla$BS, a trainable decoding procedure that outputs a set of sequences, highly valued according to the metric. Our method tightly integrates the training and decoding phases and further allows for the optimization of the task-specific metric addressing the shortcomings of standard sequence prediction. Further, we discuss the trade-offs of commonly used set-level metrics and motivate a new set-level metric that naturally evaluates the notion of “capturing the variation in the output space”. Finally, we show results on the image captioning task and find that our model outperforms standard techniques and natural ablations.

However, retooling standard sequence prediction procedures tailored towards predicting the single best output leads to the decoding of sets containing very similar sequences; failing to capture the variation in the output space. To address this, we propose $\nabla$BS, a trainable decoding procedure that outputs a set of sequences, highly valued according to the metric. Our method tightly integrates the training and decoding phases and further allows for the optimization of the task-specific metric addressing the shortcomings of standard sequence prediction. Further, we discuss the trade-offs of commonly used set-level metrics and motivate a new set-level metric that naturally evaluates the notion of “capturing the variation in the output space”. Finally, we show results on the image captioning task and find that our model outperforms standard techniques and natural ablations.

paragraphs: Some prediction problems have multiple valid sequence outputs. Returning several outputs is useful only if the collection captures meaningful alternatives; standard procedures designed to find one best sequence can instead produce a set of nearly identical candidates. This paper treats the quality of the complete output set as a learning objective.

The proposed decoding method, ∇BS, integrates training with the procedure used to generate a set of sequences. It allows optimization of a task-specific metric applied to the whole set. This gives training a direct connection to the quality of the collection produced at decoding time, including aspects that individual sequence scores may fail to capture.

The authors also examine trade-offs among common set-level metrics and motivate a new metric for capturing variation in the output space. On image captioning, their model outperforms standard techniques and natural ablations. The findings support jointly considering decoding and set-level evaluation when multiple outputs are desired, with the reported performance evidence coming from the captioning task.
summary.tldr: A trainable set decoder jointly optimizes sequence generation and set-level quality, improving image-caption collections in the reported evaluation.

title: Trainable Decoding of Sets of Sequences for Neural Sequence Models

abstract: Due to their wide field of view, omnidirectional cameras are frequently used by autonomous vehicles, drones and robots for navigation and other computer vision tasks. The images captured by such cameras, are often analyzed and classified with techniques designed for planar images that unfortunately fail to properly handle the native geometry of such images and therefore results in suboptimal performance. In this paper we aim at improving popular deep convolutional neural networks so that they can properly take into account the specific properties of omnidirectional data. In particular we propose an algorithm that adapts convolutional layers, which often serve as a core building block of a CNN, to the properties of omnidirectional images. Thus, our filters have a shape and size that adapt to the location on the omnidirectional image. We show that our method is not limited to spherical surfaces and is able to incorporate the knowledge about any kind of projective geometry inside the deep learning network. As depicted by our experiments, our method outperforms the existing deep neural network techniques for omnidirectional image classification and compression tasks.

The images captured by such cameras, are often analyzed and classified with techniques designed for planar images that unfortunately fail to properly handle the native geometry of such images and therefore results in suboptimal performance. In this paper we aim at improving popular deep convolutional neural networks so that they can properly take into account the specific properties of omnidirectional data. In particular we propose an algorithm that adapts convolutional layers, which often serve as a core building block of a CNN, to the properties of omnidirectional images. Thus, our filters have a shape and size that adapt to the location on the omnidirectional image. We show that our method is not limited to spherical surfaces and is able to incorporate the knowledge about any kind of projective geometry inside the deep learning network. As depicted by our experiments, our method outperforms the existing deep neural network techniques for omnidirectional image classification and compression tasks.

paragraphs: Omnidirectional cameras provide a wide field of view, making them useful for navigation and other vision tasks. However, their images have geometry that methods designed for planar images may handle poorly. This paper adapts convolutional neural networks so that their processing takes the properties of omnidirectional image formation into account.

The proposed algorithm changes convolutional layers by making each filter's shape and size depend on its location in the image. This gives the network a way to incorporate image geometry directly into a core operation. The authors also show that the approach is not restricted to spherical surfaces and can incorporate knowledge of other projective geometries.

Experiments show better performance than existing deep neural network techniques on omnidirectional image classification and compression. These results support the value of modifying convolution to reflect the geometry of the input in the evaluated tasks. The broader methodological contribution is a way to put known projection structure inside the network, rather than relying on planar-image processing to accommodate it implicitly.
summary.tldr: Location-dependent convolutional filters incorporate projective geometry and improve the reported classification and compression results for omnidirectional images.

title: Geometry Aware Convolutional Filters for Omnidirectional Images Representation

abstract: Efficient construction of checkpoints/snapshots is a critical tool for training and diagnosing deep learning models. In this paper, we propose a lossy compression scheme for checkpoint constructions (called LC-Checkpoint). LC-Checkpoint simultaneously maximizes the compression rate and optimizes the recovery speed, under the assumption that SGD is used to train the model. LC-Checkpoint uses quantization and priority promotion to store the most crucial information for SGD to recover, and then uses a Huffman coding to leverage the non-uniform distribution of the gradient scales. Our extensive experiments show that LC-Checkpoint achieves a compression rate up to 28{\texttimes} and recovery speedup up to 5.77{\texttimes} over a state-of-the-art algorithm (SCAR).

paragraphs: Checkpoints preserve model states that are useful for training and diagnosis, but storing and recovering them can be expensive. This paper introduces LC-Checkpoint, a lossy compression method designed to improve both checkpoint compactness and recovery speed. Its design explicitly assumes that the model is trained using stochastic gradient descent.

LC-Checkpoint combines quantization with priority promotion to retain information that is most important for SGD recovery. It then applies Huffman coding to exploit the uneven distribution of gradient scales. These components connect the storage representation to the recovery process, so the method considers what training needs after a checkpoint is restored.

The experiments report compression of up to 28 times and recovery speedups of up to 5.77 times over SCAR, the comparison method. These are reported maxima, rather than uniform gains for every checkpoint. The findings demonstrate that a checkpoint scheme tailored to SGD can improve both storage efficiency and recovery performance, with lossy storage forming an explicit part of the approach.
summary.tldr: LC-Checkpoint uses SGD-aware lossy compression to reduce checkpoint storage and accelerate recovery in the reported experiments.

title: On Efficient Constructions of Checkpoints

abstract: Deep neural networks exhibit complex learning dynamics due to their non-convex loss landscapes. Second-order optimization methods facilitate learning dynamics by compensating for ill-conditioned curvature. In this work, we investigate how curvature correction modifies the learning dynamics in deep linear neural networks and provide analytical solutions. We derive a generalized conservation law that preserves the path of parameter dynamics from curvature correction, which shows that curvature correction only modifies the temporal profiles of dynamics along the path. We show that while curvature correction accelerates the convergence dynamics of the input-output map, it can also negatively affect the generalization performance. Our analysis also reveals an undesirable effect of curvature correction that compromises stability of parameters dynamics during learning, especially with block-diagonal approximation of natural gradient descent. We introduce fractional curvature correction that resolves this problem while retaining most of the acceleration benefits of full curvature correction.

paragraphs: Curvature-aware optimization adjusts learning updates to account for the shape of a loss landscape. Although these adjustments can accelerate training, their effects on the trajectory of network parameters are more complicated. This paper investigates those effects in deep linear neural networks, where the authors can derive analytical solutions for the learning dynamics.

A generalized conservation law shows that, in the analyzed setting, curvature correction preserves the path taken by the parameters while changing how quickly they move along it. This separates the geometry of the learning trajectory from its timing. The analysis also shows faster convergence of the network’s input-output map, alongside the possibility of worse generalization.

The authors identify another adverse effect: curvature correction can destabilize parameter dynamics, particularly when natural gradient descent uses a block-diagonal approximation. They introduce fractional curvature correction to resolve this stability problem while retaining most of the acceleration from full correction. The contribution explains why faster convergence, stable parameter evolution, and good generalization need to be considered separately within this analytical setting.
summary.tldr: Analysis of deep linear networks shows how curvature correction accelerates learning while potentially harming stability and generalization.

title: Curvature-corrected learning dynamics in deep neural networks

abstract: We present a new piecewise linear regression methodology that utilises fitting a \emph{difference of convex} functions (DC functions) to the data. These are functions $f$ that may be represented as the difference $\phi_1 - \phi_2$ for a choice of \emph{convex} functions $\phi_1, \phi_2$. The method proceeds by estimating piecewise-liner convex functions, in a manner similar to max-affine regression, whose difference approximates the data. The choice of the function is regularised by a new seminorm over the class of DC functions that controls the $\ell_\infty$ Lipschitz constant of the estimate. The resulting methodology can be efficiently implemented via Quadratic programming \emph{even in high dimensions}, and is shown to have close to minimax statistical risk. We empirically validate the method, showing it to be practically implementable, and to outperform existing regression methods in accuracy on real-world datasets.

paragraphs: Piecewise linear regression represents a relationship using linear pieces that can accommodate changes in behavior across the input space. This paper constructs such an estimate as the difference between two convex functions. Each component is itself piecewise linear, fitted in a manner related to max-affine regression, and their difference is used to approximate the observed data.

The method introduces a seminorm to regularize this class of difference-of-convex functions. That regularizer controls the estimate’s Lipschitz constant in the infinity norm, providing a way to constrain how sharply its predictions can change. The representation and regularization work together to balance flexibility with control over the fitted function’s variation.

The resulting fitting procedure can be implemented efficiently through quadratic programming, including in high dimensions. The authors establish statistical risk close to the minimax benchmark and empirically demonstrate practical implementation. On real-world datasets, they report greater accuracy than existing regression methods. The contribution combines a flexible function representation, a regularizer with a clear mathematical role, and a tractable optimization procedure.
summary.tldr: Fitting a regularized difference of piecewise linear convex functions yields efficient regression with near-minimax statistical risk.

title: Piecewise Linear Regression via a Difference of Convex Functions

abstract: Machine learning models, especially deep neural networks are known to be susceptible to privacy attacks such as membership inference where an adversary can detect whether a data point was used to train a model. Such privacy risks are exacerbated when a model is used for predictions on an unseen data distribution. To alleviate privacy attacks, we demonstrate the benefit of predictive models that are based on the causal relationships between input features and the outcome. We first show that models learnt using causal structure generalize better to unseen data, especially on data from different distributions than the train distribution. Based on this generalization property, we establish a theoretical link between causality and privacy: compared to associational models, causal models provide stronger differential privacy guarantees and are more robust to membership inference attacks. Experiments on simulated Bayesian networks and the colored-MNIST dataset show that associational models exhibit upto 80% attack accuracy under different test distributions and sample sizes whereas causal models exhibit attack accuracy close to a random guess.

paragraphs: A membership inference attack tries to determine whether a particular example appeared in a model’s training data. This paper investigates how learning causal relationships between inputs and outcomes can reduce that privacy risk, especially when the model encounters a different data distribution after training.

The authors first show that models learned using causal structure generalize better to unseen data, with particular benefits under distribution changes. They then use this generalization property to establish a theoretical connection between causal learning and privacy. Relative to models based on associations, the causal models offer stronger differential privacy guarantees and greater resistance to membership inference.

Experiments use simulated Bayesian networks and colored-MNIST. Across the tested distributions and sample sizes, attacks on associational models reach accuracy as high as 80%, while attacks on causal models perform close to random guessing. These findings support causal structure as a way to alleviate privacy attacks in the studied settings, connecting how a model generalizes with how much it reveals about training membership.
summary.tldr: Learning causal relationships can improve generalization under distribution shifts and reduce vulnerability to membership inference attacks.

title: Alleviating Privacy Attacks via Causal Learning

abstract: Self-supervision as an emerging technique has been employed to train convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for more transferrable, generalizable, and robust representation learning of images. Its introduction to graph convolutional networks (GCNs) operating on graph data is however rarely explored. In this study, we report the first systematic exploration and assessment of incorporating self-supervision into GCNs. We first elaborate three mechanisms to incorporate self-supervision into GCNs, analyze the limitations of pretraining & finetuning and self-training, and proceed to focus on multi-task learning. Moreover, we propose to investigate three novel self-supervised learning tasks for GCNs with theoretical rationales and numerical comparisons. Lastly, we further integrate multi-task self-supervision into graph adversarial training. Our results show that, with properly designed task forms and incorporation mechanisms, self-supervision benefits GCNs in gaining more generalizability and robustness. Our codes are available at https://github.com/Shen-Lab/SS-GCNs.

paragraphs: Self-supervision has been useful for learning image representations, but its benefits for graph convolutional networks require separate investigation. This paper systematically studies how to incorporate self-supervision into GCNs and when doing so improves their behavior. It treats the design of the auxiliary task and the way it enters training as linked decisions.

The authors examine three incorporation mechanisms, discussing limitations of pretraining followed by finetuning and of self-training before focusing on multi-task learning. They propose three self-supervised tasks for GCNs, supported by theoretical rationales and numerical comparisons. They also integrate multi-task self-supervision into graph adversarial training to investigate robustness.

The results show gains in generalizability and robustness when the task forms and incorporation mechanisms are appropriately designed. That qualification is central to the finding: the paper supports particular ways of introducing self-supervision, rather than claiming that any auxiliary task will help. Its contribution is an organized assessment of the choices that determine whether self-supervision improves graph learning.
summary.tldr: Self-supervision improves GCN generalizability and robustness when its auxiliary tasks and training mechanisms are appropriately designed.

title: When Does Self-Supervision Help Graph Convolutional Networks?

abstract: Imitation learning in a high-dimensional environment is challenging. Most inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) methods fail to outperform the demonstrator in such a high-dimensional environment, e.g., Atari domain. To address this challenge, we propose a novel reward learning module to generate intrinsic reward signals via a generative model. Our generative method can perform better forward state transition and backward action encoding, which improves the module’s dynamics modeling ability in the environment. Thus, our module provides the imitation agent both the intrinsic intention of the demonstrator and a better exploration ability, which is critical for the agent to outperform the demonstrator. Empirical results show that our method outperforms state-of-the-art IRL methods on multiple Atari games, even with one-life demonstration. Remarkably, our method achieves performance that is up to 5 times the performance of the demonstration.

paragraphs: Learning from demonstrations in high-dimensional environments presents a challenge beyond reproducing observed behavior: an agent must explore effectively if it is to surpass its demonstrator. The paper focuses on this problem in settings such as Atari, where it reports that most inverse reinforcement learning methods struggle to exceed demonstration performance.

The proposed reward-learning module uses a generative model to produce intrinsic reward signals. It improves forward state-transition modeling and backward action encoding, strengthening its model of the environment’s dynamics. The authors connect these capabilities to two benefits: conveying the demonstrator’s underlying intention and supporting better exploration by the imitation agent.

On multiple Atari games, the method outperforms state-of-the-art inverse reinforcement learning approaches, including when supplied with a one-life demonstration. Its strongest reported result reaches up to five times the demonstration’s performance. That figure describes the reported upper end of the empirical results, while the broader finding is that dynamics-informed intrinsic rewards can help imitation move beyond the behavior directly demonstrated.
summary.tldr: A generative reward module improves imitation and exploration on Atari, with reported performance reaching up to five times the demonstration.

title: Intrinsic Reward Driven Imitation Learning via Generative Model

abstract: Kernel ridge regression is well-known to achieve minimax optimal rates in low-dimensional settings. However, its behavior in high dimensions is much less understood. Recent work establishes consistency for high-dimensional kernel regression for a number of specific assumptions on the data distribution. In this paper, we show that in high dimensions, the rotational invariance property of commonly studied kernels (such as RBF, inner product kernels and fully-connected NTK of any depth) leads to inconsistent estimation unless the ground truth is a low-degree polynomial. Our lower bound on the generalization error holds for a wide range of distributions and kernels with different eigenvalue decays. This lower bound suggests that consistency results for kernel ridge regression in high dimensions generally require a more refined analysis that depends on the structure of the kernel beyond its eigenvalue decay.
