paragraphs: Kernel ridge regression has strong statistical guarantees in low dimensions, but those guarantees do not automatically explain its behavior in high-dimensional problems. This paper examines a shared property of many common kernels: rotational invariance. The examples covered include radial basis function kernels, inner-product kernels, and fully connected neural tangent kernels of any depth.

The authors establish a lower bound on generalization error across a wide range of data distributions and kernels with different eigenvalue decay patterns. In the high-dimensional settings studied, rotational invariance leads to inconsistent estimation unless the target is a low-degree polynomial. Being such a polynomial is an exception to this obstruction, rather than a universal guarantee of successful estimation.

The result changes what a useful high-dimensional analysis must examine. Eigenvalue decay alone does not capture the kernel structure responsible for the identified failure. The paper therefore argues that consistency analyses generally need a more detailed account of kernel structure. Its contribution is to expose a structural barrier that can persist despite spectral descriptions that appear favorable.
summary.tldr: Rotational invariance creates a high-dimensional consistency barrier for common kernels unless the target is a low-degree polynomial.

title: How rotational invariance of common kernels prevents generalization in high dimensions

abstract: The usual setting for learning the structure and parameters of a graphical model assumes the availability of independent samples produced from the corresponding multivariate probability distribution. However, for many models the mixing time of the respective Markov chain can be very large and i.i.d. samples may not be obtained. We study the problem of reconstructing binary graphical models from correlated samples produced by a dynamical process, which is natural in many applications. We analyze the sample complexity of two estimators that are based on the interaction screening objective and the conditional likelihood loss. We observe that for samples coming from a dynamical process far from equilibrium, the sample complexity reduces exponentially compared to a dynamical process that mixes quickly.

However, for many models the mixing time of the respective Markov chain can be very large and i.i.d. samples may not be obtained. We analyze the sample complexity of two estimators that are based on the interaction screening objective and the conditional likelihood loss. We observe that for samples coming from a dynamical process far from equilibrium, the sample complexity reduces exponentially compared to a dynamical process that mixes quickly.

paragraphs: Learning a graphical model usually starts with independent observations from its probability distribution. That assumption can be difficult to satisfy when observations come from a Markov chain that takes a long time to mix. This paper instead studies reconstruction of binary graphical models using correlated observations generated by a dynamical process, a setting natural to many applications.

The authors analyze the number of samples needed by two estimators. One uses an interaction screening objective, and the other uses a conditional likelihood loss. Both are examined in the dynamical-data setting, making the process that produces observations part of the learning analysis rather than treating every observation as an independent draw.

The reported finding is that samples from dynamics far from equilibrium can yield an exponential reduction in sample complexity compared with a quickly mixing dynamical process. This highlights the informational role of the observation process: data gathered away from equilibrium can be particularly useful for reconstruction in the studied setting. It motivates evaluating dynamics as a source of learning information, alongside the graphical model being recovered.
summary.tldr: The studied estimators can reconstruct binary graphical models with exponentially fewer samples from far-from-equilibrium dynamics than from quickly mixing dynamics.

title: Exponential Reduction in Sample Complexity with Learning of Ising Model Dynamics

abstract: One of the ways that machine learning algorithms can help control the spread of an infectious disease is by building models that predict who is likely to become infected making them good candidates for preemptive interventions. In this work we ask: can we build reliable infection prediction models when the observed data is collected under limited, and biased testing that prioritizes testing symptomatic individuals? Our analysis suggests that when the infection is highly transmissible, incomplete testing might be sufficient to achieve good out-of-sample prediction error. Guided by this insight, we develop an algorithm that predicts infections, and show that it outperforms baselines on simulated data. We apply our model to data from a large hospital to predict Clostridioides difficile infections; a communicable disease that is characterized by both symptomatically infected and asymptomatic (i.e., untested) carriers. Using a proxy instead of the unobserved untested-infected state, we show that our model outperforms benchmarks in predicting infections.

paragraphs: Predicting who may become infected could help identify candidates for preventive intervention. Training such models is difficult when testing is limited and favors people with symptoms. The observed records then give an incomplete and biased picture of infection, since some infected people may carry the disease without being tested.

The paper investigates whether useful prediction remains possible under this testing process. Its analysis suggests that incomplete testing might still support good predictions on new data when infection is highly transmissible. Guided by that conditional finding, the authors develop an infection prediction algorithm and show that it outperforms comparison methods on simulated data.

The authors also apply the model to hospital data on Clostridioides difficile, which includes symptomatic infections and asymptomatic carriers. Because the infection status of untested people is unobserved, this evaluation uses a proxy for that state. The model outperforms benchmarks in this setting, providing empirical support for the approach while preserving the distinction between proxy-based evaluation and directly observing every infection.
summary.tldr: The paper develops an infection predictor motivated by evidence that highly transmissible diseases may remain predictable despite incomplete, symptom-biased testing.

title: Exploiting structured data for learning contagious diseases under incomplete testing

abstract: CNNs and computational models of biological vision share some fundamental principles, which opened new avenues of research. However, fruitful cross-field research is hampered by conventional CNN architectures being based on spatially and depthwise discrete representations, which cannot accommodate certain aspects of biological complexity such as continuously varying receptive field sizes and dynamics of neuronal responses. Here we propose deep continuous networks (DCNs), which combine spatially continuous filters, with the continuous depth framework of neural ODEs. This allows us to learn the spatial support of the filters during training, as well as model the continuous evolution of feature maps, linking DCNs closely to biological models. We show that DCNs are versatile and highly applicable to standard image classification and reconstruction problems, where they improve parameter and data efficiency, and allow for meta-parametrization. We illustrate the biological plausibility of the scale distributions learned by DCNs and explore their performance in a neuroscientifically inspired pattern completion task. Finally, we investigate an efficient implementation of DCNs by changing input contrast.

paragraphs: Convolutional networks and biological vision models share useful principles, but conventional networks divide both space and depth into discrete units. That structure makes it difficult to capture continuously varying receptive field sizes and evolving neuronal responses. Deep continuous networks address this mismatch by making both spatial filtering and network depth continuous.

The architecture combines spatially continuous filters with the continuous-depth framework of neural ordinary differential equations. It can learn the spatial extent of its filters during training while modeling the continuous evolution of feature maps. These two features connect the network's representation and dynamics more closely to the biological models motivating the work.

The authors demonstrate image classification and reconstruction applications, reporting improved parameter and data efficiency and support for meta-parametrization. They also examine the biological plausibility of learned scale distributions and investigate a neuroscience-inspired pattern completion task. Finally, they explore an efficient implementation through changes in input contrast, extending the study from architectural principles to practical computation.
summary.tldr: Deep continuous networks combine continuous spatial filters and neural ODE depth to learn filter scales and evolving visual representations.

title: Deep Continuous Networks

abstract: We present an analytical policy update rule that is independent of parametric function approximators. The policy update rule is suitable for optimizing general stochastic policies and has a monotonic improvement guarantee. It is derived from a closed-form solution to trust-region optimization using calculus of variation, following a new theoretical result that tightens existing bounds for policy improvement using trust-region methods. The update rule builds a connection between policy search methods and value function methods. Moreover, off-policy reinforcement learning algorithms can be derived from the update rule since it does not need to compute integration over on-policy states. In addition, the update rule extends immediately to cooperative multi-agent systems when policy updates are performed by one agent at a time.

paragraphs: The paper develops a mathematical rule for improving a stochastic policy, which describes how an agent chooses among actions. The rule is independent of a particular parameterized function approximator. This makes the update a statement about policies themselves, rather than a procedure tied to one neural network or other chosen representation.

The authors derive the rule by solving a trust-region optimization problem in closed form using calculus of variations. A trust region controls how far a policy update moves from the current policy. Their derivation follows a new result that tightens existing policy-improvement bounds, and the resulting update carries a guarantee of monotonic improvement.

The rule also connects policy search with value-function methods. Because it does not require integration over states visited by the current policy, it can support the derivation of off-policy reinforcement learning algorithms. It further extends directly to cooperative multi-agent settings when agents update one at a time. That sequential-update condition is part of the stated extension.
summary.tldr: A closed-form trust-region policy update guarantees monotonic improvement and supports off-policy learning and sequential updates in cooperative multi-agent systems.

title: An Analytical Update Rule for General Policy Optimization

abstract: When deployed, AI agents will encounter problems that are beyond their autonomous problem-solving capabilities. Leveraging human assistance can help agents overcome their inherent limitations and robustly cope with unfamiliar situations. We present a general interactive framework that enables an agent to request and interpret rich, contextually useful information from an assistant that has knowledge about the task and the environment. We demonstrate the practicality of our framework on a simulated human-assisted navigation problem. Aided with an assistance-requesting policy learned by our method, a navigation agent achieves up to a 7{\texttimes} improvement in success rate on tasks that take place in previously unseen environments, compared to fully autonomous behavior. We show that the agent can take advantage of different types of information depending on the context, and analyze the benefits and challenges of learning the assistance-requesting policy when the assistant can recursively decompose tasks into subtasks.

paragraphs: An agent facing an unfamiliar situation may need help with more than a single answer or action. This paper studies how an agent can learn to request useful information from an assistant who understands its task and environment. The central problem is making assistance part of the agent’s decision process, including interpreting what the assistant provides.

The proposed interactive framework supports rich information whose usefulness depends on context. Its practical demonstration involves navigation with simulated human assistance. The agent learns an assistance-requesting policy, allowing it to take advantage of different kinds of information in different situations. The authors also examine assistants that can recursively break a task into smaller subtasks.

In previously unseen navigation environments, the assisted agent achieves up to seven times the success rate of fully autonomous behavior. That is a reported maximum improvement in the studied setting. The work also analyzes benefits and challenges of learning to ask for help when task decomposition is available, connecting assistance quality with the structure of the task.
summary.tldr: A learned assistance-requesting policy helps navigation agents use contextually useful guidance, with up to sevenfold success-rate improvements in unseen environments.

title: A Framework for Learning to Request Rich and Contextually Useful Information from Humans

abstract: Feature selection helps reduce data acquisition costs in ML, but the standard approach is to train models with static feature subsets. Here, we consider the dynamic feature selection (DFS) problem where a model sequentially queries features based on the presently available information. DFS is often addressed with reinforcement learning, but we explore a simpler approach of greedily selecting features based on their conditional mutual information. This method is theoretically appealing but requires oracle access to the data distribution, so we develop a learning approach based on amortized optimization. The proposed method is shown to recover the greedy policy when trained to optimality, and it outperforms numerous existing feature selection methods in our experiments, thus validating it as a simple but powerful approach for this problem.

paragraphs: Feature selection can reduce the cost of acquiring data for a prediction. A fixed feature subset uses the same inputs each time, while dynamic feature selection chooses the next feature based on information already available. This paper studies that sequential setting and develops an approach based on greedily choosing features using conditional mutual information.

The greedy criterion is theoretically attractive, but computing it directly requires oracle access to the data distribution. The authors address that obstacle through amortized optimization: they learn an approach for making the selections rather than assuming that the ideal distributional information is available at decision time. This offers a simpler alternative to reinforcement learning approaches commonly used for dynamic selection.

The paper shows that the learned method recovers the greedy policy when training reaches optimality. That condition is part of the theoretical claim; the result concerns matching the greedy policy. Experiments also show improvements over numerous existing feature selection methods. Together, the findings provide both a conditional justification for the learning procedure and empirical support for choosing features as information accumulates.
summary.tldr: An amortized learning method selects features dynamically and recovers a greedy conditional-mutual-information policy when trained to optimality.

title: Learning to Maximize Mutual Information for Dynamic Feature Selection

abstract: We study the task of agnostically learning halfspaces under the Gaussian distribution. Specifically, given labeled examples $(\\mathbf{x},y)$ from an unknown distribution on $\\mathbb{R}^n \\times \\{\pm 1 \\}$, whose marginal distribution on $\\mathbf{x}$ is the standard Gaussian and the labels $y$ can be arbitrary, the goal is to output a hypothesis with 0-1 loss $\\mathrm{OPT}+\\epsilon$, where $\\mathrm{OPT}$ is the 0-1 loss of the best-fitting halfspace. We prove a near-optimal computational hardness result for this task, under the widely believed sub-exponential time hardness of the Learning with Errors (LWE) problem. Prior hardness results are either qualitatively suboptimal or apply to restricted families of algorithms. Our techniques extend to yield near-optimal lower bounds for related problems, including ReLU regression.

paragraphs: The paper studies learning a linear decision boundary when the input vectors follow a standard Gaussian distribution but their binary labels can be arbitrary. The learner aims to produce predictions whose classification error is at most epsilon above the error of the best-fitting halfspace. This is an agnostic task: the labels need not follow a perfect linear rule.

The authors establish a near-optimal computational hardness result under the widely believed assumption that Learning with Errors remains hard in sub-exponential time. The result is therefore conditional on a cryptographic hardness assumption. It addresses computational difficulty even with a specifically structured input distribution, rather than relying on unrestricted or irregular input vectors.

Previous hardness results were either qualitatively weaker or limited to restricted algorithm families. The paper strengthens this picture and extends its techniques to related problems, including ReLU regression. Its contribution is to clarify the computational barriers to approaching the best achievable prediction error, with near-optimal lower bounds rather than a new learning algorithm.
summary.tldr: Under a Learning with Errors hardness assumption, the paper proves near-optimal computational barriers for agnostic halfspace learning and related ReLU regression.

title: Near-Optimal Cryptographic Hardness of Agnostically Learning Halfspaces and ReLU Regression under Gaussian Marginals

abstract: Recently, the contrastive language-image pre-training, e.g., CLIP, has demonstrated promising results on various downstream tasks. The pre-trained model can capture enriched visual concepts for images by learning from a large scale of text-image data. However, transferring the learned visual knowledge to open-vocabulary semantic segmentation is still under-explored. In this paper, we propose a CLIP-based model named SegCLIP for the topic of open-vocabulary segmentation in an annotation-free manner. The SegCLIP achieves segmentation based on ViT and the main idea is to gather patches with learnable centers to semantic regions through training on text-image pairs. The gathering operation can dynamically capture the semantic groups, which can be used to generate the final segmentation results. We further propose a reconstruction loss on masked patches and a superpixel-based KL loss with pseudo-labels to enhance the visual representation. Experimental results show that our model achieves comparable or superior segmentation accuracy on the PASCAL VOC 2012 (+0.3% mIoU), PASCAL Context (+2.3% mIoU), and COCO (+2.2% mIoU) compared with baselines. We release the code at https://github.com/ArrowLuo/SegCLIP.

paragraphs: Language-image pretraining learns visual concepts from paired images and text, but transferring that knowledge to segmentation requires identifying where concepts occur within an image. SegCLIP addresses open-vocabulary semantic segmentation using a CLIP-based model trained without segmentation annotations. It turns patch-level visual representations into semantic regions.

The model uses a vision transformer and learnable centers that gather patches into groups during training on text-image pairs. These groups can change with the image and provide the basis for the final segmentation. Two additional objectives strengthen the visual representation: reconstruction of masked patches and a superpixel-based KL loss using pseudo-labels.

The authors report segmentation accuracy comparable to or better than baselines on PASCAL VOC 2012, PASCAL Context, and COCO, listing mIoU improvements of 0.3%, 2.3%, and 2.2%, respectively. These results support learnable patch aggregation as a way to connect image-text knowledge with spatial predictions. The annotation-free claim concerns the segmentation approach; paired images and text, together with generated pseudo-labels, remain part of its training process.
summary.tldr: SegCLIP learns to group image patches into semantic regions from image-text pairs for segmentation without segmentation annotations.

title: SegCLIP: Patch Aggregation with Learnable Centers for Open-Vocabulary Semantic Segmentation

abstract: Offline reinforcement learning suffers from the out-of-distribution issue and extrapolation error. Most policy constraint methods regularize the density of the trained policy towards the behavior policy, which is too restrictive in most cases. We propose Supported Trust Region optimization (STR) which performs trust region policy optimization with the policy constrained within the support of the behavior policy, enjoying the less restrictive support constraint. We show that, when assuming no approximation and sampling error, STR guarantees strict policy improvement until convergence to the optimal support-constrained policy in the dataset. Further with both errors incorporated, STR still guarantees safe policy improvement for each step. Empirical results validate the theory of STR and demonstrate its state-of-the-art performance on MuJoCo locomotion domains and much more challenging AntMaze domains.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning must improve a policy using an existing dataset, making unsupported decisions vulnerable to extrapolation error. Many methods address this by keeping the learned policy’s action probabilities close to those of the behavior policy that generated the data. This paper argues that matching those probabilities can constrain learning too strongly.

Supported Trust Region optimization, or STR, instead constrains the policy to the behavior policy’s support. The policy remains within the actions covered by that support while gaining more freedom to change their probabilities. STR combines this less restrictive condition with trust-region policy optimization, seeking improvement without requiring close agreement with the behavior policy’s density.

When approximation and sampling errors are absent, the authors prove strict improvement until convergence to the optimal policy within the dataset’s support constraint. Their analysis also provides safe stepwise improvement guarantees with both errors incorporated. Experiments on MuJoCo locomotion and the more challenging AntMaze domains support the theory and report state-of-the-art performance. The optimality claim is explicitly support constrained, rather than unrestricted over all possible policies.
summary.tldr: STR improves offline policies within behavior-policy support, providing improvement guarantees and strong reported performance with a less restrictive policy constraint.

title: Supported Trust Region Optimization for Offline Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Visual robotic manipulation research and applications often use multiple cameras, or views, to better perceive the world. How else can we utilize the richness of multi-view data? In this paper, we investigate how to learn good representations with multi-view data and utilize them for visual robotic manipulation. Specifically, we train a multi-view masked autoencoder which reconstructs pixels of randomly masked viewpoints and then learn a world model operating on the representations from the autoencoder. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in a range of scenarios, including multi-view control and single-view control with auxiliary cameras for representation learning. We also show that the multi-view masked autoencoder trained with multiple randomized viewpoints enables training a policy with strong viewpoint randomization and transferring the policy to solve real-robot tasks without camera calibration and an adaptation procedure. Video demonstrations are available at: https://sites.google.com/view/mv-mwm.

paragraphs: Multiple cameras give a robot richer observations, but their value can extend to learning better internal representations. This paper investigates that use of multiple views for visual manipulation. It trains a masked autoencoder to reconstruct pixels from randomly masked viewpoints, making reconstruction across views part of the representation-learning task.

A world model is then learned using the autoencoder’s representations. The authors demonstrate the approach both when control uses multiple views and when control uses only one view, with extra cameras contributing during representation learning. The latter setting shows that additional cameras can help shape the learned representation even when they are not all used for control.

The paper also trains the autoencoder with randomized viewpoints, enabling policy training under strong viewpoint randomization. The resulting policy transfers to real-robot tasks without camera calibration or an adaptation procedure in the demonstrated setting. These findings connect multi-view reconstruction with flexibility in camera placement: learning from varied perspectives can support policies that work across the viewpoint changes evaluated by the authors.
summary.tldr: Multi-view masked reconstruction learns representations that support robotic control and demonstrated real-robot transfer without camera calibration or adaptation.

title: Multi-View Masked World Models for Visual Robotic Manipulation

abstract: AI assistance continues to help advance applications in education, from language learning to intelligent tutoring systems, yet current methods for providing students feedback are still quite limited. Most automatic feedback systems either provide binary correctness feedback, which may not help a student understand how to improve, or require hand-coding feedback templates, which may not generalize to new domains. This can be particularly challenging for physical control tasks, where the rich diversity in student behavior and specialized domains make it challenging to leverage general-purpose assistive tools for providing feedback. We design and build CORGI, a model trained to generate language corrections for physical control tasks, such as learning to ride a bike. CORGI takes in as input a pair of student and expert trajectories, and then generates natural language corrections to help the student improve. We collect and train CORGI over data from three diverse physical control tasks (drawing, steering, and joint movement). Through both automatic and human evaluations, we show that CORGI can (i) generate valid feedback for novel student trajectories, (ii) outperform baselines on domains with novel control dynamics, and (iii) improve student learning in an interactive drawing task.

paragraphs: Feedback for a physical skill needs to explain how a learner should change their behavior. A simple correct-or-incorrect signal may not provide that guidance, while hand-written feedback templates can be difficult to transfer to new domains. CORGI is designed to generate natural-language corrections from examples of student and expert behavior.

The model receives a pair of trajectories: one showing the student's actions and one showing expert performance. It uses this comparison to produce a correction intended to help the student improve. The authors collect training data across drawing, steering, and joint movement, addressing varied forms of physical control within the same modeling approach.

Automatic and human evaluations support three findings. CORGI produces valid feedback for previously unseen student trajectories, outperforms baselines in domains with new control dynamics, and improves student learning in an interactive drawing task. These results connect feedback generation to an observed learning benefit in drawing, while the other evaluations examine whether useful corrections transfer across behaviors and control settings.
summary.tldr: CORGI compares student and expert trajectories to generate language corrections, with demonstrated learning benefits in an interactive drawing task.

title: Generating Language Corrections for Teaching Physical Control Tasks

abstract: Scientific Machine Learning (SciML) is concerned with the development of learned emulators of physical systems governed by partial differential equations (PDE). In application domains such as weather forecasting, molecular dynamics, and inverse design, ML-based surrogate models are increasingly used to augment or replace inefficient and often non-differentiable numerical simulation algorithms. While a number of ML-based methods for approximating the solutions of PDEs have been proposed in recent years, they typically do not adapt to the parameters of the PDEs, making it difficult to generalize to PDE parameters not seen during training. We propose a Channel Attention guided by PDE Parameter Embeddings (CAPE) component for neural surrogate models and a simple yet effective curriculum learning strategy. The CAPE module can be combined with any neural PDE solvers allowing them to adapt to unseen PDE parameters. The curriculum learning strategy provides a seamless transition between teacher-forcing and fully auto-regressive training. We compare CAPE in conjunction with the curriculum learning strategy using a PDE benchmark and obtain consistent and significant improvements over the baseline models. The experiments also show several advantages of CAPE, such as its increased ability to generalize to unseen PDE parameters without large increases inference time and parameter count. An implementation of the method and experiments are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/CAPE-ML4Sci-145B.

paragraphs: Neural PDE solvers approximate physical simulations, but their behavior must adapt when the parameters governing the equations change. The paper identifies limited parameter adaptation as a reason existing models struggle with PDE parameters absent from training. It proposes a component that makes those parameters an explicit guide to the model's processing.

Channel Attention guided by PDE Parameter Embeddings, or CAPE, uses parameter embeddings to guide channel attention in a neural solver. The component is designed to combine with any neural PDE solver. The authors also introduce a curriculum that gradually moves training from teacher forcing toward fully autoregressive operation, connecting training with the model's use of its own predictions.

On a PDE benchmark, CAPE combined with the curriculum produces consistent, significant improvements over baseline models. Experiments also show improved generalization to unseen PDE parameters without large increases in inference time or parameter count. The results support parameter-guided adaptation as a practical way to improve neural surrogates while keeping their additional computational burden modest.
summary.tldr: CAPE guides neural PDE solvers with equation parameters, improving generalization to unseen parameters with modest additional overhead.

title: Learning Neural PDE Solvers with Parameter-Guided Channel Attention

abstract: We study geodesically convex (g-convex) problems that can be written as a difference of Euclidean convex functions. This structure arises in key applications such as matrix scaling, M- estimators of scatter matrices, and Brascamp-Lieb inequalities. In particular, we exploit this structure to make use of the Convex-Concave Procedure (CCCP), which helps us bypass potentially expensive Riemannian operations and leads to very competitive solvers. Importantly, unlike existing theory for CCCP that ensures convergence to stationary points, we exploit the overall g-convexity structure and provide iteration complexity results for global optimality. We illustrate our results by specializing them to a few concrete optimization problems that have been previously studied in the machine learning literature. We hope our work spurs the study of mixed Euclidean-Riemannian optimization algorithms.

paragraphs: An optimization problem can have useful convexity in a curved geometry even when its ordinary Euclidean formulation looks different. This paper considers objectives that are geodesically convex and can also be expressed as the difference of two Euclidean convex functions. That combination appears in problems involving matrix scaling, scatter-matrix estimation, and Brascamp-Lieb inequalities.

The difference-of-convex structure lets the authors use the Euclidean Convex-Concave Procedure, or CCCP. This offers a way to avoid potentially expensive Riemannian operations while still exploiting the problem’s underlying geometry. The algorithmic opportunity comes from using one structure for computation and another for the convergence analysis.

Existing CCCP theory generally guarantees convergence to stationary points. By using overall geodesic convexity, the paper instead establishes iteration-complexity results for global optimality in the studied setting. Concrete optimization examples illustrate the results and yield competitive solvers. The stronger conclusion depends on this combined structure; it does not make arbitrary difference-of-convex problems globally solvable by CCCP.
summary.tldr: For geodesically convex objectives with a Euclidean difference-of-convex form, CCCP gains global-optimality complexity guarantees while avoiding potentially costly Riemannian operations.

title: Global optimality for Euclidean CCCP under Riemannian convexity

abstract: We propose to study and promote the robustness of a model as per its performance on a continuous geodesic interpolation of subpopulations, e.g., a class of samples in a classification problem. Specifically, (1) we augment the data by finding the worst-case Wasserstein barycenter on the geodesic connecting subpopulation distributions. (2) we regularize the model for smoother performance on the continuous geodesic path connecting subpopulation distributions. (3) Additionally, we provide a theoretical guarantee of robustness improvement and investigate how the geodesic location and the sample size contribute, respectively. Experimental validations of the proposed strategy on four datasets including CIFAR-100 and ImageNet, establish the efficacy of our method, e.g., our method improves the baselines’ certifiable robustness on CIFAR10 upto 7.7%, with 16.8% on empirical robustness on CIFAR-100. Our work provides a new perspective of model robustness through the lens of Wasserstein geodesic-based interpolation with a practical off-the-shelf strategy that can be combined with existing robust training methods.

paragraphs: This paper studies robustness by examining a model along continuous paths between subpopulation distributions, such as distributions associated with different classes. The paths are Wasserstein geodesics: distribution-level interpolations that provide a structured way to move between populations. The aim is to assess and improve performance throughout that progression.

The method combines two operations. It augments training data using a worst-case Wasserstein barycenter along a connecting geodesic, and it regularizes the model so performance varies more smoothly along the path. These steps use the same distributional geometry to identify difficult interpolations and encourage more stable behavior across them.

The authors provide a theoretical robustness-improvement guarantee and investigate the contributions of interpolation location and sample size. Experiments on four datasets, including CIFAR-100 and ImageNet, support the approach. The abstract reports improvements of up to 7.7% in certifiable robustness on CIFAR-10 and 16.8% in empirical robustness on CIFAR-100. The strategy can also be combined with existing robust-training methods, making distributional interpolation an additional training tool.
summary.tldr: Training on difficult distributional interpolations and smoothing performance along Wasserstein geodesics improves robustness in the reported theory and experiments.

title: Interpolation for Robust Learning: Data Augmentation on Wasserstein Geodesics

abstract: Estimating mutual correlations between random variables or data streams is essential for intelligent behavior and decision-making. As a fundamental quantity for measuring statistical relationships, mutual information has been extensively studied and utilized for its generality and equitability. However, existing methods often lack the efficiency needed for real-time applications, such as test-time optimization of a neural network, or the differentiability required for end-to-end learning, like histograms. We introduce a neural network called InfoNet, which directly outputs mutual information estimations of data streams by leveraging the attention mechanism and the computational efficiency of deep learning infrastructures. By maximizing a dual formulation of mutual information through large-scale simulated training, our approach circumvents time-consuming test-time optimization and offers generalization ability. We evaluate the effectiveness and generalization of our proposed mutual information estimation scheme on various families of distributions and applications. Our results demonstrate that InfoNet and its training process provide a graceful efficiency-accuracy trade-off and order-preserving properties. We will make the code and models available as a comprehensive toolbox to facilitate studies in different fields requiring real-time mutual information estimation.

paragraphs: Mutual information measures statistical dependence between variables or data streams. Estimating it can be computationally inconvenient: some neural approaches require optimization for each new estimation problem, while histogram methods lack the differentiability needed for end-to-end learning. InfoNet aims to make neural mutual-information estimation practical when results are needed quickly.

The model uses attention to process data streams and directly output an estimate. Its expensive learning phase happens beforehand through large-scale simulated training that maximizes a dual formulation of mutual information. This separates learning how to estimate dependence from applying the estimator to new inputs, removing the need for test-time optimization.

Evaluations cover several distribution families and applications, examining both effectiveness and generalization. The reported results show an efficiency-accuracy trade-off and order-preserving properties, supporting uses where estimates must also reflect relative dependence. The contribution is a reusable estimation approach whose training prepares it for new data streams, with empirical evidence that this reuse can balance speed and estimation quality.
summary.tldr: InfoNet learns from simulated data to estimate mutual information directly, avoiding neural-network optimization at test time.

title: InfoNet: Neural Estimation of Mutual Information without Test-Time Optimization

abstract: The biological functions of proteins often depend on dynamic structural ensembles. In this work, we develop a flow-based generative modeling approach for learning and sampling the conformational landscapes of proteins. We repurpose highly accurate single-state predictors such as AlphaFold and ESMFold and fine-tune them under a custom flow matching framework to obtain sequence-conditioned generative models of protein structure called AlphaFlow and ESMFlow. When trained and evaluated on the PDB, our method provides a superior combination of precision and diversity compared to AlphaFold with MSA subsampling. When further trained on ensembles from all-atom MD, our method accurately captures conformational flexibility, positional distributions, and higher-order ensemble observables for unseen proteins. Moreover, our method can diversify a static PDB structure with faster wall-clock convergence to certain equilibrium properties than replicate MD trajectories, demonstrating its potential as a proxy for expensive physics-based simulations. Code is available at https://github.com/bjing2016/alphaflow.

paragraphs: A protein’s function often depends on the range of shapes it can adopt. This paper develops models that generate collections of plausible structures from a protein sequence. The aim is to represent its conformational landscape: the structural variation that a single predicted shape cannot capture.

The authors adapt AlphaFold and ESMFold, which predict individual structures, by fine-tuning them with a custom flow matching framework. The resulting models, AlphaFlow and ESMFlow, generate structures conditioned on sequence. In training and evaluation using the PDB, the approach offers a better combination of precision and diversity than AlphaFold with MSA subsampling.

Additional training on ensembles from all-atom molecular dynamics enables the method to capture flexibility, positional distributions, and more complex ensemble properties for unseen proteins. It can also generate variation around a static PDB structure, reaching certain equilibrium properties faster in wall-clock time than replicate molecular dynamics trajectories. These findings support its potential as a proxy for expensive simulations, with the speed claim specifically tied to those properties.
summary.tldr: AlphaFlow and ESMFlow adapt protein structure predictors into generative models that capture structural ensembles and can accelerate estimation of certain equilibrium properties.

title: AlphaFold Meets Flow Matching for Generating Protein Ensembles

abstract: While recent large-scale text-to-speech (TTS) models have achieved significant progress, they still fall shorts in speech quality, similarity, and prosody. Considering that speech intricately encompasses various attributes (e.g., content, prosody, timbre, and acoustic details) that pose significant challenges for generation, a natural idea is to factorize speech into individual subspaces representing different attributes and generate them individually. Motivated by it, we propose a TTS system with novel factorized diffusion models to generate natural speech in a zero-shot way. Specifically, 1) we design a neural codec with factorized vector quantization (FVQ) to disentangle speech waveform into subspaces of content, prosody, timbre, and acoustic details; 2) we propose a factorized diffusion model, which generates attributes in each subspace following its corresponding prompt. With this factorization design, our method can effectively and efficiently model the intricate speech with disentangled subspaces in a divide-and-conquer way. Experimental results show that our method outperforms the state-of-the-art TTS systems on quality, similarity, prosody, and intelligibility.

A factorized diffusion model then generates the attributes in their respective spaces, guided by the corresponding prompts. This divides a complicated generation problem into parts while keeping the representation organized around properties that matter for the resulting speech.

The authors report that this design models speech effectively and efficiently. In their experiments, NaturalSpeech 3 outperforms leading text-to-speech systems on quality, similarity, prosody, and intelligibility. These results span both how the generated voice sounds and how clearly it communicates the intended content. The paper's central contribution is the coordinated use of factorization in the speech codec and the generative model, so that both stages work with the same separation of attributes.
summary.tldr: NaturalSpeech 3 separates speech attributes in its codec and diffusion models, improving zero-shot speech synthesis in the reported evaluations.

title: NaturalSpeech 3: Zero-Shot Speech Synthesis with Factorized Codec and Diffusion Models

abstract: We introduce LaGTran, a novel framework that utilizes text supervision to guide robust transfer of discriminative knowledge from labeled source to unlabeled target data with domain gaps. While unsupervised adaptation methods have been established to address this problem, they show limitations in handling challenging domain shifts due to their exclusive operation within the pixel-space. Motivated by our observation that semantically richer text modality has more favorable transfer properties, we devise a transfer mechanism to use a source-trained text-classifier to generate predictions on the target text descriptions, and utilize these predictions as supervision for the corresponding images. Our approach driven by language guidance is surprisingly easy and simple, yet significantly outperforms all prior approaches on challenging datasets like GeoNet and DomainNet, validating its extreme effectiveness. To further extend the scope of our study beyond images, we introduce a new benchmark called Ego2Exo to study ego-exo transfer in videos and find that our language-aided approach LaGTran yields significant gains in this highly challenging and non-trivial transfer setting. Code, models, and proposed datasets are publicly available at https://tarun005.github.io/lagtran/.

paragraphs: Transferring a visual classifier to a new domain is difficult when the target data look different and lack labels. LaGTran uses text descriptions to help move discriminative knowledge across that gap. The approach is motivated by the authors' observation that semantically rich text has more favorable transfer properties than working exclusively with visual appearance.

The framework trains a text classifier on the source domain, then applies it to descriptions of target-domain examples. Those predictions become supervision for the corresponding target images. Language therefore provides an intermediate route for transferring class information from labeled source data to unlabeled visual data in a different domain.

The authors report substantial improvements over prior approaches on challenging image datasets including GeoNet and DomainNet. They also introduce Ego2Exo, a benchmark for transferring between egocentric and exocentric video views, and find significant gains there. These results extend the method's evaluated scope beyond images. The contribution is a simple transfer mechanism in which predictions from text supply training guidance for visual recognition under substantial domain differences.
summary.tldr: LaGTran uses predictions from text descriptions to supervise visual domain adaptation, improving transfer across tested image and video domains.

title: Tell, Don’t Show: Language Guidance Eases Transfer Across Domains in Images and Videos

abstract: We study the infinite-horizon distributionally robust (DR) control of linear systems with quadratic costs, where disturbances have unknown, possibly time-correlated distribution within a Wasserstein-2 ambiguity set. We aim to minimize the worst-case expected regret—the excess cost of a causal policy compared to a non-causal one with access to future disturbance. Though the optimal policy lacks a finite-order state-space realization (i.e., it is non-rational), it can be characterized by a finite-dimensional parameter. Leveraging this, we develop an efficient frequency-domain algorithm to compute this optimal control policy and present a convex optimization method to construct a near-optimal state-space controller that approximates the optimal non-rational controller in the $\mathit{H}_\infty$-norm. This approach avoids solving a computationally expensive semi-definite program (SDP) that scales with the time horizon in the finite-horizon setting.

paragraphs: This paper studies control of linear systems with quadratic costs over an infinite horizon. Disturbance distributions are unknown and may include correlations across time, but belong to a Wasserstein-2 ambiguity set. The objective is worst-case expected regret: the additional cost of a causal controller compared with a controller that knows future disturbances.

The optimal policy has an unusual structure. It cannot be represented exactly by a finite-order state-space controller, yet a finite-dimensional parameter can characterize it. The authors use this property to develop an efficient algorithm that computes the optimal policy in the frequency domain. A compact characterization therefore remains useful even when an exact finite-order realization is unavailable.

For constructing a state-space controller, the paper introduces a convex optimization method that approximates the optimal policy in the H-infinity norm and yields a near-optimal controller. This approach avoids the expensive semidefinite program whose size scales with the horizon in the finite-horizon setting. The contribution connects an infinite-horizon optimality target with a computable finite-order approximation.
summary.tldr: A frequency-domain method computes an infinite-horizon robust regret-optimal policy and supports a near-optimal finite-order controller approximation.

title: Infinite-Horizon Distributionally Robust Regret-Optimal Control

abstract: When there exists uncertainty, AI machines are designed to make decisions so as to reach the best expected outcomes. Expectations are based on true facts about the objective environment the machines interact with, and those facts can be encoded into AI models in the form of true objective probability functions. Accordingly, AI models involve probabilistic machine learning in which the probabilities should be objectively interpreted. We prove under some basic assumptions when machines can learn the true objective probabilities, if any, and when machines cannot learn them.
originalAbstract: When there exists uncertainty, AI machines are designed to make decisions so as to reach the best expected outcomes. Accordingly, AI models involve probabilistic machine learning in which the probabilities should be objectively interpreted. We prove under some basic assumptions when machines can learn the true objective probabilities, if any, and when machines cannot learn them.

paragraphs: When an AI system chooses an action under uncertainty, it can compare the expected outcomes of its alternatives. Those expectations depend on probabilities. This paper examines a foundational question behind that process: when can a machine learn probabilities that describe objective facts about its environment?

The authors frame probabilities as properties of the environment that a model aims to represent. Under this interpretation, learning a probability function is a claim about recovering something objectively true. The qualification that such probabilities exist is part of the question itself. Their existence and a machine’s ability to learn them are therefore separate issues that the paper brings into focus.

The contribution is theoretical: under basic assumptions, the authors prove results identifying when true objective probabilities can be learned and when they cannot. These positive and negative results place conditions around the probabilistic learning that supports decisions based on expected outcomes. The stated conclusion is conditional, rather than a blanket assertion that machines can always recover environmental probabilities or that such recovery is impossible.
summary.tldr: The paper proves conditional results about when machines can and cannot learn true objective probabilities.

title: Can Machines Learn the True Probabilities?

abstract: How do we infer a 3D scene from a single image in the presence of corruptions like rain, snow or fog? Straightforward domain randomization relies on knowing the family of corruptions ahead of time. Here, we propose a Bayesian approach—dubbed robust inverse graphics (RIG)—that relies on a strong scene prior and an uninformative uniform corruption prior, making it applicable to a wide range of corruptions. Given a single image, RIG performs posterior inference jointly over the scene and the corruption. We demonstrate this idea by training a neural radiance field (NeRF) scene prior and using a secondary NeRF to represent the corruptions over which we place an uninformative prior. RIG, trained only on clean data, outperforms depth estimators and alternative NeRF approaches that perform point estimation instead of full inference. The results hold for a number of scene prior architectures based on normalizing flows and diffusion models. For the latter, we develop reconstruction-guidance with auxiliary latents (ReGAL)—a diffusion conditioning algorithm that is applicable in the presence of auxiliary latent variables such as the corruption. RIG demonstrates how scene priors can be used beyond generation tasks.

paragraphs: Recovering a three-dimensional scene from one image becomes harder when rain, snow, fog, or other corruptions obscure it. Training with randomized corruptions requires anticipating their family. Robust inverse graphics instead combines a strong prior over scenes with an uninformative uniform prior over corruption, aiming to handle a broad range of disturbances.

Given an image, the method jointly performs posterior inference over the scene and the corruption. The authors implement this using a learned neural radiance field scene prior and a second neural radiance field for corruption. This formulation explicitly represents both possible scene explanations and the additional latent corruption responsible for the observed image.

Although trained only on clean data, the method outperforms the tested depth estimators and alternative NeRF approaches that use point estimation. Results hold with scene priors based on normalizing flows and diffusion models. For diffusion priors, the authors introduce ReGAL, a conditioning algorithm that accommodates auxiliary latent variables such as corruption. The findings demonstrate a use of learned scene priors for reconstruction beyond generation.
summary.tldr: Joint Bayesian inference over scenes and corruption enables robust single-image reconstruction using priors trained only on clean data.

title: Robust Inverse Graphics via Probabilistic Inference

abstract: Transformer-based large language models have displayed impressive in-context learning capabilities, where a pre-trained model can handle new tasks without fine-tuning by simply augmenting the query with some input-output examples from that task. Despite the empirical success, the mechanics of how to train a Transformer to achieve ICL and the corresponding ICL capacity is mostly elusive due to the technical challenges of analyzing the nonconvex training problems resulting from the nonlinear self-attention and nonlinear activation in Transformers. To the best of our knowledge, this paper provides the first theoretical analysis of the training dynamics of Transformers with nonlinear self-attention and nonlinear MLP, together with the ICL generalization capability of the resulting model. Focusing on a group of binary classification tasks, we train Transformers using data from a subset of these tasks and quantify the impact of various factors on the ICL generalization performance on the remaining unseen tasks with and without data distribution shifts. We also analyze how different components in the learned Transformers contribute to the ICL performance. Furthermore, we provide the first theoretical analysis of how model pruning affects ICL performance and prove that proper magnitude-based pruning can have a minimal impact on ICL while reducing inference costs. These theoretical findings are justified through numerical experiments.

paragraphs: In-context learning lets a pretrained model handle a new task by receiving examples alongside a query, without fine-tuning. Explaining how training produces this ability is difficult because nonlinear attention and nonlinear activation functions create a nonconvex optimization problem. This paper analyzes both training dynamics and the resulting ability to generalize in Transformers that retain those nonlinear components.

The analysis focuses on a group of binary-classification tasks. Transformers are trained on a subset and evaluated theoretically on unseen tasks, both with and without distribution shifts. The authors quantify how different factors affect generalization and examine how components of the learned model contribute to in-context performance. This links the training process to behavior on tasks outside the training subset.

The paper also studies pruning and proves that appropriate magnitude-based pruning can reduce inference costs while having minimal impact on in-context learning. Numerical experiments support the theoretical findings. The scope matters: these are results for the analyzed task family and suitable pruning, rather than a guarantee that arbitrary pruning preserves in-context performance in every Transformer.
summary.tldr: The paper analyzes how nonlinear Transformers learn and generalize in context, including conditions under which magnitude-based pruning has minimal impact.

title: How Do Nonlinear Transformers Learn and Generalize in In-Context Learning?

abstract: Contextual dueling bandits, where a learner compares two options based on context and receives feedback indicating which was preferred, extends classic dueling bandits by incorporating contextual information for decision-making and preference learning. Several algorithms based on the upper confidence bound (UCB) have been proposed for linear contextual dueling bandits. However, no algorithm based on posterior sampling has been developed in this setting, despite the empirical success observed in traditional contextual bandits. In this paper, we propose a Thompson sampling algorithm, named FGTS.CDB, for linear contextual dueling bandits. At the core of our algorithm is a new Feel-Good exploration term specifically tailored for dueling bandits. This term leverages the independence of the two selected arms, thereby avoiding a cross term in the analysis. We show that our algorithm achieves nearly minimax-optimal regret, i.e., $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(d\sqrt T)$, where $d$ is the model dimension and $T$ is the time horizon. Finally, we evaluate our algorithm on synthetic data and observe that FGTS.CDB outperforms existing algorithms by a large margin.

paragraphs: In contextual dueling bandits, a learner chooses two options using the current context and observes which option is preferred. The feedback is a comparison rather than a separate reward for each choice. This paper develops a posterior-sampling approach for the linear version of this problem, where earlier algorithms had used upper confidence bounds.

The proposed algorithm, FGTS.CDB, adapts Thompson sampling through a specially designed Feel-Good exploration term. Its construction uses independence between the two selected options to avoid a cross term in the mathematical analysis. This is the central mechanism supporting the paper’s theoretical treatment of exploration in the paired-choice setting.

The authors prove regret scaling of approximately d times the square root of T, up to logarithmic factors, where d is model dimension and T is the time horizon. They characterize this rate as nearly minimax optimal. Synthetic-data experiments also show FGTS.CDB outperforming existing algorithms by a large margin. The paper thus supplies both a near-optimal theoretical guarantee and empirical evidence within its synthetic evaluations.
summary.tldr: FGTS.CDB brings Thompson sampling to linear contextual dueling bandits with nearly minimax-optimal regret and strong synthetic-data results.

title: Feel-Good Thompson Sampling for Contextual Dueling Bandits

abstract: Both Evolutionary Algorithms (EAs) and Reinforcement Learning (RL) have demonstrated powerful capabilities in policy search with different principles. A promising direction is to combine the respective strengths of both for efficient policy optimization. To this end, many works have proposed various mechanisms to integrate EAs and RL. However, it is still unclear which of these mechanisms are complementary and can be fully combined. In this paper, we revisit different mechanisms from five perspectives: 1) Interaction Mode, 2) Individual Architecture, 3) EAs and operators, 4) Impact of EA on RL, and 5) Fitness Surrogate and Usage. We evaluate the effectiveness of each mechanism and experimentally analyze the reasons for the more effective mechanisms. Using the most effective mechanisms, we develop EvoRainbow and EvoRainbow-Exp, which outperform strong baselines and provide state-of-the-art performance across various tasks with distinct characteristics. To promote community development, we release the code on https://github.com/yeshenpy/EvoRainbow.

paragraphs: Evolutionary algorithms and reinforcement learning offer different ways to search for effective policies. Many methods combine them, but it remains unclear which integration mechanisms work well together. This paper examines that design question systematically, aiming to identify combinations that support more effective policy optimization.

The analysis organizes existing mechanisms into five perspectives: how the two approaches interact, how individual policies are structured, which evolutionary algorithms and operators are used, how evolution affects reinforcement learning, and how fitness surrogates are constructed and applied. The authors evaluate individual mechanisms and use experiments to investigate why the more effective choices help.

They then assemble the most effective mechanisms into EvoRainbow and EvoRainbow-Exp. Across tasks with different characteristics, these methods outperform strong baselines and achieve the state-of-the-art performance reported in the abstract. The contribution includes both the resulting algorithms and an empirical examination of design choices. This makes the work relevant to understanding how evolutionary and reinforcement-learning components can be combined, as well as to obtaining stronger policy-search performance.
summary.tldr: EvoRainbow combines empirically effective evolutionary and reinforcement-learning mechanisms to improve policy search across varied tasks.

title: EvoRainbow: Combining Improvements in Evolutionary Reinforcement Learning for Policy Search

abstract: Graph-based methods, pivotal for label inference over interconnected objects in many real-world applications, often encounter generalization challenges, if the graph used for model training differs significantly from the graph used for testing. This work delves into Graph Domain Adaptation (GDA) to address the unique complexities of distribution shifts over graph data, where interconnected data points experience shifts in features, labels, and in particular, connecting patterns. We propose a novel, theoretically principled method, Pairwise Alignment (Pair-Align) to counter graph structure shift by mitigating conditional structure shift (CSS) and label shift (LS). Pair-Align uses edge weights to recalibrate the influence among neighboring nodes to handle CSS and adjusts the classification loss with label weights to handle LS. Our method demonstrates superior performance in real-world applications, including node classification with region shift in social networks, and the pileup mitigation task in particle colliding experiments. For the first application, we also curate the largest dataset by far for GDA studies. Our method shows strong performance in synthetic and other existing benchmark datasets.

paragraphs: A graph model can struggle when the graph used for testing differs from the graph used for training. Differences can involve node features, labels, and the patterns of connections between nodes. Pair-Align addresses this graph domain adaptation problem by explicitly accounting for changes in structure and in the distribution of labels.

The method separates conditional structure shift from label shift. It handles the former by assigning edge weights that recalibrate how neighboring nodes influence one another. It handles the latter by weighting labels in the classification loss. These two adjustments connect the adaptation mechanism to different sources of mismatch, within an approach the authors describe as theoretically principled.

The paper reports superior performance for social-network node classification across regions and for pileup mitigation in particle-collision experiments, alongside strong synthetic and benchmark results. It also contributes a social-network dataset described as the largest for graph domain adaptation at the time of the study. The findings support adapting both neighborhood influence and label contributions when transferring models between graphs.
summary.tldr: Pair-Align improves graph transfer by reweighting edges for structural shifts and classification losses for label shifts.

title: Pairwise Alignment Improves Graph Domain Adaptation

abstract: Adapting pre-trained large language models to different domains in natural language processing requires two key considerations: high computational demands and model’s inability to continual adaptation. To simultaneously address both issues, this paper presents COPAL (COntinual Pruning in Adaptive Language settings), an algorithm developed for pruning large language generative models under a continual model adaptation setting. While avoiding resource-heavy finetuning or retraining, our pruning process is guided by the proposed sensitivity analysis. The sensitivity effectively measures model’s ability to withstand perturbations introduced by the new dataset and finds model’s weights that are relevant for all encountered datasets. As a result, COPAL allows seamless model adaptation to new domains while enhancing the resource efficiency. Our empirical evaluation on a various size of LLMs show that COPAL outperforms baseline models, demonstrating its efficacy in efficiency and adaptability.

paragraphs: Adapting a pretrained language model to successive domains raises two connected problems: computation is expensive, and adaptation must account for more than the latest dataset. COPAL addresses these together through continual pruning. It uses the selection of model weights as a means of adaptation while avoiding resource-intensive fine-tuning or retraining.

The pruning decisions are guided by a sensitivity analysis. This analysis measures how well the model withstands perturbations introduced by a new dataset and identifies weights relevant across the datasets encountered so far. The history of adaptation therefore informs which parts of the model are retained, rather than treating each new domain as an isolated pruning problem.

Experiments across language models of different sizes report better results than the evaluated baselines, supporting the method's efficiency and adaptability. The contribution is a way to connect compression with ongoing domain adaptation: reducing model resources and responding to new data become parts of the same process. The stated evidence concerns that continual adaptation setting and the models included in the empirical evaluation.
summary.tldr: COPAL uses sensitivity-guided continual pruning to adapt language models across domains without resource-heavy fine-tuning or retraining.

title: COPAL: Continual Pruning in Large Language Generative Models

abstract: Feature selection is a crucial task in settings where data is high-dimensional or acquiring the full set of features is costly. Recent developments in neural network-based embedded feature selection show promising results across a wide range of applications. Concrete Autoencoders (CAEs), considered state-of-the-art in embedded feature selection, may struggle to achieve stable joint optimization, hurting their training time and generalization. In this work, we identify that this instability is correlated with the CAE learning duplicate selections. To remedy this, we propose a simple and effective improvement: Indirectly Parameterized CAEs (IP-CAEs). IP-CAEs learn an embedding and a mapping from it to the Gumbel-Softmax distributions’ parameters. Despite being simple to implement, IP-CAE exhibits significant and consistent improvements over CAE in both generalization and training time across several datasets for reconstruction and classification. Unlike CAE, IP-CAE effectively leverages non-linear relationships and does not require retraining the jointly optimized decoder. Furthermore, our approach is, in principle, generalizable to Gumbel-Softmax distributions beyond feature selection.

paragraphs: Feature selection can reduce the cost of collecting high-dimensional data, but jointly learning selected features and a decoder can be unstable. This paper identifies a connection between that instability in Concrete Autoencoders and the repeated selection of the same feature. It proposes a small change in how the selection distributions are parameterized.

Indirectly Parameterized Concrete Autoencoders learn an embedding and a mapping from that embedding to the parameters of Gumbel–softmax distributions. This indirect representation changes the optimization of feature choices while retaining a neural embedded-selection framework. The approach can exploit nonlinear relationships and does not require separately retraining the jointly optimized decoder.

Across reconstruction and classification datasets, IP-CAE consistently improves generalization and training time relative to standard CAE. The authors also suggest that the parameterization principle could extend beyond feature selection. That broader possibility is a methodological implication, while the concrete empirical evidence reported in the abstract concerns the evaluated feature-selection tasks.
summary.tldr: Indirect parameterization stabilizes Concrete Autoencoder feature selection and improves training speed and generalization in the reported tests.

title: Indirectly Parameterized Concrete Autoencoders

abstract: Cloud-based AI services offer numerous benefits but also introduce vulnerabilities, allowing for tampering with deployed DNN models, ranging from injecting malicious behaviors to reducing computing resources. Fingerprint samples are generated to query models to detect such tampering. In this paper, we present Intersecting-Boundary-Sensitive Fingerprinting (IBSF), a novel method for black-box integrity verification of DNN models using only top-1 labels. Recognizing that tampering with a model alters its decision boundary, IBSF crafts fingerprint samples from normal samples by maximizing the partial Shannon entropy of a selected subset of categories to position the fingerprint samples near decision boundaries where the categories in the subset intersect. These fingerprint samples are almost indistinguishable from their source samples. We theoretically establish and confirm experimentally that these fingerprint samples’ expected sensitivity to tampering increases with the cardinality of the subset. Extensive evaluation demonstrates that IBSF surpasses existing state-of-the-art fingerprinting methods, particularly with larger subset cardinality, establishing its state-of-the-art performance in black-box tampering detection using only top-1 labels. The IBSF code is available at https://github.com/CGCL-codes/IBSF.

paragraphs: A deployed neural network may be altered after it has been provided as a service. Fingerprinting checks model integrity by submitting specially chosen inputs and examining the responses. IBSF addresses a restrictive black-box setting in which verification can use only the model's top-ranked class label, rather than scores or internal computations.

The method exploits the fact that tampering changes decision boundaries. Starting from normal inputs, it maximizes partial Shannon entropy over a chosen subset of categories. This positions fingerprint inputs near locations where boundaries among those categories intersect, while keeping them almost indistinguishable from their source inputs. Such locations make the returned label sensitive to changes in the model.

The authors theoretically establish and experimentally confirm that expected tampering sensitivity increases as the selected category subset grows. Extensive evaluation reports stronger detection than existing fingerprinting methods, particularly with larger subsets. The result makes boundary intersections a useful design principle for integrity checks that must work with the limited information supplied by top-1 labels.
summary.tldr: IBSF detects model tampering using top-1 labels from fingerprint inputs placed near intersections of multiple class boundaries.

title: Intersecting-Boundary-Sensitive Fingerprinting for Tampering Detection of DNN Models

abstract: Multimodal learning with variational autoencoders (VAEs) requires estimating joint distributions to evaluate the evidence lower bound (ELBO). Current methods, the product and mixture of experts, aggregate single-modality distributions assuming independence for simplicity, which is an overoptimistic assumption. This research introduces a novel methodology for aggregating single-modality distributions by exploiting the principle of consensus of dependent experts (CoDE), which circumvents the aforementioned assumption. Utilizing the CoDE method, we propose a novel ELBO that approximates the joint likelihood of the multimodal data by learning the contribution of each subset of modalities. The resulting CoDE-VAE model demonstrates better performance in terms of balancing the trade-off between generative coherence and generative quality, as well as generating more precise log-likelihood estimations. CoDE-VAE further minimizes the generative quality gap as the number of modalities increases. In certain cases, it reaches a generative quality similar to that of unimodal VAEs, which is a desirable property that is lacking in most current methods. Finally, the classification accuracy achieved by CoDE-VAE is comparable to that of state-of-the-art multimodal VAE models.

paragraphs: Multimodal variational autoencoders must combine information from individual modalities to estimate joint distributions and evaluate their training objective. The paper argues that common product- and mixture-of-experts approaches make an overly optimistic independence assumption when aggregating those distributions. It proposes a way to account for dependence when deciding how different sources of information should contribute.

The method uses consensus of dependent experts, abbreviated CoDE. It introduces a new evidence lower bound that approximates the joint likelihood by learning the contribution of each subset of modalities. This makes combinations of modalities part of the aggregation process, providing a mechanism for incorporating relationships that an independence-based treatment overlooks.

It also reduces the generative quality gap as modality count increases and, in some cases, reaches quality similar to unimodal VAEs. Classification accuracy remains comparable to state-of-the-art multimodal VAE models. The findings suggest that explicitly accommodating dependence can improve generation and likelihood estimation while retaining competitive classification performance.
summary.tldr: CoDE-VAE accounts for dependence between modalities, improving reported generation trade-offs and likelihood estimates while retaining competitive classification accuracy.

title: Aggregation of Dependent Expert Distributions in Multimodal Variational Autoencoders

abstract: A key task in certain democratic processes is to produce a concise slate of statements that proportionally represents the full spectrum of user opinions. This task is similar to committee elections, but unlike traditional settings, the candidate set comprises all possible statements of varying lengths, and so it can only be accessed through specific queries. Combining social choice and large language models, prior work has approached this challenge through a framework of generative social choice. We extend the framework in two fundamental ways, providing theoretical guarantees even in the face of approximately optimal queries and a budget limit on the overall length of the slate. Using GPT-4o to implement queries, we showcase our approach on datasets related to city improvement measures and drug reviews, demonstrating its effectiveness in generating representative slates from unstructured user opinions.
