paragraphs: Summarizing many people’s views into a short list of statements resembles a committee election, except the candidates are all statements that could be written. That candidate space is effectively accessed through generation and evaluation queries. This paper extends generative social choice to make the resulting summaries more realistically constrained.

The framework now provides theoretical guarantees when queries are only approximately optimal and when the total length of the selected statements is limited. Both changes matter for language-model implementations: generated candidates need not be the best possible statements, and a useful slate must fit within a concise communication budget.

Using GPT-4o to implement the queries, the authors demonstrate the method on city-improvement opinions and drug reviews. The examples support its ability to produce proportionally representative slates from unstructured input. The contribution combines a stronger theoretical model with applications; representativeness is evaluated through the framework’s social-choice criteria rather than a claim that every participant endorses every chosen statement.
summary.tldr: Generative social choice gains guarantees for imperfect queries and length budgets when producing representative summaries of public opinions.

title: Generative Social Choice: The Next Generation

abstract: In fully-dynamic consistent clustering, we are given a finite metric space $(M,d)$, and a set $F\subseteq M$ of possible locations for opening centers. Data points arrive and depart, and the goal is to maintain an approximately optimal clustering solution at all times while minimizing the recourse, the total number of additions/deletions of centers over time. Specifically, we study fully dynamic versions of the classical $k$-center, facility location, and $k$-median problems. We design algorithms that, given a parameter $\beta\geq 1$, maintain an $O(\beta)$-approximate solution at all times, and whose total recourse is bounded by $O(\log |F| \log \Delta) \cdot OPT_{rec}^{\beta}$. Here $OPT_{rec}^{\beta}$ is the minimal recourse of an offline algorithm that maintains a $\beta$-approximate solution at all times, and $\Delta$ is the metric aspect ratio. We obtain our results via a reduction to the recently proposed Positive Body Chasing framework of [Bhattacharya Buchbinder Levin Saranurak, FOCS 2023], which we show gives fractional solutions to our clustering problems online. Our contribution is to round these fractional solutions while preserving the approximation and recourse guarantees. We complement our positive results with logarithmic lower bounds which show that our bounds are nearly tight.

paragraphs: When data points continually arrive and depart, a clustering algorithm must balance solution quality against the disruption of changing its centers. This paper studies that balance for dynamic k-center, facility location, and k-median problems. It measures disruption through recourse: the total number of center additions and deletions over time, with centers chosen from a fixed finite set of possible locations.

For a parameter beta of at least one, the algorithms maintain solutions whose approximation factor is O(beta). Their recourse is compared with the smallest recourse achievable by an offline algorithm that maintains beta-approximate solutions throughout. The resulting overhead is O(log |F| log Delta), where F is the candidate-center set and Delta describes the metric’s distance range.

The method reduces clustering to Positive Body Chasing, obtaining fractional solutions online before rounding them into clustering solutions. The central contribution is rounding while preserving both quality and recourse guarantees. Logarithmic lower bounds show that the resulting bounds are nearly tight, clarifying how much stability can be achieved alongside approximate clustering quality.
summary.tldr: The paper gives dynamic clustering algorithms with approximate solution quality and nearly tight bounds on center changes relative to an offline comparator.

title: Competitively Consistent Clustering

abstract: Recently differential privacy has been used for a number of streaming, data structure, and dynamic graph problems as a means of hiding the internal randomness of the data structure, so that multiple possibly adaptive queries can be made without sacrificing the correctness of the responses. Although these works use differential privacy to show that for some problems it is possible to tolerate $T$ queries using $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{T})$ copies of a data structure, such results only apply to numerical estimation problems, and only return the cost of an optimization problem rather than the solution itself. In this paper we investigate the use of differential privacy for adaptive queries to search problems, which are significantly more challenging since the responses to queries can reveal much more about the internal randomness than a single numerical query. We focus on two classical search problems: nearest neighbor queries and regression with arbitrary turnstile updates. We identify key parameters to these problems, such as the number of $c$-approximate near neighbors and the matrix condition number, and use different differential privacy techniques to design algorithms returning the solution point or solution vector with memory and time depending on these parameters. We give algorithms for each of these problems that achieve similar tradeoffs.

paragraphs: Randomized data structures can face difficulties when later queries depend on earlier answers, because responses may expose their internal randomness. Differential privacy has been used to protect that randomness and preserve correctness across adaptive queries. Earlier results addressed numerical estimates, including an optimization problem's cost. This paper studies returning an actual solution, which can reveal substantially more information.

The authors focus on nearest-neighbor search and regression under arbitrary turnstile updates. Their algorithms return a solution point or a solution vector, respectively. They identify problem-specific parameters that influence the required resources, including the number of approximately near neighbors and the matrix condition number, and apply different differential-privacy techniques to these search settings.

The resulting memory and time costs depend on those parameters, with related trade-offs obtained for both problems. The contribution extends privacy-based protection of internal randomness beyond scalar answers. It also shows why the richer output of a search query requires attention to the structure of the underlying problem when designing algorithms for repeated adaptive use.
summary.tldr: The paper uses differential privacy to support adaptive nearest-neighbor and regression searches, with resource costs depending on key problem parameters.

title: On Differential Privacy for Adaptively Solving Search Problems via Sketching

abstract: We study the problem of clustering a set of items based on bandit feedback. Each of the $n$ items is characterized by a feature vector, with a possibly large dimension $d$. The items are partitioned into two unknown groups, such that items within the same group share the same feature vector. We consider a sequential and adaptive setting in which, at each round, the learner selects one item and one feature, then observes a noisy evaluation of the item’s feature. The learner’s objective is to recover the correct partition of the items, while keeping the number of observations as small as possible. We provide an algorithm which relies on finding a relevant feature for the clustering task, leveraging the Sequential Halving algorithm. With probability at least $1-\delta$, we obtain an accurate recovery of the partition and derive an upper bound on the required budget . Furthermore, we derive an instance-dependent lower bound, which is tight in some relevant cases.

paragraphs: This paper studies clustering when the learner cannot inspect complete feature vectors directly. Instead, each observation measures one chosen feature of one chosen item and includes noise. The goal is to recover two unknown groups while making as few observations as possible, even when many features are available.

The setting assumes that every item within a group has the same underlying feature vector. The algorithm exploits this structure by searching for a feature useful for separating the groups. It uses Sequential Halving as part of that search and chooses observations adaptively, so its measurement decisions can respond to the information obtained so far.

The authors establish accurate recovery with probability at least 1−δ and give an upper bound on the observation budget. They also derive a lower bound that depends on the particular instance and matches the achievable requirements in some relevant cases. Together, these results characterize both a successful strategy and portions of its efficiency limits under the stated two-group model.
summary.tldr: An adaptive algorithm finds a useful feature for recovering two groups from noisy measurements, with probability guarantees and observation-budget bounds.

title: Clustering Items through Bandit Feedback: Finding the Right Feature out of Many

abstract: Pre-trained Vision-Language Models (VLMs) exhibit strong zero-shot classification abilities, demonstrating great potential for generating weakly supervised labels. Unfortunately, existing weakly supervised learning methods are short of ability in generating accurate labels via VLMs. In this paper, we propose a novel weakly supervised labeling setting, namely True-False Labels (TFLs) which can achieve high accuracy when generated by VLMs. The TFL indicates whether an instance belongs to the label, which is randomly and uniformly sampled from the candidate label set. Specifically, we theoretically derive a risk-consistent estimator to explore and utilize the conditional probability distribution information of TFLs. Besides, we propose a convolutional-based Multi-modal Prompt Retrieving (MRP) method to bridge the gap between the knowledge of VLMs and target learning tasks. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed TFL setting and MRP learning method. The code to reproduce the experiments is at https://github.com/Tranquilxu/TMP.

paragraphs: Vision-language models can recognize classes without task-specific training, making them promising sources of weak supervision. However, converting their knowledge into accurate training labels remains challenging. This paper proposes a different labeling format: randomly and uniformly choose one candidate class, then ask whether an instance belongs to that class.

The resulting true-false label records membership in the sampled class rather than supplying a complete class assignment. The authors argue that vision-language models can generate these labels with high accuracy. They derive a risk-consistent estimator that uses the conditional probability information contained in this supervision, giving the learning method a theoretical foundation tied to the proposed labeling process.

The paper also introduces a convolution-based multi-modal prompt retrieval method to connect pretrained vision-language knowledge with the target task. Experiments support both the true-false labeling setting and the retrieval-based learning method. Together, the contributions show a way to use a simpler supervision question while still extracting information needed for the broader classification problem.
summary.tldr: The paper learns from vision-language-model-generated true-false class labels using a risk-consistent estimator and multi-modal prompt retrieval.

title: Learning from True-False Labels via Multi-modal Prompt Retrieving

abstract: Bridging contrastive language-image pre-training (CLIP) to video action recognition has attracted growing interest. Human actions are inherently rich in spatial and temporal contexts, involving dynamic interactions among people, objects, and the environment. Accurately recognizing actions requires effectively capturing these fine-grained elements and modeling their relationships with language. However, most existing methods rely on cosine similarity–practically equivalent to the Pearson correlation coefficient–between global tokens for video-language alignment. As a result, they have limited capacity to model complex dependencies and tend to overlook local tokens that encode critical spatio-temporal cues. To overcome these limitations, we propose BDC-CLIP, a novel framework that leverages Brownian Distance Covariance (BDC) to align visual and textual representations. Our method can capture complex relationships–both linear and nonlinear–between all visual and textual tokens, enabling fine-grained modeling in space, time, and language. BDC-CLIP achieves state-of-the-art performance across zero-shot, few-shot, base-to-novel, and fully supervised action recognition settings, demonstrating its effectiveness and broad applicability.

paragraphs: Recognizing an action in video depends on relationships among people, objects, surroundings, and movement over time. Adapting CLIP to this task requires connecting those visual details to language. The paper argues that commonly used alignment methods compress too much of this information into global tokens, then compare those summaries using cosine similarity.

BDC-CLIP changes the comparison mechanism to Brownian Distance Covariance. It uses relationships among all visual and textual tokens, allowing local spatial and temporal cues to contribute to alignment with language. The method can represent both linear and nonlinear dependencies. This matters because an action’s meaning may depend on combinations of details that a similarity score between whole-video and whole-text summaries does not adequately capture.

The authors report state-of-the-art action recognition across zero-shot, few-shot, base-to-novel, and fully supervised settings. These results cover different amounts of supervision and different relationships between training and evaluation categories. They support the usefulness of richer video-language alignment across the evaluated settings, with fine-grained token relationships forming the core methodological change.
summary.tldr: BDC-CLIP aligns all video and text tokens through Brownian Distance Covariance to improve action recognition across multiple supervision settings.

title: BDC-CLIP: Brownian Distance Covariance for Adapting CLIP to Action Recognition

abstract: The logistic loss (a.k.a. cross-entropy loss) is one of the most popular loss functions used for multiclass classification. It is also the loss function of choice for next-token prediction in language modeling. It is associated with the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence and the softargmax operator. In this work, we propose to construct new convex loss functions based on $f$-divergences. Our loss functions generalize the logistic loss in two directions: i) by replacing the KL divergence with $f$-divergences and ii) by allowing non-uniform reference measures. We instantiate our framework for numerous $f$-divergences, recovering existing losses and creating new ones. By analogy with the logistic loss, the loss function generated by an $f$-divergence is associated with an operator, that we dub $f$-softargmax. We derive a novel parallelizable bisection algorithm for computing the $f$-softargmax associated with any $f$-divergence. On the empirical side, one of the goals of this paper is to determine the effectiveness of loss functions beyond the classical cross-entropy in a language model setting, including on pre-training, post-training (SFT) and distillation. We show that the loss function generated by the $\alpha$-divergence (which is equivalent to Tsallis $\alpha$-negentropy in the case of unit reference measures) with $\alpha=1.5$ performs well across several tasks.

paragraphs: Cross-entropy is widely used for classification and next-token prediction. This paper constructs a broader family of convex losses by extending its relationship with KL divergence. The framework replaces KL with other f-divergences and also permits non-uniform reference measures, giving two ways to move beyond the usual loss while retaining a common mathematical construction.

Each resulting loss has an associated operator called f-softargmax, analogous to the operator paired with logistic loss. The authors derive a parallelizable bisection algorithm for computing this operator for any f-divergence. They instantiate the framework with numerous divergences, recovering known losses as well as creating new ones.

A loss based on alpha-divergence with alpha equal to 1.5 performs well across several tasks. With unit reference measures, it corresponds to Tsallis alpha-negentropy. The contribution combines a general recipe and computational tool with evidence that a particular alternative is useful across multiple language-model training settings.
summary.tldr: A framework generates convex alternatives to cross-entropy from f-divergences, with an efficient operator algorithm and promising language-model results.

title: Loss Functions and Operators Generated by f-Divergences

abstract: With the widespread deployment of long-context large language models (LLMs), there has been a growing demand for efficient support of high-throughput inference. However, as the key-value (KV) cache expands with the sequence length, the increasing memory footprint and the need to access it for decoding both result in low throughput when serving long-context LLMs. While various dynamic sparse attention methods have been proposed to accelerate inference while maintaining generation quality, they either fail to sufficiently reduce GPU memory usage or introduce significant decoding latency by offloading the KV cache to the CPU. We present ShadowKV, a high-throughput long-context LLM inference system that stores the low-rank key cache and offloads the value cache to reduce the memory footprint for larger batch sizes and longer sequences. To minimize decoding latency, ShadowKV employs an accurate KV selection strategy that reconstructs minimal sparse KV pairs on-the-fly. By evaluating ShadowKV on benchmarks like RULER, LongBench, and models such as Llama-3.1-8B and GLM-4-9B-1M, we demonstrate that it achieves up to 6$\times$ larger batch sizes and 3.04$\times$ higher throughput on an A100 GPU without sacrificing accuracy, even surpassing the performance achievable with infinite batch size under the assumption of infinite GPU memory.

paragraphs: Long-context language models retain a growing key-value cache during generation. Both storing that cache and accessing it for each decoding step can reduce serving throughput. Sparse attention can reduce work, but existing methods may leave too much data on the GPU or introduce substantial delays when moving cached data from the CPU.

ShadowKV combines a low-rank key cache with an offloaded value cache to reduce GPU memory requirements. Its selection strategy reconstructs a small set of sparse key-value pairs as needed, aiming to limit decoding latency. The memory savings allow larger batches and longer sequences, while selective reconstruction addresses the cost of retrieving the relevant context.

Evaluations include RULER, LongBench, Llama-3.1-8B, and GLM-4-9B-1M. On an A100 GPU, the authors report up to six times larger batches and 3.04 times higher throughput without sacrificing accuracy. They also report exceeding a comparison with infinite batch size under an infinite-GPU-memory assumption, showing that the claimed throughput benefit extends beyond simply fitting more requests into memory.
summary.tldr: ShadowKV combines compact key storage, value offloading, and selective reconstruction to improve long-context inference throughput.

title: ShadowKV: KV Cache in Shadows for High-Throughput Long-Context LLM Inference

abstract: Cross-domain few-shot segmentation (CD-FSS) is proposed to first pre-train the model on a source-domain dataset with sufficient samples, and then transfer the model to target-domain datasets where only a few training samples are available for efficient finetuning. There are majorly two challenges in this task: (1) the domain gap and (2) finetuning with scarce data. To solve these challenges, we revisit the adapter-based methods, and discover an intriguing insight not explored in previous works: the adapter not only helps the fine-tuning of downstream tasks but also naturally serves as a domain information decoupler. Then, we delve into this finding for an interpretation, and we find the model’s inherent structure could lead to a natural decoupling of domain information. Building upon this insight, we propose the Domain Feature Navigator (DFN), which is a structure-based decoupler instead of loss-based ones like current works, to capture domain-specific information, thereby directing the model’s attention towards domain-agnostic knowledge. Moreover, to prevent the potential excessive overfitting of DFN during the source-domain training, we further design the SAM-SVN method to constrain DFN from learning sample-specific knowledge. On target domains, we freeze the model and fine-tune the DFN to learn knowledge specific to target domains. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method surpasses the state-of-the-art method in CD-FSS significantly by 2.69% and 4.68% average MIoU in 1-shot and 5-shot scenarios, respectively.
originalAbstract: Cross-domain few-shot segmentation (CD-FSS) is proposed to first pre-train the model on a source-domain dataset with sufficient samples, and then transfer the model to target-domain datasets where only a few training samples are available for efficient finetuning. There are majorly two challenges in this task: (1) the domain gap and (2) finetuning with scarce data. To solve these challenges, we revisit the adapter-based methods, and discover an intriguing insight not explored in previous works: the adapter not only helps the fine-tuning of downstream tasks but also naturally serves as a domain information decoupler. Then, we delve into this finding for an interpretation, and we find the model’s inherent structure could lead to a natural decoupling of domain information. Building upon this insight, we propose the Domain Feature Navigator (DFN), which is a structure-based decoupler instead of loss-based ones like current works, to capture domain-specific information, thereby directing the model’s attention towards domain-agnostic knowledge. Moreover, to prevent the potential excessive overfitting of DFN during the source-domain training, we further design the SAM-SVN method to constrain DFN from learning sample-specific knowledge. On target domains, we freeze the model and fine-tune the DFN to learn knowledge specific to target domains. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method surpasses the state-of-the-art method in CD-FSS significantly by 2.69% and 4.68% average MIoU in 1-shot and 5-shot scenarios, respectively.

paragraphs: Cross-domain few-shot segmentation transfers a model trained with plentiful source data to a different domain with only a few annotated examples. It must handle both the change in domain and the risk of fitting too closely to scarce target data. This paper revisits adapters and finds that they can also separate domain information through the model’s structure.

Building on that interpretation, the authors introduce the Domain Feature Navigator, or DFN. It captures domain-specific information to direct the model toward knowledge that transfers across domains. The separation comes from architecture rather than a dedicated separation loss. A further method, SAM-SVN, constrains DFN during source training so that it does not excessively learn details specific to individual samples.

For target-domain adaptation, the rest of the model is frozen while DFN is fine-tuned on domain-specific knowledge. The reported experiments improve average MIoU over the state-of-the-art method by 2.69% in the one-shot setting and 4.68% in the five-shot setting. These findings support using the adapter’s structural role to address both domain transfer and limited-data adaptation.
summary.tldr: A structurally designed adapter separates domain information and improves cross-domain segmentation with very few labeled examples.

title: Adapter Naturally Serves as Decoupler for Cross-Domain Few-Shot Semantic Segmentation

abstract: Leveraging Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to create embodied agents offers a promising avenue for tackling real-world tasks. While language-centric embodied agents have garnered substantial attention, MLLM-based embodied agents remain underexplored due to the lack of comprehensive evaluation frameworks. To bridge this gap, we introduce EmbodiedBench, an extensive benchmark designed to evaluate vision-driven embodied agents. EmbodiedBench features: (1) a diverse set of 1,128 testing tasks across four environments, ranging from high-level semantic tasks (e.g., household) to low-level tasks involving atomic actions (e.g., navigation and manipulation); and (2) six meticulously curated subsets evaluating essential agent capabilities like commonsense reasoning, complex instruction understanding, spatial awareness, visual perception, and long-term planning. Through extensive experiments, we evaluated 24 leading proprietary and open-source MLLMs within EmbodiedBench. Our findings reveal that: MLLMs excel at high-level tasks but struggle with low-level manipulation, with the best model, GPT-4o, scoring only $28.9\%$ on average. EmbodiedBench provides a multifaceted standardized evaluation platform that not only highlights existing challenges but also offers valuable insights to advance MLLM-based embodied agents. Our code and dataset are available at [https://embodiedbench.github.io](https://embodiedbench.github.io).

Six curated subsets examine capabilities including commonsense reasoning, understanding complex instructions, spatial awareness, visual perception, and long-term planning. This structure allows evaluation across different demands instead of treating embodied performance as a single undifferentiated ability.

The authors test 24 proprietary and open-source models. They find strong performance on high-level tasks but substantial difficulty with low-level manipulation; the best model, GPT-4o, achieves an average score of 28.9%. These results identify a gap between broad task understanding and effective action, while providing a standardized platform for tracking improvements across those capabilities.
summary.tldr: EmbodiedBench tests vision-driven agents across 1,128 tasks and reveals substantial weaknesses in low-level manipulation.

title: EmbodiedBench: Comprehensive Benchmarking Multi-modal Large Language Models for Vision-Driven Embodied Agents

abstract: We propose a novel method for simulating conditioned diffusion processes (diffusion bridges) in Euclidean spaces. By training a neural network to approximate bridge dynamics, our approach eliminates the need for computationally intensive Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods or reverse-process modeling. Compared to existing methods, it offers greater robustness across various diffusion specifications and conditioning scenarios. This applies in particular to rare events and multimodal distributions, which pose challenges for score-learning- and MCMC-based approaches. We propose a flexible variational family for approximating the diffusion bridge path measure which is partially specified by a neural network. Once trained, it enables efficient independent sampling at a cost comparable to sampling the unconditioned (forward) process.

paragraphs: A diffusion bridge is a diffusion process constrained by conditioning information. Simulating these processes can be expensive, particularly when the required events are rare or the relevant distribution has multiple modes. This paper proposes learning the bridge dynamics with a neural network for diffusion processes in Euclidean spaces.

The method constructs a flexible variational family that approximates the probability distribution over entire bridge paths. A neural network specifies part of this family and is trained to approximate the conditioned dynamics. This formulation removes the need for computationally intensive Markov Chain Monte Carlo sampling or a model of the reverse process.

Once training is complete, the approach produces independent samples at a cost comparable to simulating the unconditioned forward process. The authors report greater robustness than existing methods across diffusion specifications and conditioning scenarios, particularly for rare events and multimodal distributions. The important efficiency claim concerns sampling after training: learning a reusable approximation makes conditioned path generation substantially more direct, while retaining flexibility across the types of processes and conditions studied.
summary.tldr: A neural approximation of diffusion-bridge dynamics enables efficient independent sampling after training, including challenging rare-event and multimodal settings.

title: Neural Guided Diffusion Bridges

abstract: Recent advancements in large language model (LLM)-based agents have demonstrated that collective intelligence can significantly surpass the capabilities of individual agents, primarily due to well-crafted inter-agent communication topologies. Despite the diverse and high-performing designs available, practitioners often face confusion when selecting the most effective pipeline for their specific task: Which topology is the best choice for my task, avoiding unnecessary communication token overhead while ensuring high-quality solution? In response to this dilemma, we introduce G-Designer, an adaptive, efficient, and robust solution for multi-agent deployment, which dynamically designs task-aware, customized communication topologies. Specifically, G-Designer models the multi-agent system as a multi-agent network, leveraging a variational graph auto-encoder to encode both the nodes (agents) and a task-specific virtual node, and decodes a task-adaptive and high-performing communication topology. Extensive experiments on six benchmarks showcase that G-Designer is: (1) high-performing, achieving superior results on MMLU with accuracy at $84.50\%$ and on HumanEval with pass@1 at $89.90\%$; \textbf{(2) task-adaptive}, architecting communication protocols tailored to task difficulty, reducing token consumption by up to $95.33\%$ on HumanEval; and \textbf{(3) adversarially robust}, defending against agent adversarial attacks with merely $0.3\%$ accuracy drop.

paragraphs: Groups of language model agents can benefit from collaboration, but the pattern of communication affects both solution quality and token consumption. G-Designer addresses the choice of who should communicate with whom. It constructs a communication topology adapted to the task, allowing the structure of the agent team’s interactions to change with its requirements.

The method represents the agents as nodes in a network and adds a virtual node describing the task. A variational graph auto-encoder encodes this combined information and decodes a customized communication network. These results support the method’s reported combination of task adaptation, efficiency, and robustness, with the largest token reduction describing an observed maximum.
summary.tldr: G-Designer learns task-specific communication networks for agent teams, showing strong benchmark performance, reduced token use, and adversarial robustness.

title: G-Designer: Architecting Multi-agent Communication Topologies via Graph Neural Networks

abstract: Model stealing poses a significant security risk in machine learning by enabling attackers to replicate a black-box model without access to its training data, thus jeopardizing intellectual property and exposing sensitive information. Recent methods that use pre-trained diffusion models for data synthesis improve efficiency and performance but rely heavily on manually crafted prompts, limiting automation and scalability, especially for attackers with little expertise. To assess the risks posed by open-source pre-trained models, we propose a more realistic threat model that eliminates the need for prompt design skills or knowledge of class names. In this context, we introduce Stealix, the first approach to perform model stealing without predefined prompts. Stealix uses two open-source pre-trained models to infer the victim model’s data distribution, and iteratively refines prompts through a genetic algorithm, progressively improving the precision and diversity of synthetic images. Our experimental results demonstrate that Stealix significantly outperforms other methods, even those with access to class names or fine-grained prompts, while operating under the same query budget. These findings highlight the scalability of our approach and suggest that the risks posed by pre-trained generative models in model stealing may be greater than previously recognized.

paragraphs: Model stealing attempts to reproduce a black-box model from its outputs without possessing its training data. This paper tests a less expertise-dependent threat model to assess the security implications of pretrained generators.

Stealix combines two open-source pretrained models to infer information about the target distribution and evolves prompts with a genetic algorithm. Iterative refinement improves the precision and diversity of synthesized images used in the replication study. The emphasis is on automating the prompting component rather than requiring a predefined prompt collection.

Under equal query budgets, experiments outperform compared methods, including some with access to class names or detailed prompts. The contribution is evidence that generative-model assistance can lower practical barriers to model replication. These benchmark results characterize the studied threat model; they do not establish that every protected model can be copied without restriction or additional assumptions.
summary.tldr: Stealix shows that automated prompt evolution can strengthen black-box model replication without predefined prompts or class-name knowledge.

title: Stealix: Model Stealing via Prompt Evolution

abstract: Model depth is a double-edged sword in deep learning: deeper models achieve higher accuracy but require higher computational cost. To efficiently train models at scale, progressive training (also known as model expansion) scales up model capacity during training and significantly reduces computation with little performance degradation. In this work, we study the depth expansion of large-scale models through the lens of optimization theory and feature learning, offering insights on the initialization of new layers, hyperparameter transfer, learning rate schedule, and timing of model expansion. Specifically, we propose zero/one-layer progressive training to achieve an optimal tradeoff between computation and loss, with a comprehensive ablations on our expansion strategy. For example, zero/one-layer progressive training on GPT2 can save $\approx 80%$ compute, or equivalently achieve an $\approx 5\times$ acceleration, while attaining a loss comparable to that of a fully trained 60-layer model with 7B parameters, thus demonstrating a mixing behavior in terms of loss. Furthermore, scaling laws on LLAMA3 and DeepSeekV3 models show a $3\sim 5\times$ improvement in compute efficiency, with an increasing advantage at larger scales.

paragraphs: Progressive training grows a model during training, reducing the computation spent using its full capacity. This paper studies expansion in depth through optimization theory and feature learning. It examines how to initialize added layers, transfer hyperparameters, choose learning-rate schedules, and decide when expansion should happen.

The proposed zero/one-layer progressive-training strategy aims for an optimal trade-off between computation and loss, with ablations examining the expansion choices. The approach makes the model’s growth schedule part of training design. Its motivation is that obtaining the benefits of a deep final model need not require paying the full computational cost of that depth throughout training.

In the highlighted GPT2 experiment, the strategy saves approximately 80% of computation, equivalent to roughly fivefold acceleration, while reaching loss comparable to a fully trained 60-layer, 7B-parameter model. Scaling-law results for LLAMA3 and DeepSeekV3 show three- to fivefold improvements in compute efficiency, with larger advantages at greater scale. These findings concern the reported computation–loss trade-off and support depth expansion as an efficient training strategy.
summary.tldr: Zero/one-layer progressive training expands model depth during learning, reporting comparable loss with substantial compute savings and stronger efficiency at larger scales.

title: Scaling depth capacity via zero/one-layer model expansion

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) show strong reasoning abilities, yet their reliability is hindered by hallucinations, where fluent reasoning becomes factually or logically incorrect. Most existing uncertainty-based detectors rely on sequence-level averaging, which ignores the step-wise dynamics of reasoning and often misclassifies hard-but-correct or easy-but-wrong samples. We propose a dynamic perspective that models reasoning as a trajectory on a latent Evidence Manifold, where each step is supported by local evidence. Hallucinations are characterized as Evidence Drops, i.e., sudden declines in local evidence support that indicate topological deviations from this manifold. Based on this insight, we design a training-free and model-agnostic detector that identifies hallucinations via the worst-case Evidence Drop and enables step-level error localization. Experiments on GSM8K, MATH, and ProcessBench show consistent improvements over sequence-level uncertainty baselines in selective accuracy and risk–coverage trade-offs.

paragraphs: This paper detects hallucinations by examining how evidence support changes during a reasoning sequence. Averaging uncertainty across an entire answer can hide an abrupt mistake or confuse difficult correct reasoning with confident incorrect reasoning. The authors therefore focus on local changes between reasoning steps.

Their framework represents reasoning as a path on a latent evidence manifold, where each step has local evidential support. A sudden decrease in that support is treated as an Evidence Drop and interpreted as a departure from the supported reasoning path. The detector uses the worst such drop to flag a response and can identify the step where the suspected error occurs.

The method requires no training and is described as model-agnostic. Evaluations on GSM8K, MATH, and ProcessBench report consistent improvements over sequence-level uncertainty baselines in selective accuracy and risk–coverage trade-offs. These measures concern the quality of answers retained as uncertain cases are excluded. The findings support tracking local reasoning dynamics when deciding which outputs to trust.
summary.tldr: A training-free detector flags hallucinations through sharp local drops in reasoning support and can locate the suspected erroneous step.

title: Mind the Gap: Catching Hallucinations via Evidence Drop on the Reasoning Manifold

abstract: The problem of optimising functions with intractable gradients frequently arises in machine learning and statistics, ranging from maximum marginal likelihood estimation procedures to fine-tuning of generative models. Stochastic approximation methods for this class of problems typically require inner sampling loops to obtain (biased) stochastic gradient estimates, which rapidly becomes computationally expensive. In this work, we develop sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) samplers for optimisation of functions with intractable gradients. Our approach replaces expensive inner sampling methods with efficient SMC approximations, which can result in significant computational gains. We establish convergence results for the basic recursions defined by our methodology which SMC samplers approximate. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on the reward-tuning of energy-based models within various settings.

paragraphs: Some optimization problems have gradients that cannot be computed directly. Examples include maximum marginal likelihood estimation and tuning generative models. Stochastic approximation handles such problems using estimated gradients, but obtaining each estimate can require an inner sampling procedure. Repeating that procedure throughout optimization can become a major computational expense, even when the resulting estimates remain biased.

The paper develops sequential Monte Carlo samplers for this setting. The approach replaces expensive inner sampling methods with SMC approximations, aiming to make the sampling work within optimization more efficient. Its proposed benefit is computational: the authors state that this substitution can deliver substantial gains when optimizing functions with intractable gradients.

The theoretical results establish convergence for the underlying recursions that the SMC samplers approximate. This distinction identifies what the stated guarantees cover. Experiments demonstrate the approach on reward-based tuning of energy-based models in several settings. Together, the theory and experiments present a route to reducing the cost of sampling-dependent optimization while connecting the practical approximation to an analyzed recursive procedure.
summary.tldr: Sequential Monte Carlo approximations can reduce the expensive inner sampling needed to optimize objectives with intractable gradients.

title: Efficient Stochastic Optimisation via Sequential Monte Carlo

abstract: Reasoning large language models exhibit complex reasoning behaviors via extended chain-of-thought generation that are highly fragile to information loss during decoding, creating critical challenges for KV cache compression. Existing token-dropping methods directly disrupt reasoning chains by removing intermediate steps, while head-reallocation methods, designed for retrieval tasks, fail to preserve the heads essential for generative reasoning. However, no existing method can identify which attention heads genuinely maintain reasoning consistency and control generation termination. To address this, we propose RLKV, which uses reinforcement learning as a probe to discover which heads contribute to reasoning quality by directly optimizing their cache usage against actual generation outcomes. This discovery naturally leads to an efficient compression strategy: we allocate full KV cache to reasoning-critical heads while aggressively compressing others with constant-size KV cache. Experiments reveal that a fraction of heads proves essential for reasoning, enabling 20–60% cache reduction with near-lossless performance across diverse tasks and models, and up to 2.06x end-to-end speedup at 60% reduction.

paragraphs: Long reasoning sequences require models to retain information during generation, making their key-value caches costly but difficult to compress safely. Dropping tokens can remove intermediate reasoning information, while head-allocation strategies developed for retrieval may overlook heads that preserve reasoning consistency or help determine when generation should stop.

RLKV uses reinforcement learning to investigate which attention heads matter for actual generation outcomes. It optimizes their cache usage against reasoning quality, turning compression decisions into a probe of head importance. The resulting strategy keeps full caches for reasoning-critical heads and assigns aggressively compressed, constant-size caches to the others.

Experiments find that a fraction of heads is essential for reasoning across the tested tasks and models. This enables cache reductions of 20–60% with near-lossless performance, and up to a 2.06-fold end-to-end speedup at 60% reduction. The findings support allocating memory according to a head’s demonstrated contribution to reasoning, with the reported preservation of performance remaining near-lossless rather than an exact guarantee of unchanged outputs.
summary.tldr: RLKV learns which attention heads need full memory, enabling 20–60% cache reduction with near-lossless reasoning performance.

title: Which Heads Matter for Reasoning? RL-Guided KV Cache Compression

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can reveal and amplify societal biases during chain-of-thought (CoT) generation. We present COFT (Chain of Fair Thought), a training-free decoding method that applies token-level fairness control at decode time, with distribution-free marginal validity guarantees (under exchangeability) for any frozen causal language model. COFT operates in three stages. First, it creates a masked counterfactual prompt by replacing sensitive spans with neutral tokens. Second, it compares the factual and masked logit distributions through lightweight logit fusion to attenuate attribute-driven biases. Third, it uses dual-branch split-conformal calibration to certify per-step candidate token sets at a user-chosen risk level. We evaluate COFT across six models and multiple bias benchmarks. Our method reduces standard bias metrics by 30–55% (median 38%) while preserving task utility and language quality. Reasoning accuracies remain unchanged within run-to-run noise margins. The computational overhead is modest, equivalent to one additional cached forward pass ($<$=11%). COFT offers a clear, auditable path to safer CoT generation with significant bias reduction, negligible utility loss, and no requirement for retraining, auxiliary classifiers, or weight access.

paragraphs: COFT addresses societal bias expressed during a language model’s generated reasoning by changing token selection at inference time. It works with a frozen causal language model, so the intervention does not require retraining. The method aims to reduce the influence of sensitive attributes while retaining useful reasoning and fluent language.

First, COFT constructs a second prompt in which sensitive spans are replaced with neutral tokens. It then combines information from the original and masked prompts’ token-score distributions to attenuate attribute-driven bias. Finally, dual-branch split-conformal calibration produces candidate token sets at a user-selected risk level. Its distribution-free marginal validity guarantee depends on exchangeability and applies to these per-step sets.

Across six models and multiple bias benchmarks, COFT reduces standard bias measures by 30–55%, with a median reduction of 38%. Reasoning accuracy stays within run-to-run noise margins, while task utility and language quality are preserved. Reported computational overhead is at most 11%, equivalent to one additional cached forward pass. The contribution combines an explicit decoding intervention with calibrated token sets and measured bias reductions.
summary.tldr: COFT combines masked-prompt comparisons and conformal calibration to reduce measured reasoning biases without retraining, with validity guarantees under exchangeability.

title: COFT: Counterfactual–Conformal Decoding for Fair Chain-of-Thought Reasoning in Large Language Models

abstract: LoRA adapts large language models (LLMs) by restricting updates to low-rank subspaces of pre-trained weights. While this substantially reduces training cost, the effectiveness of adaptation critically depends on which subspace is chosen at initialization: a poor initialization that allocates capacity to task-irrelevant directions can severely hinder downstream performance. Existing initialization strategies primarily rely on the intrinsic properties of pre-trained weights, implicitly assuming that weight geometry alone reflects task relevance. However, such criteria overlook how the model interacts with the downstream data distribution. In this work, we formulate LoRA initialization as identifying the degree of impact of directions in parameter space under the target data distribution. We argue that data-aware sensitivity, rather than weight-only magnitude, should govern the choice of adaptation subspaces. Building on this perspective, we propose a Fisher-guided framework that leverages curvature information induced by downstream data to characterize how parameter perturbations influence model predictions. This perspective yields a principled, task-dependent criterion for selecting LoRA directions that better align adaptation with the target objective. Empirical results across diverse tasks and modalities demonstrate that data-aware initialization consistently and significantly improves downstream performance over existing approaches.

Building on this perspective, we propose a Fisher-guided framework that leverages curvature information induced by downstream data to characterize how parameter perturbations influence model predictions. This perspective yields a principled, task-dependent criterion for selecting LoRA directions that better align adaptation with the target objective. Empirical results across diverse tasks and modalities demonstrate that data-aware initialization consistently and significantly improves downstream performance over existing approaches.

paragraphs: LoRA reduces fine-tuning cost by allowing weight updates only within a small, low-rank subspace. That restriction makes the initial choice of directions consequential: limited adaptation capacity can be spent on directions that matter little for the target task. This paper examines how to choose those directions using downstream data.

The authors argue that properties of pretrained weights alone do not adequately describe task relevance. Their Fisher-guided framework instead uses curvature information induced by the target data distribution to characterize how parameter changes affect model predictions. This supplies a task-dependent criterion for selecting the subspace in which LoRA will learn.

Experiments across varied tasks and modalities show consistent, significant downstream improvements over existing initialization approaches. The findings support treating initialization as an informed allocation of adaptation capacity, using the model’s interaction with target data to guide that allocation. The contribution is specifically a better starting subspace for low-rank fine-tuning, with empirical evidence that data-aware sensitivity is more useful than relying only on pretrained weight geometry.
summary.tldr: The paper initializes LoRA using target-data Fisher information to select adaptation directions that better affect task-relevant predictions.

title: Learning in the Fisher Subspace: A Guided Initialization for LoRA Fine-Tuning

abstract: Evaluating the performance of large language models (LLMs) from human preference data is crucial for obtaining LLM leaderboards. However, many existing approaches either rely on restrictive parametric assumptions or lack valid uncertainty quantification when flexible machine learning methods are used. In this paper, we propose a nonparametric statistical framework, called DMLRank, for comparing and ranking LLMs from preference data using debiased machine learning (DML). For this, we introduce generalized average ranking scores (GARS), which generalize commonly used ranking models, including the Bradley-Terry model or PageRank/ Rank centrality with complex human responses such as ties. DMLRank comes with the following advantages: (i) It produces statistically efficient estimates of GARS ranking scores. (ii) It naturally allows to incorporate black-box machine learning methods for estimation. (iii) It can be combined with pre-trained LLM evaluators (e.g., using LLM-as-a-judge). (iv) It suggests optimal policies for collecting preference data under budget constraints. We demonstrate these advantages both theoretically and empirically using both synthetic and real-world preference datasets. In summary, our framework provides practitioners with powerful, state-of-the-art methods for comparing or ranking LLMs for leaderboards.

The authors support these advantages through theory and experiments on synthetic and real preference datasets. The contribution links ranking, uncertainty, and data collection: practitioners can use expressive estimation tools while assessing model comparisons and deciding how to spend their evaluation budget.
summary.tldr: DMLRank combines flexible preference modeling with statistically grounded ranking estimates and budget-aware preference collection.

title: Nonparametric LLM Evaluation from Preference Data

abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) are rapidly evolving toward true multimodal reasoning, with visual search representing a concrete instantiation of the thinking-with-images paradigm. However, LVLM visual search faces two key challenges: incompatibility among intrinsic capabilities after post-training, and interference in long multi-step reasoning contexts. To address these, we identify two novel insights. First, self-regulation between pre- and post-training LVLMs leverages the intrinsic single-step capabilities of the pre-training model to mitigate capability deterioration and long-context interference. Second, probability-based prophetic sampling, replacing naive prompting, provides a probabilistic interface where the pre-training model acts as a prophet and the post-training model selectively accepts prophetic tokens under its output distribution, preserving coherent multi-step reasoning. Building on these insights, we introduce SeProD, a self-prophetic decoding framework that leverages intrinsic single-step capabilities to enable coherent multi-step reasoning in a training-free, plug-and-play manner. Experiments show that SeProD consistently improves multiple visual-search LVLMs across all 12 splits of 4 visual search benchmarks, as well as across general VQA benchmarks, without added computational overhead, thanks to its parallel prophetic acceptance mechanism.

paragraphs: Visual search asks a vision-language model to carry out reasoning grounded in images over multiple steps. The paper identifies two obstacles: post-training can make intrinsic capabilities less compatible, and long reasoning contexts can interfere with their use. SeProD addresses these problems by coordinating the single-step strengths of a pre-training model with a post-training model's multi-step reasoning.

The pre-training model proposes tokens through probability-based prophetic sampling. The post-training model selectively accepts those proposals according to its own output distribution, providing a probabilistic way to incorporate guidance while maintaining coherent reasoning. This self-regulation is implemented during decoding, making SeProD training-free and usable as a plug-in framework.

Experiments show consistent improvements across multiple visual-search models on all 12 splits of four visual-search benchmarks, as well as on general visual question answering benchmarks. The authors report no additional computational overhead, attributing this to parallel prophetic acceptance. The results support using complementary capabilities from pre- and post-training models during generation to reduce interference in extended visual reasoning.
summary.tldr: SeProD coordinates pre- and post-training models during decoding to improve visual search without further training or reported computational overhead.

title: Self-Prophetic Decoding to Unlock Visual Search in LVLMs

abstract: Training instability in modern deep learning systems is frequently triggered by rare but extreme gradient-norm spikes, which can induce oversized parameter updates, corrupt optimizer state, and lead to slow recovery or divergence. Widely used safeguards such as gradient clipping mitigate these failures but require threshold tuning and indiscriminately truncate large updates. We propose GradientStabilizer, a lightweight, drop-in gradient transform that preserves the instantaneous gradient direction while replacing the update magnitude with a statistically stabilized estimate derived from running gradient-norm statistics. We prove that the resulting stabilized magnitude is uniformly bounded on spike steps, independent of the spike size, and show how this boundedness controls optimizer state evolution in adaptive methods. Across LLM pre-training (FP16), quantization-aware pre-training (FP4), ImageNet classification, reinforcement learning, and time-series forecasting, GradientStabilizer consistently improves training stability, widens stable learning-rate regions, and reduces divergence relative to clipping-based baselines, even substantially reducing Adam’s sensitivity to weight-decay strength.

paragraphs: Rare spikes in gradient size can destabilize neural-network training by causing oversized updates and disturbing the optimizer’s accumulated state. Gradient clipping helps, but its threshold needs tuning and it truncates large gradients without distinguishing their statistical context. GradientStabilizer addresses the magnitude of these training signals using information accumulated over time.

The method preserves the current gradient’s direction while replacing its magnitude with a stabilized estimate computed from running gradient-norm statistics. The authors prove that this stabilized magnitude stays uniformly bounded on spike steps, independently of how large the spike is. They also show how that bound controls the evolution of internal state in adaptive optimizers.

Experiments span FP16 language-model pretraining, FP4 quantization-aware pretraining, ImageNet classification, reinforcement learning, and time-series forecasting. The authors report consistently improved stability, wider ranges of stable learning rates, and less divergence than clipping-based alternatives. They also report substantially reduced sensitivity of Adam to weight-decay strength. Together, the theoretical and empirical results support magnitude stabilization as a lightweight intervention across the tested training settings.
summary.tldr: GradientStabilizer preserves gradient direction while statistically stabilizing magnitude, with bounded responses to spikes and improved stability across tested training settings.

title: GradientStabilizer: Fix the Norm, Not the Gradient

abstract: Conventional wisdom suggests that reasoning models fail when problems exceed their capabilities. However, we find that frontier reasoning models sometimes possess the necessary capabilities to solve problems but fail due to premature self-doubt – a phenomenon informally known as context anxiety. We provide the first systematic study of context anxiety, demonstrating that it arises, in part, from a model’s inability to accurately estimate the tokens required to complete a task. We also show that context anxiety leads to material efficiency losses when models operate under perceived constraints. Building on this analysis, we further show that models can learn alternative strategies for solving long-horizon problems without exhibiting context anxiety, suggesting that performance improvements may be achievable not through scaling model capabilities, but by improving models’ ability to accurately assess and adapt to their own limitations.

paragraphs: A failed reasoning attempt does not always mean a model lacks the ability to solve the problem. This paper studies cases where frontier reasoning models have the needed capabilities but stop short because of premature self-doubt, described as context anxiety. The distinction matters because it points to a different source of failure.

The authors find that context anxiety arises partly from inaccurate estimates of how many tokens a task will require. When models perceive themselves as constrained, this behavior also causes material efficiency losses. The issue therefore concerns how models assess and respond to their available reasoning space, as well as the reasoning skills they possess.

The study further shows that models can learn alternative strategies for long-horizon problems without exhibiting context anxiety. This suggests a route to better performance through more accurate self-assessment and adaptation to limitations. The claim is qualified: inaccurate token estimation explains part of the phenomenon, and the results suggest that some improvements may be achievable without scaling underlying model capabilities.
summary.tldr: Some reasoning failures stem from inaccurate estimates of required context, and models can learn strategies that reduce this context anxiety.

title: Lost in Context: Addressing Context Anxiety in Large Language Models

abstract: Triangles capture higher-order structures in graphs and are fundamental to applications such as clustering and network analysis. To enable efficient use of such structures at scale, we study the problem of triangle cut sparsification, which aims to reduce the graph size while approximately preserving triangle counts across every cut. We investigate quantum algorithms for this problem, using triangle listing as our main technical ingredient. In particular, we present a quantum algorithm for triangle listing that, for a graph with $n$ vertices, $m$ edges, and $t$ triangles, runs in time $T_{\mathrm{q\text{-}list}} =\widetilde{O}\left(\min(n^{5/4}t^{7/12} + n^{7/6}t^{7/9}, m + m^{3/4}t^{1/2},n^{3/2}t^{1/2})\right)$, improving upon the best known classical bounds over a broad range of parameters. Our algorithm is based on a heavy–light vertex partition and an extension of triangle detection via quantum walks and Grover search. Leveraging this result, we design a quantum algorithm for constructing $\varepsilon$-triangle cut sparsifiers of size $\tilde{O}(n/\varepsilon^2)$ in time $\widetilde{O}(T_{\mathrm{q\text{-}list}} + \sqrt{mn}/\varepsilon)$. Finally, we demonstrate applications to clustering algorithms based on triangle-related measures and prove a lower bound of $\Omega(n/\varepsilon^2)$ on the size of any $\varepsilon$-triangle cut sparsifiers.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to shrink a graph while approximately preserving triangle counts across every cut, meaning every partition of its vertices into two sides. Triangles represent higher-order structure useful for clustering and network analysis. Preserving their behavior across cuts lets a smaller representation retain this information about the original graph.

The main technical ingredient is a quantum algorithm for listing triangles. It combines a heavy–light partition of vertices with quantum walks and Grover search. Its running-time bound takes the best of three expressions involving the numbers of vertices, edges, and triangles, improving on the best known classical bounds across a broad parameter range.

Using that listing procedure, the authors construct triangle-cut sparsifiers of size approximately n/ε², up to logarithmic factors. Construction time combines triangle listing with an additional term approximately √(mn)/ε. They also prove a size lower bound of Ω(n/ε²), so the size guarantee matches it up to logarithmic factors. Applications to triangle-based clustering connect these theoretical results to graph-analysis methods that depend on higher-order relationships.
summary.tldr: Quantum triangle-listing algorithms enable compact triangle-cut sparsifiers with size guarantees matching a proved lower bound up to logarithmic factors.

title: Quantum Algorithms for Triangle Cut Sparsification

abstract: Expressive policies based on flow-matching have been successfully applied in reinforcement learning (RL) more recently due to their ability to model complex action distributions from offline data. These algorithms build on standard policy gradients, which assume that there is no unmeasured confounding in the data. However, this condition does not necessarily hold for pixel-based demonstrations when a mismatch exists between the demonstrator’s and the learner’s sensory capabilities, leading to implicit confounding biases in offline data. We address the challenge by investigating the problem of confounded observations in offline RL from a causal perspective. We develop a novel causal offline RL objective that optimizes policies’ worst-case performance that may arise due to confounding biases. Based on this new objective, we introduce a practical implementation that learns expressive flow-matching policies from confounded demonstrations, employing a deep discriminator to assess the discrepancy between the target policy and the nominal behavioral policy. Experiments across 25 pixel-based tasks demonstrate that our proposed confounding-robust augmentation procedure achieves a success rate 120% that of confounding-unaware, state-of-the-art offline RL methods.

We address the challenge by investigating the problem of confounded observations in offline RL from a causal perspective. paragraphs: Learning a policy from recorded demonstrations can be misleading when the demonstrator and learner have different sensory capabilities. In pixel-based tasks, the demonstrator may act on information the learner cannot observe. This creates hidden confounding: apparent relationships in the demonstrations can reflect information missing from the learner's inputs.

The paper addresses this problem for expressive policies built with flow matching. It introduces a causal offline reinforcement learning objective that optimizes worst-case policy performance under possible confounding biases. A practical implementation learns from the confounded demonstrations and uses a deep discriminator to assess how the target policy differs from the nominal behavior policy.

Across 25 pixel-based tasks, the proposed augmentation achieves a success rate 120% of that obtained by state-of-the-art methods that do not account for confounding. This means a rate 1.2 times as high, rather than a 120% increase. The findings support accounting explicitly for sensory mismatch when learning complex action distributions from offline demonstrations.
summary.tldr: A causal worst-case objective improves flow-matching policies learned from demonstrations with hidden sensory confounding.

title: Causal Flow Q-Learning for Robust Offline Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Online model editing for multimodal large language models (MLLMs) requires assimilating a stream of corrections under tight compute and memory budgets. Yet editors developed for text-only LLMs often degrade on MLLMs: visually dominant activations skew the statistics that shape updates, causing cross-modal conflict, while sequential writes become entangled in a shared edit space and amplify long-horizon interference, causing inter-edit interference. To address these, we propose M-ORE, a modality-decoupled online recursive editor for lifelong MLLM adaptation. M-ORE is derived from a unified proximal-projection formulation and admits a closed-form update with a Sherman-Morrison recursion, yielding constant per-edit overhead. It maintains module-wise locality statistics for the text stack and the visual projector to avoid visually dominated update shaping and performs continual updates in a fixed orthogonal low-rank edit subspace via a Sherman-Morrison recursion to mitigate long-horizon interference. Experiments on multiple MLLM backbones and online editing benchmarks show that our M-ORE method consistently improves reliability, generality, and locality over strong baselines, while achieving favorable quality-efficiency scaling. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/lab-klc/M-ORE.

paragraphs: A multimodal language model receiving a continuing stream of corrections must update efficiently without disrupting unrelated behavior. The paper identifies two obstacles. Strong visual activations can dominate the statistics used to shape edits, creating conflict between modalities, while successive edits can interfere with one another over long sequences.

M-ORE addresses these problems through separate update statistics for the text stack and visual projector. It performs continual changes within a fixed, orthogonal, low-rank edit subspace. A unified proximal-projection formulation yields a closed-form update, and a Sherman-Morrison recursion keeps the overhead of each edit constant as corrections accumulate.

Separating the statistics targets visually dominated update shaping, while the structured edit space aims to reduce interference across corrections. Experiments on multiple multimodal backbones and online editing benchmarks report consistent improvements in reliability, generality, and locality over strong baselines. The results also show favorable quality-efficiency scaling, supporting the method's suitability for repeated adaptation under tight computational and memory budgets.
summary.tldr: M-ORE separates modality-specific editing statistics and uses recursive low-rank updates to improve continual multimodal model correction.

title: Modality-Decoupled Online Recursive Editing

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown promising potential in materials science, enabling tasks ranging from knowledge retrieval to property prediction. Existing materials science benchmarks mainly focus on perceptual or knowledge-based tasks, largely ignoring the structure modelling tasks, a core challenge in real scientific workflows. In practice, constructing and manipulating atomic structures is one of the most creative and least automated steps in materials research. In this work, we introduce AtomWorld, a benchmark designed to evaluate the abilities of LLMs on structure modifications. The benchmark includes ten fundamental actions under four widely used modelling categories, enabling verifiable evaluation metrics. We find that Gemini 2.5 Pro generally performs the best. While the success rate decreases markedly with increasing modelling complexity, with particularly low success rates (below 12% for rotation) for operations involving complex spatial relations. Our results suggest that contemporary LLMs are better suited as copilots for materials structure modelling rather than fully unsupervised autonomous scientific agents. Beyond evaluation, AtomWorld also serves as a testbed and playground for developing future structure-aware models, including reinforcement learning and agentic approaches.

paragraphs: AtomWorld evaluates whether language models can modify atomic structures, an important part of materials research that involves more than recalling scientific facts. Existing materials benchmarks emphasize knowledge or perception, leaving structure construction and manipulation comparatively untested. The paper brings this spatial work into an evaluation where the correctness of modifications can be checked.

The benchmark organizes ten basic actions into four commonly used modelling categories. This structure lets the authors examine performance across different operations and levels of complexity. Its emphasis on verifiable modifications matters because a model's ability to discuss a material does not establish that it can correctly change the arrangement of its atoms.

Gemini 2.5 Pro generally performs best in the reported evaluation, but success drops substantially as modelling becomes more complex. Rotation is especially difficult, with success rates below 12%. These findings support using current models as supervised copilots for structure modelling. AtomWorld also provides a setting for developing and evaluating future models that better understand atomic geometry.
summary.tldr: AtomWorld tests language models on atomic structure modifications and finds substantial weaknesses in complex spatial operations.

title: AtomWorld: A Benchmark for Evaluating Spatial Reasoning in Large Language Models on Material Structures

abstract: Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) has established itself as a powerful and widely adopted optimizer for training machine learning models. By explicitly minimizing the sharpness of the loss landscape, SAM often improves generalization while delivering strong empirical performance. However, SAM and its variants, like most training algorithms, are sensitive to the choice of learning rate, which is typically selected through extensive hyperparameter tuning or predefined schedulers. In this work, motivated by recent advances on the effectiveness of stochastic Polyak step sizes for Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD), we derive Polyak schedulers tailored to SAM-style updates, yielding novel adaptive algorithms in both deterministic and stochastic settings. In the smooth setting, we prove linear convergence for strongly convex objectives and an $\mathcal{O}(1/T)$ convergence rate for convex objectives in the deterministic case. In the stochastic setting, we establish analogous convergence guarantees up to a neighborhood of the optimum. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed Polyak schedulers achieve performance comparable to or better than carefully tuned SAM baselines, while substantially reducing the need for learning-rate tuning.

paragraphs: Sharpness-Aware Minimization, or SAM, trains models by explicitly accounting for the sharpness of the loss landscape. It often improves generalization, but its performance depends on choosing a suitable learning rate. That choice commonly requires repeated tuning or a predefined schedule, adding work around an otherwise effective optimizer.

The authors derive adaptive Polyak-type learning-rate schedulers specifically for SAM-style updates. They develop versions for both deterministic optimization and stochastic training. Tailoring the scheduler to SAM matters because its update rule differs from ordinary stochastic gradient descent, where stochastic Polyak step sizes have already shown promise.

For smooth objectives, the deterministic analysis proves linear convergence under strong convexity and an O(1/T) rate under convexity, where T counts iterations. The stochastic results provide analogous guarantees only up to a neighborhood of the optimum. Experiments find performance comparable to or better than carefully tuned SAM baselines while substantially reducing learning-rate tuning. Together, these results support adaptive scheduling through both conditional mathematical guarantees and observed training performance.
summary.tldr: SAM-specific Polyak schedulers reduce learning-rate tuning while providing conditional convergence guarantees and competitive empirical performance.

title: Adaptive Sharpness-Aware Minimization with a Polyak-type Step size: A Theory-Grounded Scheduler

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have been augmented with web search to overcome the limitations of the static knowledge boundary by accessing up-to-date information from the open Internet. While this integration enhances model capability, it also introduces a distinct safety threat surface: the retrieval and citation process has the potential risk of exposing users to harmful or low-credibility web content. Existing red-teaming methods are largely designed for standalone LLMs as they primarily focus on unsafe generation, ignoring risks emerging from the complex search workflow. To address this gap, we propose CREST-Search, a pioneering red-teaming framework for LLMs with web search. The cornerstone of CREST-Search is three novel attack strategies that generate seemingly benign search queries yet induce unsafe citations. It also employs an iterative in-context refinement mechanism to strengthen adversarial effectiveness under black-box constraints. In addition, we construct a search-specific harmful dataset, WebSearch-Harm, which enables fine-tuning a specialized red-teaming model to improve query quality. Our experiments demonstrate that CREST-Search can effectively bypass safety filters and systematically expose vulnerabilities in web search-based LLM systems, underscoring the necessity of the development of robust search models.

A system can expose users to harmful or low-credibility material through its sources. Red-teaming focused mainly on unsafe generated text can miss vulnerabilities in this broader search workflow.

CREST-Search is a framework for evaluating that threat surface. It uses three attack strategies to create apparently benign search queries that induce unsafe citations. An iterative in-context refinement process improves adversarial effectiveness under black-box constraints. The contribution is an evaluation approach centered on what a model retrieves and cites as well as what it writes. These findings support treating the retrieval-and-citation process as an explicit part of safety testing when language models access the open web.
summary.tldr: CREST-Search reveals safety weaknesses in web-enabled LLMs by testing whether benign-looking queries can induce unsafe citations.

title: When Search Goes Wrong: Red-Teaming Web-Augmented Large Language Models

abstract: We introduce a constrained optimization framework for training transformers that behave like optimization descent algorithms. Specifically, we enforce layerwise descent constraints on the objective function and replace standard empirical risk minimization (ERM) with a primal-dual training scheme. This approach yields models whose intermediate representations decrease the loss monotonically in expectation across layers. We apply our method to both unrolled transformer architectures and conventional pretrained transformers on tasks of video denoising and text classification. Across these settings, we observe that constrained transformers achieve stronger robustness to perturbations and maintain higher out-of-distribution generalization, while preserving competitive in-distribution performance.

paragraphs: This paper trains transformers so that their layers behave more like successive steps of an optimization algorithm.
