Training therefore considers how the model progresses internally, alongside the quality of its final output.

The authors impose descent constraints at individual layers and use a primal-dual training scheme to balance the prediction objective with those constraints. The resulting models decrease the objective monotonically across layers in expectation. That qualification matters: the stated property concerns expected behavior, rather than requiring every layer to improve the loss for every individual example.

The method is applied to both unrolled architectures and conventional pretrained transformers, using video denoising and text classification tasks. In these settings, the authors observe stronger resistance to perturbations and better generalization outside the training distribution while retaining competitive performance within it. The findings suggest that controlling intermediate computational progress can be useful for robustness.
summary.tldr: Layerwise optimization constraints improve transformer robustness in the studied tasks while making loss decrease across layers in expectation.

title: A Constrained Optimization Perspective of Unrolled Transformers

abstract: Sub-bit model compression targets storage below one bit per weight; as magnitudes are aggressively compressed, the sign bit becomes a fixed-cost bottleneck. Across Transformers, CNNs, and MLPs, learned sign matrices resist low-rank approximation and are spectrally indistinguishable from an i.i.d. Rademacher baseline. This randomness gives rise to the lower bound of sub-bit model compression—the one-bit wall. Despite this apparent randomness, most weights retain their initialization signs; flips primarily occur via rare near-zero boundary crossings, suggesting that sign-pattern randomness is largely inherited from initialization. We formalize this behavior with sign lock-in theory, a stopping-time analysis of sign flips under SGD noise. Under bounded updates and a rare re-entry condition into a small neighborhood of zero, the number of effective sign flips exhibits a geometric tail. Building on this mechanism, we introduce a from-scratch low-rank sign-template training method that prevents the emergence of this one-bit wall.

paragraphs: Compressing a model below one bit per weight becomes difficult when weight magnitudes are heavily compressed but their positive or negative signs still require storage. Across Transformers, convolutional networks, and multilayer perceptrons, the authors find that learned sign matrices resist low-rank approximation. The authors then introduce training from scratch with a low-rank sign template to prevent this barrier from emerging. title: Sign Lock-In: Randomly Initialized Weight Signs Persist and Bottleneck Sub-Bit Model Compression

abstract: Stochastic differential equations (SDEs) and stochastic partial differential equations (SPDEs) are fundamental for modeling stochastic dynamics across the natural sciences and modern machine learning. Learning their solution operators with deep learning models promises fast solvers and new perspectives on classical learning tasks. In this work, we build on Wiener–chaos expansions (WCE) to design neural operator (NO) architectures for SDEs and SPDEs: we project driving noise paths onto orthonormal Wick–Hermite features and use NO backbones to parameterize the corresponding chaos coefficients governed by deterministic equations, enabling reconstruction of S(P)DE solutions from the observed noise trajectories. Empirically, we achieve competitive accuracy across several tasks, including standard SPDE benchmarks and SDE-based diffusion one-step image sampling, topological graph interpolation, financial extrapolation, parameter estimation, and manifold SDE flood forecasting. We further explore a law-matching setting where the Brownian trajectories paired with training solutions are unobserved, and show that the proposed framework remains effective by sampling auxiliary Brownian paths from the prescribed noise prior. These results suggest WCE-based neural operators are a practical and scalable approach to learning SDE/SPDE solution operators across domains. Our source code can be found in https://github.com/EEthanShi/SDENO.

paragraphs: Stochastic differential equations describe dynamics driven partly by randomness, while their partial-differential counterparts also capture variation across space. This paper develops neural operators for learning their solution mappings. Its central move is to organize the random input through a Wiener–chaos expansion, giving the learning architecture a structured way to represent how noise influences solutions.

The method projects noise trajectories onto orthonormal Wick–Hermite features. Neural operator backbones then represent the expansion coefficients, which are governed by deterministic equations. Combining the features and learned coefficients reconstructs solutions for observed noise paths. This separates the representation of randomness from learning the corresponding coefficient functions within a single framework.

Experiments report competitive accuracy on tasks ranging from standard stochastic-equation benchmarks to image sampling, graph interpolation, financial extrapolation, parameter estimation, and flood forecasting. The authors also examine distribution matching when training solutions lack paired Brownian trajectories. Sampling auxiliary paths from the prescribed noise prior remains effective in that setting, supporting the framework’s practical promise across the tested domains.
summary.tldr: The method combines structured expansions of random noise with neural operators to learn stochastic differential-equation solutions across multiple domains.

title: Expanding the Chaos: Neural Operator for Stochastic (Partial) Differential Equations

abstract: Zeroth-order (ZO) methods are widely used when gradients are unavailable or prohibitively expensive, including black-box learning and memory-efficient fine-tuning of large models, yet their optimization dynamics in deep learning remain underexplored. In this work, we provide an explicit step size condition that exactly captures the (mean-square) linear stability of a family of ZO methods based on the standard two-point estimator. Our characterization reveals a sharp contrast with first-order (FO) methods: whereas FO stability is governed solely by the largest Hessian eigenvalue, mean-square stability of ZO methods depends on the entire Hessian spectrum. Since computing the full Hessian spectrum is infeasible in practical neural network training, we further derive tractable stability bounds that depend only on the largest eigenvalue and the Hessian trace. Empirically, we find that full-batch ZO methods operate at the edge of stability: ZO-GD, ZO-GDM, and ZO-Adam consistently stabilize near the predicted stability boundary across CNNs, ResNets, and Transformers on vision tasks. Our results highlight an implicit regularization effect specific to ZO methods, where large step sizes primarily regularize the Hessian trace, whereas in FO methods they regularize the top eigenvalue.

paragraphs: Zeroth-order optimization uses function evaluations when gradients are unavailable or too expensive. This paper studies the stability of a family of methods using the standard two-point estimator. It derives an explicit step-size condition that exactly characterizes mean-square linear stability, providing a theoretical boundary for how large an update can be in that analysis.

This links observed training dynamics to a broader measure of curvature than the sharpest direction alone.
summary.tldr: Zeroth-order stability depends on the full Hessian spectrum, and full-batch experiments find training near the predicted boundary with trace-focused implicit regularization.

title: Zeroth-Order Optimization at the Edge of Stability

abstract: To enhance the interpretability of multimodal large language models’ outputs, recent efforts explored Grounded Visual Reasoning (GVR), in which the model is trained to select relevant image regions before answering the question. However, the multi-round “ground-then-answer” and reasoning nature of these methods imposes much more computational costs compared to non-GVR methods. To attain efficient and effective GVR, in this paper, we propose a novel paradigm called Reason with Thumbnails, Answer with Focus (RTAF), which feeds the model with low-resolution images to reason the relevant regions and high-resolution crops to answer the final answer. Our motivation arises from the observation that, in many cases, the key area required to answer questions can be inferred from the low-resolution thumbnails, without the need for a full-resolution image. Additionally, for extreme cases where thumbnails lack sufficient information (leading to undirected region guessing and increased computation), we equip the model with a tool to access higher-resolution images. For training efficiency, we adopt pure reinforcement learning (i.e., GRPO) and design a suite of reward functions to supervise the model’s behavior, alongside a resolution-aware training data selection strategy. Finally, our model, based on Qwen2.5-VL, achieves significant improvements across a range of benchmarks with reduced computation, demonstrating the effectiveness and efficiency of our proposed RTAF, e.g., compared to the non-GVR model Qwen2.5-VL, our model achieves a performance gain of 5.8 while using comparable visual tokens (471 vs. 391). Against state-of-the-art GVR methods, RTAF reduces visual token usage by half while delivering superior performance.

paragraphs: Grounded visual reasoning makes a model select relevant image regions before answering, improving the interpretability of its response. Repeated visual inspection and reasoning can be costly. RTAF reduces this burden by using a low-resolution thumbnail to locate relevant areas, then supplying high-resolution crops for the final answer.

The approach rests on the observation that thumbnails often contain enough information to identify where to look. When they do not, the model can invoke a tool to access higher-resolution imagery, avoiding prolonged unguided region selection. Training uses GRPO reinforcement learning, rewards designed to supervise model behavior, and a data selection strategy that accounts for image resolution.

Compared with the non-grounded Qwen2.5-VL model, the abstract reports a performance gain of 5.8 with comparable visual-token usage, 471 versus 391. Against state-of-the-art grounded reasoning methods, it uses half as many visual tokens while achieving better performance. These findings support allocating visual detail according to the stage of reasoning and the information needed.
summary.tldr: RTAF locates relevant regions using thumbnails and answers from detailed crops, reducing visual-token costs while improving evaluated performance.

title: Reason with Thumbnails, Answer with Focus: An Efficient and Effective Paradigm for Multimodal Grounded Visual Reasoning

abstract: Conditioned Sequence Models (CSMs) learn policies by treating return-to-go (RTG) as a control signal. However, existing CSMs often treat the RTGs as simple numerical inputs rather than aligning them with the performance of their policies. In this paper, we propose Q-ALIGN DT, a framework that enforces this alignment by ensuring the $Q$-value of the output policy is consistent with the input RTG. By leveraging a $Q$ function to provide dense guidance to CSMs and further fine-tuning it using an RTG-perturbation technique with the CSM, our method ensures that higher RTGs are consistently mapped to trajectories with higher expected returns. Theoretically, we show that Q-ALIGN DT can efficiently learn the desired policy and output a near-optimal one when the RTG is sufficiently high. Empirically, we demonstrate through extensive experiments that Q-ALIGN DT achieves superior controllability and performance across the D4RL benchmark. Remarkably, our model effectively learns a structured family of policies that maintains precise alignment and generalizes to tasks like velocity-tracking where prior methods fail.

paragraphs: Return-conditioned sequence models use a requested future return as an input for selecting behavior. Yet supplying a larger number does not by itself establish that the resulting policy will perform better. Q-ALIGN DT connects this control input to the policy's expected performance using a Q function.

The framework guides the sequence model so that the value of its output policy agrees with the requested return-to-go. It also fine-tunes the Q function together with the sequence model through return perturbation. This dense guidance is designed to produce an ordered family of behaviors, with higher requested returns corresponding consistently to trajectories with higher expected returns.

The theoretical analysis shows efficient learning of the desired policy and a near-optimal output when the requested return is sufficiently high. Experiments across D4RL report improved controllability and performance. The learned policy family also generalizes to velocity-tracking tasks where prior approaches fail. The contribution is therefore both performance-oriented and behavioral: the conditioning number gains a more precise relationship to what the model actually does.
summary.tldr: Q-ALIGN DT aligns requested returns with policy values, improving control and supporting near-optimal behavior when the requested return is sufficiently high.

title: Return-to-Go Is More Than a Number: Q-Guided Alignment for Return-Conditioned Supervised Learning

abstract: In standard Transformer architectures, semantic importance is often conflated with activation magnitude, obscuring the geometric structure of latent representations. To disentangle these factors, we introduce PRISM, a complex-valued architecture designed to isolate the computational role of phase. By enforcing a strict unit-norm constraint (|z| = 1) and replacing attention with gated harmonic convolutions, the model is encouraged to utilize subtractive interference in the frequency domain to suppress noise, rather than relying on magnitude-based gating. We utilize this constrained regime to study a hybrid architecture—fusing phase-based routing with standard attention—which achieves improved parameter efficiency and representation quality compared to baselines in our evaluated settings. Mechanistically, interventional ablations indicate that the model carries substantial task-relevant information in phase: preserving phase largely maintains performance, whereas disrupting phase causes severe degradation. Together, these results suggest that phase-based spectral interference is a usable computational mechanism for neural sequence modeling at the evaluated scale.

paragraphs: The paper investigates whether phase can carry useful information for neural sequence modeling independently of activation magnitude. Standard transformer representations can entangle the importance of a feature with its size. PRISM creates a constrained setting for studying an alternative by using complex-valued representations whose magnitude is fixed at one.

summary.tldr: PRISM provides experimental evidence that phase-based interference can carry task-relevant information and improve sequence modeling in the evaluated settings.

title: Language as a Wave Phenomenon: Semantic Phase Locking and Interference in Neural Networks

abstract: Transformer-based Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) have recently emerged as a promising paradigm to sequential modeling, combining the strong representational capabilities of Transformers with the sparse spike-driven computation of SNNs. Within such position-agnostic architectures, positional encoding is critical for injecting order information, allowing the model to distinguish token positions, capture sequential dependencies, and represent relative relationships among tokens. However, existing positional encoding methods for SNNs are largely inherited from ANNs and, in doing so, undermine the spike-driven computational properties that are central to spiking transformers. To address this limitation, we propose the Spiking Positional Encoding (SPE), a method designed specifically for Spiking Transformers, aimed at encoding relative positional information while preserving both spike-driven computation and the linear complexity of spiking self-attention. The core component of SPE is the Positional Encoding Leaky Integrate-and-Fire (PE-LIF) neuron, which incorporates position-dependent signals into neuronal thresholds and implicitly propagates this information through spike trains via continuous firing and membrane potential reset dynamics. Extensive experiments on thirteen NLP benchmarks demonstrate that SPE consistently outperforms existing SNN positional encoding methods, strengthens the sequence modeling capability, and improves energy efficiency without introducing additional trainable parameters. Code is available at https://github.com/CayleyZ/SPE.

Spiking transformers add a second requirement: that this information preserve computation through sparse spikes. The paper argues that positional encodings borrowed from conventional neural networks can undermine the computational properties that make spiking architectures attractive.

summary.tldr: SPE encodes position through spiking-neuron thresholds and dynamics, improving sequence modeling without additional trainable parameters.

title: Positional Encoding for Spiking Transformers

abstract: Stochastic variance-reduced algorithms such as Stochastic Average Gradient (SAG) and SAGA, and their deterministic counterparts like the Incremental Aggregated Gradient (IAG) method, have been extensively studied in large-scale machine learning. Despite their popularity, existing analyses for these algorithms are disparate, relying on different proof techniques tailored to each method. Furthermore, the original proof of SAG is known to be notoriously involved, requiring computer-aided analysis. Focusing on finite-sum optimization with smooth and strongly convex objectives, our main contribution is to develop a single unified convergence analysis that applies to all three algorithms: SAG, SAGA, and IAG. Our analysis features two key steps: (i) establishing a bound on delays due to sub-sampling using simple concentration tools, and (ii) carefully designing a novel Lyapunov function that accounts for such delays. The resulting proof is short and modular, providing high-probability bounds for SAG and SAGA that can be seamlessly extended to non-convex objectives and Markovian sampling. As an immediate byproduct of our new analysis technique, we obtain the best known rates for the IAG algorithm, significantly improving upon prior bounds.

paragraphs: SAG, SAGA, and IAG solve optimization problems by reusing gradient information from different parts of a dataset. Their convergence has traditionally been explained through separate mathematical arguments, with the original SAG proof particularly complicated. This paper develops one analysis covering all three methods, making their shared behavior easier to understand.

The main setting is finite-sum optimization with smooth, strongly convex objectives. The proof first bounds how old gradient information can become because only some components are sampled at each step. It then builds a Lyapunov function, a mathematical measure of progress, that explicitly accounts for these delays. Together, these steps connect sampling behavior to convergence.

The resulting argument is short and modular, with high-probability guarantees for SAG and SAGA. The authors also describe extensions to non-convex objectives and Markovian sampling. For IAG, the same technique produces the best known convergence rates reported in the abstract, improving earlier bounds. The contribution is therefore both a simpler common explanation and stronger guarantees for an existing algorithm.
summary.tldr: A unified proof explains convergence of SAG, SAGA, and IAG while improving known convergence bounds for IAG.

title: A Short and Unified Convergence Analysis of the SAG, SAGA, and IAG Algorithms

abstract: Large language model (LLM) answer engines are increasingly used for information seeking, shifting visibility from ranked lists to synthesized answers. This enables Generative Engine Optimization (GEO), which targets LLM answer engines’ evidence pool and generation. We analyze the search engine optimization (SEO) to the GEO transition to identify two risks: (i) concentrated influence from low contestability and system sensitivity, and (ii) undisclosed commercial influence embedded in evidence and reasoning. We then formalize a general GEO pipeline to locate where optimization acts and compare academic and industry practices, revealing a third risk (iii) academic–industry blind spots driven by visibility and evaluation asymmetries between offline setups and deployed systems. This position argues the need for answer-level governance and measurement: stronger contestability, high-precision disclosure, black-box auditing of material influence, and deployment-aligned metrics for exposure persistence.

paragraphs: This position paper examines what changes when people seek information through AI-generated answers instead of ranked search results. Generative Engine Optimization targets both the evidence available to an answer engine and its generation process. The authors analyze this transition to identify how efforts to gain visibility can influence the answers people receive.

They identify concentrated influence when systems are sensitive to optimization and that influence is difficult to contest. They also highlight commercial influence that can enter evidence and reasoning without being disclosed. By formalizing a general optimization pipeline and comparing academic with industry practices, they identify another problem: offline research and deployed systems expose different information and use different evaluation conditions.

The resulting governance proposal focuses on answers themselves. The authors call for stronger opportunities to contest influence, precise disclosure, and black-box audits of material effects on outputs. They also advocate metrics that capture how exposure persists in deployed systems. The central implication is that measuring visibility alone misses how optimization shapes synthesized information.
summary.tldr: Optimizing AI answer engines creates risks of concentrated and undisclosed influence that the authors argue require answer-level auditing and governance.

title: Position: Generative Engine Optimization Creates Underexamined Risks, Governance Must Target Concentration, Disclosure, and Academic Blind Spots

abstract: As large language models (LLMs) transition from research prototypes to real-world systems, customization has emerged as a central bottleneck. While text prompts can already customize LLM behavior, we argue that text-only prompting does not constitute a suitable control interface for scalable, stable, and inference-only customization. This position paper argues that model providers should expose vector prompt inputs as part of the public interface for customizing LLMs. We support this position with diagnostic evidence showing that vector prompt tuning continues to improve with increasing supervision whereas text-based prompt optimization saturates early, and that vector prompts exhibit dense, global attention patterns indicative of a distinct control mechanism. abstract: A logistic regression classification algorithm is developed for problems in which the feature vectors may be missing data (features). Single or multiple imputation for the missing data is avoided by performing analytic integration with an estimated conditional density function (conditioned on the nonmissing data). Conditional density functions are estimated using a Gaussian mixture model (GMM), with parameter estimation performed using both expectation maximization (EM) and Variational Bayesian EM (VB-EM). Using widely available real data, we demonstrate the general advantage of the VB-EM GMM estimation for handling incomplete data, vis-à-vis the EM algorithm. Moreover, it is demonstrated that the approach proposed here is generally superior to standard imputation procedures.

paragraphs: This paper develops logistic regression for examples whose feature vectors contain missing entries. Its central idea is to account for the missing values through analytic integration. The calculation uses an estimated distribution of the missing features conditioned on the observed features, allowing the classifier to work with uncertainty about the unavailable information.

The conditional distributions are estimated with a Gaussian mixture model. The authors investigate two ways to fit that model: expectation maximization and variational Bayesian expectation maximization. This makes estimation of the missing-feature distribution an explicit part of the classification method. The resulting procedure avoids both single imputation and multiple imputation, which would supply replacement values for the missing entries.

Experiments on widely available real datasets show a general advantage for the variational Bayesian mixture estimates over the ordinary expectation-maximization estimates. They also show that the proposed classification approach is generally superior to standard imputation procedures. The results support integrating over estimated conditional distributions as a useful treatment of incomplete features in the evaluated problems.
summary.tldr: The method handles missing features in logistic regression by integrating over conditional Gaussian-mixture distributions instead of imputing values.
